law-india-constitution.title: India's Constitution: rights, rules & how the country runs
law-india-constitution.description: From the Preamble to Parliament, courts, federalism and elections: how India's Constitution works and what it means for you, explained for children, students and adults.

courses.title: Rules, fairness and our Constitution (for kids)
courses.summary: Why we have rules, what India's Constitution is, and the rights and duties every child has, told through stories from a classroom, a cricket match and a village.
outcomes: Learners can explain why groups need fair rules
Learners can say what the Constitution is and when it began
Learners can name some rights children have, like going to school and being safe
Learners can name duties they can do every day
Learners know that 1098 is a free helpline for children in India

lessons.title: Why do we need rules?

story.title: The cricket match that went wrong

scenes.text: Aarav, Zoya and their friends start a cricket match in the park. Nobody decides the rules first.
Aarav is out, but says 'first ball is a trial ball!' Zoya says a hit over the wall is six; others say it is out. Everyone shouts.
Grandpa Joseph says: 'Let's agree on rules before you play, and the same rules for everyone.' They write five rules on a paper.
Now the game is fun again. Even when Zoya is out, she says 'that's fair', because the rules were agreed before.

steps.title: What is a rule?
steps.body:
A **rule** tells us what we should do or should not do. Rules help people live, play and work together **without fighting**.

- At home: brush your teeth, put toys back.
- At school: raise your hand to speak, do not push in the line.
- On the road: stop at the red light.
steps.say: A rule tells us what to do or not do, so people can live and play together without fighting.

steps.title: Fair rules are the same for everyone
steps.body:
A rule is **fair** when it is the same for everyone and everyone knows it before the game starts.

If only the tallest child can bat, that is **unfair**. If everyone gets a turn to bat, that is **fair**.

steps.title: A country needs rules too
steps.body: A school has rules. A country has rules too. Rules made by the government for the whole country are called **laws**. For example, there is a law that every child aged 6 to 14 has the right to go to school free.

steps.title: Rules can be changed, the fair way
steps.body: If a rule feels unfair, we do not break it secretly. We **talk**, give reasons, and agree on a better rule together. Grown-ups do this for the country by voting and through Parliament.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With your family, make **three rules** for screen time or for a game. Check: Is each rule the same for everyone? Does everyone know it? Write them and stick them on the fridge.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: This is learning, not legal advice. If something ever feels wrong or unsafe, tell a trusted grown-up. In India, children can call **1098** (Childline) for help, and anyone can call **112** in an emergency. Families can get free legal help on **15100**.

activity.prompt: Is this rule fair or unfair?

items.text: Everyone gets one turn on the swing, then the next child
Only boys can be class monitor
Everyone puts their own plate in the sink
The rule changes in the middle of the game to help one team
Anyone who wants can join the drawing club
A child is not allowed to play because of their religion

quiz.q: Why do we need rules?
options: So that grown-ups can be bossy
So people can live and play together without fighting
quiz.why: The answer is "So people can live and play together without fighting". Reason: Rules help everyone know what to do, so things are fair and peaceful. The other choices, such as "So that grown-ups can be bossy" and "Rules are not needed", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What makes a rule fair?
options: It is the same for everyone and known before
quiz.why: The answer is "It is the same for everyone and known before". Reason: A fair rule treats everyone the same way and is known in advance. The other choices, such as "It helps only my friends" and "It changes whenever I lose", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Rules made for a whole country are called…
quiz.why: The answer is "Laws". Reason: Rules for the whole country are called laws. The other choices, such as "Games" and "Homework", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: If you think a rule is unfair, what is the best thing to do?
options: Talk about it and suggest a better rule
quiz.why: The answer is "Talk about it and suggest a better rule". Reason: We change rules the fair way: by talking, giving reasons and agreeing. The other choices, such as "Break it secretly" and "Shout at everyone", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Our Constitution: India's big rulebook

scenes.text: On 26 January, Priya watches the Republic Day parade on TV with her Nani in Lucknow.
'Nani, what is a Republic?' she asks. Nani smiles: 'It means the people choose their leaders. No king or queen rules us.'
'On this day in 1950, our Constitution started. It is the big rulebook of India. Even the Prime Minister must follow it.'
Priya says, 'So it is like our class rules, but for the whole country!' 'Exactly,' says Nani.

steps.title: What is the Constitution?
steps.body:
The **Constitution of India** is the most important book of rules for our country. It says:

- how leaders are chosen,
- what rights every person has,
- what duties citizens have,
- how laws are made.

Every other law must follow the Constitution.
steps.say: The Constitution is India's most important rulebook. Every other law must follow it.

steps.title: Two special days
steps.body:
- **26 November 1949**: the Constitution was adopted (accepted). We celebrate this as **Constitution Day** (Samvidhan Divas).
- **26 January 1950**: the Constitution came into force. We celebrate this as **Republic Day**.

steps.title: Who wrote it?
steps.body: Many leaders from all over India worked together in the **Constituent Assembly** for almost three years. **Dr B. R. Ambedkar** led the Drafting Committee, so he is often called the main architect of the Constitution. **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was the President of the Assembly, and later India's first President.

steps.title: The Preamble: the promise at the start
steps.body:
The Constitution begins with the **Preamble**, which starts with the words **'We, the People of India'**. It promises everyone:

- **Justice**: fair treatment
- **Liberty**: freedom to think, speak and believe
- **Equality**: everyone is equal
- **Fraternity**: we are like brothers and sisters, one nation

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Read the first line of the Preamble aloud: *'We, the People of India…'*. Then tell someone at home what **Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity** mean in your own words.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: This is learning, not legal advice. If something ever feels wrong or unsafe, tell a trusted grown-up. In India, children can call **1098** (Childline) for help, and anyone can call **112** in an emergency. Families can get free legal help on **15100**.

activity.prompt: Match the big word to its meaning
pairs: Freedom to think, speak and believe
Feeling like one family as a nation
People choose their leaders, no king

quiz.q: When did India's Constitution come into force?
quiz.why: It came into force on 26 January 1950, which is why we celebrate Republic Day on 26 January.

quiz.q: Who led the Drafting Committee of the Constitution?
quiz.why: The answer is "Dr B. R. Ambedkar". Reason: Dr B. R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the Drafting Committee. The other choices, such as "Rabindranath Tagore" and "Mahatma Gandhi", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The Preamble begins with which words?
quiz.why: The Preamble starts 'We, the People of India', showing the power comes from the people.

quiz.q: Must the Prime Minister follow the Constitution?
options: No, the Prime Minister is above it
quiz.why: The answer is "Yes, everyone must follow it". Reason: Nobody is above the Constitution, not even the most powerful leaders. The other choices, such as "No, the Prime Minister is above it", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: My rights and my duties

scenes.text: Ravi, age 11, stopped going to school to help at a brick kiln near his village in Rajasthan.
His old teacher, Sunita Ma'am, visits his parents. 'Every child aged 6 to 14 has the right to free school. And children must not do dangerous work.'
The panchayat helps the family get support. Ravi returns to school and gets his books and midday meal.
Ravi now helps plant trees at school. 'Rights help me,' he says, 'and duties are how I help others.'

steps.title: What is a right?
steps.body:
A **right** is something every person should have, just because they are a human being. The Constitution protects many rights. Some important ones for children:

- **Right to education**: free and compulsory school for children aged 6 to 14.
- **Right to equality**: no one should be treated badly because of religion, caste, gender or where they were born.
- **Protection from dangerous work**: children below 14 must not work in factories, mines or other dangerous jobs.
- **Right to life and safety.**

steps.title: What is a duty?
steps.body:
A **duty** is something we should do for others and for our country. The Constitution lists **Fundamental Duties**. Some you can do today:

- Respect the National Flag and National Anthem.
- Protect nature: trees, rivers, animals.
- Take care of public property: do not break benches or scribble on walls.
- Treat everyone as brothers and sisters, and respect women and girls.

steps.title: Rights and duties go together
steps.body:
**You have a right to a clean park. Your duty is to not throw litter.**

**You have a right to be safe. Your duty is to not hurt or bully others.**

When everyone does their duties, everyone's rights are protected.

steps.title: If a child needs help
steps.body: If you or a friend is hurt, scared, made to work, or someone touches you in a way that feels wrong, **tell a trusted grown-up**: a parent, teacher or relative. In India, children can call **1098** (Childline), free, any time. It is never your fault.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make a **'rights and duties' chart**: on one side write 3 rights you have, on the other side write a matching duty for each one.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: This is learning, not legal advice. If something ever feels wrong or unsafe, tell a trusted grown-up. In India, children can call **1098** (Childline) for help, and anyone can call **112** in an emergency. Families can get free legal help on **15100**.

activity.prompt: Is it a right or a duty?

items.text: Going to school free (age 6 to 14)
Protecting trees and animals
Being treated equally
Not damaging public buses and parks
Being safe from dangerous work as a child
Respecting the National Flag

quiz.q: Children of which age have the right to free and compulsory education?
quiz.why: The answer is "6 to 14 years". Reason: The Right to Education covers children aged 6 to 14. The other choices, such as "Only 18 and above" and "Only 2 to 4 years", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which of these is a duty?
quiz.why: The answer is "Protecting nature". Reason: Protecting the environment is one of our Fundamental Duties. The other choices, such as "Being treated equally" and "Going to school free", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What number can a child in India call for help?
quiz.why: The answer is "1098". Reason: 1098 is Childline, a free helpline for children. The other choices, such as "1234" and "0000", do not fit the question. (Question: What number can a child in India call for help?)

quiz.q: A child below 14 working in a dangerous factory is…
quiz.why: The Constitution forbids employing children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.

questions.q: Rules help us to…
questions.why: The answer is "Live and play together fairly". Reason: Rules make life fair and peaceful. The other choices, such as "Fight more" and "Do whatever we like", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which day is Republic Day?
questions.why: The answer is "26 January". Reason: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950. The other choices, such as "14 November" and "5 September", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which day is Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas)?
questions.why: The answer is "26 November". Reason: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949. The other choices, such as "1 May" and "15 August", do not fit the question.

questions.q: What does 'Equality' mean?
questions.why: The answer is "Everyone is treated as equal". Reason: Equality means equal treatment for everyone. The other choices, such as "Some people are more important" and "Only adults have rights", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Laws are…
questions.why: The answer is "Rules for a whole country". Reason: Laws are rules made for the whole country. The other choices, such as "Stories" and "Rules for one game only", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Who is called the main architect of the Constitution?
questions.why: The answer is "Dr B. R. Ambedkar". Reason: He chaired the Drafting Committee. The other choices, such as "Sachin Tendulkar" and "C. V. Raman", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Not throwing litter in the park is…
questions.why: The answer is "A duty". Reason: Keeping public places clean is our duty. The other choices, such as "A punishment" and "A right", do not fit the question.

questions.q: 'Fraternity' in the Preamble means…
options: Feeling like one family as a nation
questions.why: The answer is "Feeling like one family as a nation". Reason: Fraternity is brotherhood and sisterhood among all people. The other choices, such as "Having lots of money" and "Winning a game", do not fit the question.

questions.q: In a Republic, who chooses the leaders?
questions.why: The answer is "The people". Reason: In a republic the people choose their leaders and there is no hereditary king. The other choices, such as "Only rich people" and "A king", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Meena's friend says a man at the shop touched her in a way that felt wrong and told her to keep it secret. What should Meena's friend do?
options: Tell a trusted adult or call 1098
questions.why: Unsafe secrets should always be told to a trusted adult. 1098 helps children. It is never the child's fault.

questions.q: Which rule is fair?
options: Everyone bowls one over in turn
Only the captain's friends can bowl
questions.why: The answer is "Everyone bowls one over in turn". Reason: A fair rule gives everyone the same chance. The other choices, such as "Only the captain's friends can bowl" and "Girls cannot bat", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Every other law in India must follow…
questions.why: The answer is "The Constitution". Reason: The Constitution is the highest law; other laws must agree with it. The other choices, such as "A cricket rulebook" and "Any one person's wish", do not fit the question.

courses.title: The Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Duties and Directive Principles
courses.summary: A complete, story-led guide to the heart of India's Constitution: how it was made, what the Preamble promises, each group of Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) with real situations, the writs that enforce them, the Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) and the Directive Principles (Articles 36–51). Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can explain how and when the Constitution was made and what each word of the Preamble means
Learners can name the six groups of Fundamental Rights and match situations to the right Article
Learners can explain 'reasonable restrictions' and why rights are not unlimited
Learners can name the five writs and when each is used
Learners can distinguish Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles from Fundamental Rights

lessons.title: How the Constitution was made, and what the Preamble promises

scenes.text: In a Pune school debate, Ishaan says: 'The word secular was always in our Preamble.' His opponent Fatima says: 'No, it was added later.'
Their teacher, Mr D'Souza, asks both to check. They find that 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

'So was India not secular before 1976?' asks Ishaan. Mr D'Souza explains that freedom of religion and equal treatment were already in the Fundamental Rights; the amendment made the idea explicit in the Preamble.
Both students win a point: Fatima for the fact, Ishaan for the deeper idea.

steps.title: The Constituent Assembly
steps.body:
India's Constitution was written by the **Constituent Assembly**, which first met on **9 December 1946**. **Dr Rajendra Prasad** was its President and **Dr B. R. Ambedkar** chaired the **Drafting Committee**.

The Assembly debated every article in public, for almost three years. The Constitution was **adopted on 26 November 1949** (now Constitution Day) and came **into force on 26 January 1950** (Republic Day). 26 January was chosen because on that date in 1930 the Indian National Congress had declared the goal of *Purna Swaraj* (complete independence).

It is one of the longest written constitutions in the world and borrowed ideas from many places: parliamentary government from Britain, fundamental rights and judicial review from the USA, Directive Principles from Ireland, and more, all adapted to Indian needs.

steps.title: The Preamble, word by word
steps.body:
**'We, the People of India'**: power comes from the people, not from a king or a foreign ruler.

- **Sovereign**: India decides its own internal and external matters.
- **Socialist**: the State aims to reduce inequality of income and opportunity (added 1976).
- **Secular**: the State has no official religion and treats all religions equally (added 1976).
- **Democratic**: government is elected by the people.
- **Republic**: the head of state (the President) is elected, not hereditary.

It promises **Justice** (social, economic, political), **Liberty** (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), **Equality** (of status and opportunity) and **Fraternity** (assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation).

steps.title: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution?
steps.body: Yes. In the **Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)** the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and helps interpret it. It can be amended (as in 1976), but the **basic structure** it reflects, such as democracy and secularism, cannot be destroyed. The Preamble itself is not directly enforceable in court; you cannot sue only because 'fraternity' is missing, but courts use it to read other articles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the dates: **adopted 26 Nov 1949**, **in force 26 Jan 1950**.
- Saying the Preamble always had 'socialist' and 'secular': these were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.
- Thinking 'Republic' and 'Democracy' mean the same. The UK is a democracy but not a republic (it has a hereditary monarch). India is both.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick one Preamble ideal and find **one news story** this week that shows it being protected or challenged. Write two lines: which ideal, and why.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

activity.prompt: Put these events in order

events.text: Purna Swaraj declared on 26 January
Constituent Assembly first meets (9 December)
India becomes independent (15 August)
Constitution adopted (26 November)
Constitution comes into force (26 January)
Kesavananda Bharati case: basic structure doctrine
42nd Amendment adds 'socialist', 'secular', 'integrity'

quiz.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly?
quiz.why: Dr Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee; Dr Rajendra Prasad was President of the Assembly.

quiz.q: Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976)?
quiz.why: The answer is "Socialist, Secular, Integrity". Reason: The 42nd Amendment added 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity'. The other choices, such as "Justice, Liberty" and "Republic, Fraternity", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: India is a 'Republic' because…
options: Its head of state is elected, not hereditary
quiz.why: The answer is "Its head of state is elected, not hereditary". Reason: A republic has an elected (not hereditary) head of state. The other choices, such as "It is a large country" and "It has a Parliament", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why was 26 January chosen for the Constitution to come into force?
options: It was the day of independence
Purna Swaraj had been declared on 26 January 1930
quiz.why: The answer is "Purna Swaraj had been declared on 26 January 1930". Reason: It honoured the 1930 Purna Swaraj declaration. The other choices, such as "It was chosen at random" and "It was Dr Ambedkar's birthday", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Preamble is part of the Constitution?
quiz.why: The answer is "Kesavananda Bharati (1973)". Reason: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) also laid down the basic structure doctrine. The other choices, such as "Maneka Gandhi (1978)" and "Puttaswamy (2017)", do not fit the question.

sources: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala (1973)

lessons.title: Right to Equality (Articles 14–18)

scenes.text: Kavya, 23, from Madurai, sees a state government advertisement for clerks: 'Only male candidates may apply.'
She is angry. Her brother says, 'The government can choose whoever it likes.'
Her aunt, a lawyer, explains Article 16: equality of opportunity in public employment; no discrimination on grounds of sex, among others.
With help from the District Legal Services Authority, Kavya files a writ petition in the High Court. The court stays the advertisement until it is corrected.

steps.title: Article 14: equality before law
steps.body:
**Article 14**: the State shall not deny to any person **equality before the law** or the **equal protection of the laws**.

- *Equality before law* (from British law): no one is above the law, from a peon to a minister.
- *Equal protection* (from US law): people in similar situations must be treated alike.

This applies to **every person** in India, including foreigners.

Article 14 does **not** ban all classification. The State may treat groups differently if there is a **reasonable classification**: a clear difference between the groups, connected to the purpose of the law (for example, lower income-tax rates for senior citizens). It bans **arbitrary** action: the Supreme Court has said arbitrariness is the opposite of equality.

steps.title: Article 15 and 16: no discrimination
steps.body:
**Article 15**: the State shall not discriminate against any **citizen** only on grounds of **religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth**. No citizen can be barred from shops, restaurants, wells, tanks, bathing ghats or public roads on these grounds.

**Article 16**: equality of opportunity in **public employment** (government jobs).

Both articles allow **special provisions**: for women and children (15(3)), for socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (15(4), 16(4)), and for economically weaker sections (15(6), 16(6), added in 2019). These are seen as tools to reach **real equality**, not exceptions to it.

steps.title: Article 17 and 18
steps.body:
**Article 17** abolishes **untouchability** and forbids its practice in any form. Enforcing any disability arising out of untouchability is an offence punishable by law (see the Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989).

**Article 18** abolishes **titles** (like 'Rai Bahadur'), except military and academic distinctions. National awards such as the Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are allowed, but they must not be used as a prefix or suffix to a name.

steps.title: Worked example: is this valid?
steps.body:
**Case A**: A state reserves seats in a government college for SC/ST students. **Valid**: a special provision under Article 15(4).

**Case B**: A private café refuses entry to a person because of caste. **Unlawful**: Article 15(2) applies to shops and public restaurants, and Article 17 forbids untouchability.

**Case C**: A government office pays women less than men for the same work. **Invalid** under Articles 14 and 16; also against the principle of equal pay for equal work (Article 39(d), a Directive Principle).

**Case D**: A law gives free bus passes only to students. **Valid**: students are a reasonable class connected to the aim of supporting education.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Article 15 and 16 protect foreigners: they protect **citizens**; Article 14 protects **all persons**.
- Thinking reservation 'violates equality'. The Supreme Court has held that special provisions can be a facet of equality, within limits it has set.
- Thinking Fundamental Rights apply against everyone. Most apply against the **State** (defined in Article 12), but some, like Articles 15(2), 17 and 24, also apply against private persons.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Look at any public notice (a school rule, a job advert, a housing society rule). Ask: does it treat people differently? If yes, is there a **reasonable** reason linked to its purpose?

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

activity.prompt: Match the Article to what it guarantees
pairs: Equality before law and equal protection of laws
No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth

quiz.q: Article 14 protects…
quiz.why: The answer is "All persons, including foreigners". Reason: Article 14 uses the word 'person', so it covers everyone in India. The other choices, such as "Only citizens" and "Only adults", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which of these is a ground listed in Article 15?
quiz.why: The answer is "Place of birth". Reason: Article 15 lists religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth. The other choices, such as "Height" and "Political party", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A law giving lower tax rates to senior citizens is…
options: Valid if it is a reasonable classification
quiz.why: The answer is "Valid if it is a reasonable classification". Reason: Article 14 permits reasonable classification linked to the law's purpose. The other choices, such as "Only valid in some states" and "A Fundamental Duty", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Can a person write 'Padma Shri' as a title before their name?
options: No, national awards must not be used as titles
quiz.why: The Supreme Court has held these awards are not titles under Article 18 and should not be used as prefixes or suffixes.

quiz.q: Article 17 applies…
quiz.why: Untouchability is forbidden in any form and its practice is punishable, whoever does it.

sources: Indra Sawhney v Union of India (1992)

lessons.title: Freedoms, life and liberty (Articles 19–22)

story.title: Arjun's post and the 3 a.m. knock

scenes.text: Arjun, a college student in Guwahati, posts a sharp cartoon criticising a local minister's road project.
Late at night, police arrive and take him to the station without saying why.
His sister Rina calls a legal-aid lawyer. The lawyer insists: he must be told the grounds of arrest, may consult a lawyer, and must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.
The magistrate finds criticism of a government project is protected speech, and Arjun is released. 'Criticism is not a crime,' the lawyer tells him.

steps.title: Article 19: six freedoms for citizens
steps.body:
Article 19(1) gives every **citizen** the right to:

- (a) freedom of **speech and expression** (courts have read in freedom of the press and the right to information),
- (b) **assemble peaceably and without arms**,
- (c) form **associations, unions** or co-operative societies,
- (d) **move freely** throughout India,
- (e) **reside and settle** in any part of India,
- (g) practise any **profession, occupation, trade or business**.

(Clause (f), the right to property, was removed in 1978. Property is now a legal right under **Article 300A**: no one can be deprived of property except by authority of law.)

steps.title: Reasonable restrictions
steps.body:
No freedom is absolute. Clauses 19(2) to 19(6) allow **reasonable restrictions** by law, for example, on speech, in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

Three tests courts apply:

- The restriction must be **by a law**, not just an order without legal basis.
- It must be for one of the **listed purposes**.
- It must be **reasonable and proportionate**: not more than needed.

In **Shreya Singhal (2015)** the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act because its vague words ('annoying', 'offensive') punished protected speech.

steps.title: Articles 20 and 21: protection and life
steps.body:
**Article 20** (for all persons):

- No punishment under a law made *after* the act was done (no retrospective criminal law).
- No **double jeopardy**: not prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence.
- No one accused can be **compelled to be a witness against himself**.

**Article 21**: *'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.'* After **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**, that procedure must be **fair, just and reasonable**. Courts have read into Article 21 the rights to live with dignity, livelihood, a clean environment, speedy trial, free legal aid, shelter, health, and **privacy** (**Puttaswamy, 2017**, nine judges).

**Article 21A** (added 2002): free and compulsory education for children aged **6 to 14**.

steps.title: Article 22: rights when arrested
steps.body:
A person who is arrested must:

- be **informed, as soon as may be, of the grounds** of arrest,
- have the right to **consult and be defended by a lawyer** of their choice,
- be **produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours** (excluding travel time), and not be kept longer without the magistrate's order.

These protections do not apply in the same way to *preventive detention* laws, which Article 22 regulates separately with an advisory board.

steps.title: Worked example: which Article?
steps.body:
- A town bans all protests forever, even peaceful ones → Article **19(1)(b)**; a total, permanent ban is unlikely to be a reasonable restriction.
- A worker from Bihar is told he cannot settle in Mumbai → Article **19(1)(e)**.
- Police beat a suspect to force a confession → Articles **20(3)** and **21**.
- A slum is demolished without notice or hearing → Article **21** (procedure must be fair).
- Your private photos are collected by a government app without legal basis → **privacy** under Article 21.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Say aloud the three things every arrested person is entitled to (grounds, lawyer, magistrate within 24 hours). Teach them to one family member; they may need it one day.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

a.text: You are Rina. Police have taken your brother Arjun at night for a social-media post. You are at the police station. What do you do first?

choices.label: Politely ask the officer for the grounds of arrest and which section is applied
choices.feedback: Good. Article 22 and the criminal procedure law require the grounds to be told; you are entitled to ask.

choices.label: Shout at the officers and try to pull Arjun out
choices.feedback: This can lead to your own arrest and does not help Arjun.

b.text: The officer gives a section number. Arjun has no lawyer and you cannot afford one.

choices.label: Call NALSA legal aid 15100 / the District Legal Services Authority
choices.feedback: Correct. Free legal aid is available to people in custody, whatever their income.

choices.label: Wait until morning and hope he is let go
choices.feedback: Waiting silently gives up protections. A lawyer can watch the 24-hour limit and seek bail.

c.text: The officers warn you. You calm down. What now?

choices.label: Ask calmly for the grounds of arrest
choices.feedback: Better: calm, firm questions work.

d.text: A legal-aid lawyer comes. Arjun is produced before a magistrate within 24 hours. The lawyer argues criticism of a road project is protected speech. He is released on bail.

e.text: In the morning you learn Arjun has not yet seen a magistrate. You call legal aid now and a lawyer helps. Lesson: act early; rights work best when someone asserts them.

quiz.q: Which freedom is NOT in Article 19(1) today?
quiz.why: Property was removed from Article 19 in 1978 and is now a legal right under Article 300A.

quiz.q: A person arrested must be produced before a magistrate within…
quiz.why: The answer is "24 hours (excluding travel time)". Reason: Article 22(2) sets 24 hours, excluding journey time. The other choices, such as "12 hours" and "7 days", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which case held that the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable?
quiz.why: The answer is "Maneka Gandhi (1978)". Reason: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) transformed Article 21. The other choices, such as "Indra Sawhney (1992)" and "Shreya Singhal (2015)", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Why was Section 66A of the IT Act struck down?
options: Its vague words punished protected speech
quiz.why: In Shreya Singhal (2015) the Court found it vague and an unreasonable restriction on speech.

quiz.q: Article 20(3) means…
options: An accused cannot be forced to be a witness against himself
quiz.why: The answer is "An accused cannot be forced to be a witness against himself". Reason: Article 20(3) protects against self-incrimination. The other choices, such as "Trials must be in English" and "Police can force confessions", do not fit the question.

sources: Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978)
K. S. Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017)
Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015)

lessons.title: Against exploitation, freedom of religion, culture, education and constitutional remedies (Articles 23–32)

story.title: The letter that became a case

scenes.text: In a stone quarry, Baldev and his family work for years to 'repay' a small loan, never paid wages, never allowed to leave.
A social worker, Anita, writes a simple letter to the Supreme Court describing the conditions.
The Court treats the letter as a petition (a Public Interest Litigation) and orders an inquiry.
The workers are freed as bonded labourers and the state is told to rehabilitate them. Baldev's children start school.

steps.title: Articles 23 and 24: against exploitation
steps.body:
**Article 23** prohibits **traffic in human beings, begar (forced unpaid labour) and other forms of forced labour**. The Supreme Court has held that paying less than the minimum wage can amount to forced labour. Bonded labour is abolished by the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976.

**Article 24**: no child below **14** shall be employed in any **factory, mine or other hazardous employment**. The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 (as amended in 2016) bans employing children under 14 in almost all work (with narrow family-enterprise exceptions outside school hours) and bans adolescents (14–18) in hazardous work.

steps.title: Articles 25–28: freedom of religion
steps.body:
- **Article 25**: all persons are equally entitled to **freedom of conscience** and the right freely to **profess, practise and propagate** religion, subject to public order, morality, health and other Fundamental Rights. The State may regulate secular activities linked to religion and may make laws for social reform.
- **Article 26**: religious denominations may manage their own religious affairs and institutions.
- **Article 27**: no one can be forced to pay taxes to promote a particular religion.
- **Article 28**: no religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by State funds.

Courts protect practices that are **essential** to a religion, and the State can still act against harmful practices (for example, instant triple talaq was held invalid in 2017).

steps.title: Articles 29 and 30: culture and education
steps.body:
**Article 29**: any section of citizens with a distinct **language, script or culture** has the right to conserve it; no citizen can be denied admission to a State-run or State-aided institution only on grounds of religion, race, caste or language.

**Article 30**: religious and linguistic **minorities** have the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.

steps.title: Article 32 and the five writs
steps.body:
**Article 32** lets anyone go directly to the **Supreme Court** to enforce Fundamental Rights. Dr Ambedkar called it the **'very soul' and 'heart'** of the Constitution. **Article 226** gives **High Courts** a similar (and wider) power.

The five **writs**:

- **Habeas corpus** ('produce the body'): bring a detained person before court; release if detention is illegal.
- **Mandamus** ('we command'): order a public official or body to do a public duty it is failing to do.
- **Prohibition**: stop a lower court/tribunal from acting beyond its jurisdiction (while the case is pending).
- **Certiorari**: quash an order already passed by a lower court/tribunal without jurisdiction or with a clear error.
- **Quo warranto** ('by what authority'): ask a person holding a public office to show their legal right to it.

**PIL**: since the late 1970s–80s, courts let public-spirited people, even through letters, file cases for those who cannot approach courts themselves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing **prohibition** (before the order, case pending) with **certiorari** (after the order, to quash it).
- Thinking mandamus can be issued against the President or a private person: it lies against public authorities, not the President or Governors personally, and generally not against private persons.
- Thinking Fundamental Rights can never be suspended: during a national emergency, Article 19 can be suspended and enforcement of other rights can be suspended, but **never Articles 20 and 21** (after the 44th Amendment, 1978).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: For each writ, invent a one-line situation from your town. Example: *'The municipality refuses to issue my birth certificate despite all documents'* → mandamus.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

cards.back: 'Produce the body': court checks if a detention is legal; frees the person if not.
'We command': orders a public authority to perform a legal duty it is neglecting.
Stops a lower court or tribunal from continuing a case beyond its powers.
Quashes an order already passed by a lower court or tribunal without jurisdiction or with error.
'By what authority?': challenges someone holding a public office illegally.
Right to approach the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights.
Bans human trafficking, begar and forced labour.
Minorities may set up and run educational institutions.

quiz.q: Which writ would you use if a friend has been illegally detained?
quiz.why: Habeas corpus asks the authority to produce the detained person and justify the detention.

quiz.q: Dr Ambedkar called which Article the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
quiz.why: The answer is "Article 32". Reason: Article 32 makes rights enforceable directly in the Supreme Court. The other choices, such as "Article 21" and "Article 368", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Article 24 forbids employing children below 14 in…
options: Any work at all, including chores
quiz.why: Article 24 covers factories, mines and hazardous work; a separate Act goes further.

quiz.q: Which rights can never be suspended even during a national emergency?
quiz.why: After the 44th Amendment (1978), Articles 20 and 21 remain enforceable in an emergency.

quiz.q: A person is appointed to a public office without the required qualification. Which writ challenges this?
quiz.why: The answer is "Quo warranto". Reason: Quo warranto asks 'by what authority' the person holds the office. The other choices, such as "Prohibition" and "Mandamus", do not fit the question.

sources: Bandhua Mukti Morcha v Union of India (1984)

lessons.title: Fundamental Duties and Directive Principles

scenes.text: Nandini, a retired teacher in Bengaluru, watches her neighbourhood lake fill with garbage and sewage.
She organises residents to stop dumping (a Fundamental Duty: protect the environment) and to clean the banks every Sunday.
When the city still lets sewage flow in, the residents file a petition. The court relies on Article 21 (clean environment) and Article 48A (a Directive Principle) to order a cleanup plan.
Two years later, birds are back. 'Duties for us, directions for the State, and rights for all,' Nandini tells her grandson.

steps.title: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A)
Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV, Articles 36–51)
steps.body:
These are **instructions to the State** for making laws and policies, inspired partly by the Irish Constitution. **Article 37**: they are **not enforceable by any court**, but are **fundamental in the governance** of the country.

Examples:

- **Article 39**: adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work for men and women, no concentration of wealth, protection of children.
- **Article 39A**: equal justice and **free legal aid** (the basis of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987).
- **Article 40**: organise **village panchayats** (made real by the 73rd Amendment).
- **Article 44**: try to secure a **uniform civil code** for citizens.
- **Article 45**: early childhood care and education for children below 6.
- **Article 47**: raise nutrition and public health.
- **Article 48A**: protect the environment, forests and wildlife.
- **Article 50**: separate the judiciary from the executive.
- **Article 51**: promote international peace and respect for international law.

steps.title: Rights vs Duties vs Directive Principles
steps.body:
- **Who it binds**: Rights mainly limit the **State**; DPSPs guide the **State**; Duties are for **citizens**.
- **Enforceable in court?** Rights: **yes** (Articles 32, 226). DPSPs: **no** (Article 37). Duties: not directly, though laws may enforce some (e.g., insulting the National Flag is punishable under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971).
- **Nature**: Rights are mostly 'negative' (the State must not do X). DPSPs are 'positive' (the State should do Y).

Courts try to **harmonise** them: in **Minerva Mills (1980)** the Supreme Court said the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself part of the basic structure.

steps.title: Directive Principles in action
steps.body: Many famous laws and schemes trace back to DPSPs: the **Minimum Wages Act** and **Maternity Benefit Act** (Article 39, 42), the **73rd and 74th Amendments** creating panchayats and municipalities (Article 40), the **Legal Services Authorities Act** (Article 39A), the **Midday Meal** in schools (Article 47) and the **Wildlife Protection Act** (Article 48A).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Choose **one** Fundamental Duty and do something concrete for it this week, such as returning lost public property, planting a tree, or checking a viral claim scientifically before forwarding it.

activity.prompt: Fundamental Right, Directive Principle or Fundamental Duty?

items.text: Equality before law (Art 14)
State should secure a uniform civil code (Art 44)
Develop scientific temper
Freedom of speech (Art 19)
Organise village panchayats (Art 40)
Safeguard public property
Free legal aid (Art 39A)
Protection from forced labour (Art 23)

quiz.q: Fundamental Duties were added by…
quiz.why: The answer is "The 42nd Amendment (1976)". Reason: The 42nd Amendment inserted Article 51A. The other choices, such as "The 73rd Amendment (1992)" and "The original Constitution", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which Article says Directive Principles are not enforceable by courts?
quiz.why: The answer is "Article 37". Reason: Article 37: not enforceable, but fundamental in governance. The other choices, such as "Article 51A" and "Article 32", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The 11th Fundamental Duty (2002) concerns…
options: Parents providing education to children aged 6–14
quiz.why: The answer is "Parents providing education to children aged 6–14". Reason: It was added with Article 21A by the 86th Amendment. The other choices, such as "Military service" and "Paying taxes", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Free legal aid is a Directive Principle under…
quiz.why: The answer is "Article 39A". Reason: Article 39A led to the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 and NALSA. The other choices, such as "Article 50" and "Article 48A", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which case said the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure?
quiz.why: The answer is "Minerva Mills (1980)". Reason: Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980). The other choices, such as "Maneka Gandhi (1978)" and "Vishaka (1997)", do not fit the question.

sources: Constitution of India, Parts IV and IVA
Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980)

questions.q: The Constitution came into force on…
questions.why: The answer is "26 January 1950". Reason: Adopted 26 Nov 1949; in force 26 Jan 1950. The other choices, such as "26 November 1949" and "15 August 1947", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which word in the Preamble means India has no official religion and treats all religions equally?
questions.why: The answer is "Secular". Reason: Secular, added in 1976. The other choices, such as "Republic" and "Sovereign", do not fit the question. (Question: Which word in the Preamble means India has no official religion and treats all religions equally?)

questions.q: Right to education for children aged 6–14 is in…
questions.why: The answer is "Article 21A". Reason: Article 21A was added by the 86th Amendment (2002). The other choices, such as "Article 14" and "Article 32", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which right is available to foreigners as well as citizens?
questions.why: The answer is "Article 21 life and personal liberty". Reason: Article 21 uses 'person'; Articles 16, 19 and 29 are for citizens. The other choices, such as "Article 19 freedoms" and "Article 16 public employment", do not fit the question.

questions.q: The right to property today is…
questions.why: The answer is "A legal/constitutional right under Article 300A". Reason: The 44th Amendment (1978) moved it to Article 300A. The other choices, such as "A Fundamental Duty" and "A Fundamental Right under Article 19", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which writ quashes an order already passed by a lower tribunal without jurisdiction?
questions.why: The answer is "Certiorari". Reason: Certiorari quashes; prohibition prevents. The other choices, such as "Habeas corpus" and "Mandamus", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Article 15 allows special provisions for…
options: Women and children, and backward classes, SCs and STs
questions.why: The answer is "Women and children, and backward classes, SCs and STs". Reason: Articles 15(3) and 15(4). The other choices, such as "Only rich people" and "Only foreigners", do not fit the question.

questions.q: The right to privacy was declared a Fundamental Right in…
questions.why: The answer is "Puttaswamy (2017)". Reason: A nine-judge bench in Puttaswamy (2017). The other choices, such as "Kesavananda Bharati (1973)" and "Maneka Gandhi (1978)", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A municipal officer refuses, without reason, to issue a trade licence you are legally entitled to. The most suitable writ is…
questions.why: The answer is "Mandamus". Reason: Mandamus commands a public authority to do its legal duty. The other choices, such as "Certiorari" and "Habeas corpus", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which statement about Directive Principles is correct?
options: They guide the State but are not enforceable by courts
questions.why: The answer is "They guide the State but are not enforceable by courts". Reason: Article 37. The other choices, such as "Courts can enforce them directly" and "They were added in 1976", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A law makes an act punishable and applies it to acts done five years before the law was passed. This violates…
questions.why: The answer is "Article 20(1)". Reason: Article 20(1) bars retrospective criminal punishment. The other choices, such as "Article 19(1)(a)" and "Article 30", do not fit the question.

questions.q: During a national emergency, which rights remain enforceable after the 44th Amendment?
questions.why: The answer is "Articles 20 and 21". Reason: Article 359 as amended protects Articles 20 and 21. The other choices, such as "Articles 14 and 15 only" and "None", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A state law classifies people for a benefit. Under Article 14, which test applies?
options: The law must treat everyone identically in every way
The classification must be based on an intelligible difference with a rational link to the law's object, and not be arbitrary
questions.why: The answer is "The classification must be based on an intelligible difference with a rational link to the law's object, and not be arbitrary". Reason: Reasonable classification plus the rule against arbitrariness.

questions.q: Why did the Supreme Court hold in Minerva Mills (1980) that Parliament could not give Directive Principles total primacy over all Fundamental Rights?
options: Because the balance between Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure
questions.why: The answer is "Because the balance between Parts III and IV is part of the basic structure". Reason: Harmony and balance between rights and directives is basic structure. The other choices, such as "Because DPSPs are unimportant" and "Because DPSPs were added late", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which Fundamental Duty relates to how you treat a viral health rumour?
options: Develop scientific temper and spirit of inquiry
questions.why: The answer is "Develop scientific temper and spirit of inquiry". Reason: Scientific temper means checking evidence before believing or spreading claims. The other choices, such as "Defend the country" and "Strive for excellence", do not fit the question.

Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can explain the parliamentary system and the roles of the President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
Learners can compare Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha in composition, term and powers

lessons.title: Who runs the government? President, Prime Minister and ministers

scenes.text: Meher, a Class 12 student in Chandigarh, watches news of an old political crisis: a government loses a confidence vote in the Lok Sabha by a single vote.
'Why does one vote in the Lok Sabha decide who is Prime Minister? I thought people elected the PM,' she asks her father, Gurpreet.
He explains: in a parliamentary system, people elect MPs; the PM stays only as long as a majority of Lok Sabha MPs support the government.
Meher realises: 'So the government is answerable to Parliament every single day, not just once in five years.'

steps.title: Three organs of the State
steps.body:
- **Legislature** makes laws: Parliament (Union) and State Legislatures.
- **Executive** implements laws: President, Prime Minister, Council of Ministers and the civil services (and Governors, Chief Ministers at state level).
- **Judiciary** interprets laws and settles disputes: Supreme Court, High Courts and subordinate courts.

India follows a **separation of functions with checks and balances**, not a strict separation: ministers are also members of Parliament, and courts can review laws and executive actions.

steps.title: The President
steps.body:
The **President** is the head of the State and the Supreme Commander of the armed forces. All executive action is taken in the President's name.

- **Election**: indirectly, by an electoral college of the **elected members of both Houses of Parliament** and the **elected members of State Legislative Assemblies** (and of certain Union Territories with legislatures), using proportional representation by single transferable vote.
- **Qualifications**: citizen of India, at least **35 years** old, qualified to be a Lok Sabha member.
- **Term**: 5 years; can be removed by **impeachment** for violation of the Constitution (Article 61).

Under **Article 74**, the President acts on the **aid and advice of the Council of Ministers** headed by the PM. The President may send advice back once for reconsideration, but must then act on it. The President also has important powers like granting **pardons** (Article 72) and issuing **ordinances** (Article 123) when Parliament is not in session; an ordinance lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved.

steps.title: Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
steps.body:
The **Prime Minister** is the head of the government. The President appoints as PM the person who can **command a majority in the Lok Sabha**, and appoints other ministers on the PM's advice.

- The Council of Ministers is **collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha** (Article 75(3)). If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the whole government must resign.
- Its size cannot exceed **15%** of the total strength of the Lok Sabha (91st Amendment, 2003).
- A minister who is not an MP must become one within **six months**.
- The **Cabinet** is the smaller inner group of senior ministers that takes the key decisions.

The **Vice-President** is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and acts as President if that office falls vacant.

steps.title: Worked example: the majority mark
steps.body:
The Lok Sabha has **543** elected seats. A simple majority is more than half: **272**.

If Party A wins 240 seats and its allies win 35, the alliance has 275 → it can claim majority and its leader is invited to form the government. If the alliance later falls to 268 because some allies withdraw support, the government may face a **no-confidence motion**; if it loses, the Council of Ministers must resign.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'The people directly elect the PM': no, voters elect MPs; the PM is the leader who has majority support in the Lok Sabha.
- 'The President can refuse any law or advice': the President is a constitutional head and acts on ministerial advice, with limited discretion.
- 'Ministers must be Lok Sabha MPs': a minister can be from either House, or become an MP within six months.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find out who your **MP**, **MLA** and local **ward councillor/sarpanch** are. Write one thing each of them is responsible for.

quiz.q: Who elects the President of India?
options: Elected MPs and elected MLAs (electoral college)
quiz.why: An electoral college of elected members of Parliament and State Assemblies elects the President.

quiz.q: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to…
quiz.why: The answer is "The Lok Sabha". Reason: Article 75(3): collective responsibility to the House of the People. The other choices, such as "The President" and "The Rajya Sabha", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Minimum age to become President is…
quiz.why: The answer is "35". Reason: Article 58 requires at least 35 years. The other choices, such as "25" and "45", do not fit the question. (Question: Minimum age to become President is…)

quiz.q: A person who is not an MP is made a minister. Within how long must they become an MP?
quiz.why: The answer is "Six months". Reason: Article 75(5): six consecutive months. The other choices, such as "One month" and "One year", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The maximum size of the Council of Ministers is…
options: 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
quiz.why: The answer is "15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha". Reason: Set by the 91st Amendment (2003). The other choices, such as "Any number" and "50 ministers", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Parliament: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha

scenes.text: Tenzin, a political science student from Sikkim, gets a visitor pass to watch Parliament in New Delhi.
At 11 a.m. it is Question Hour. An MP from Kerala asks the Railway Minister why a train route has been cancelled; the minister must answer.
Later, in Zero Hour, MPs raise urgent local issues: floods, a bridge collapse, a farmers' protest.
'Parliament is not only for making laws,' Tenzin writes. 'It is where the government has to explain itself in public.'

steps.title: What Parliament is
steps.body:
Under **Article 79**, Parliament consists of the **President** and two Houses:

- **Lok Sabha** (House of the People): directly elected.
- **Rajya Sabha** (Council of States): represents the States and Union Territories.

The President is part of Parliament because a bill becomes law only after the President's assent, though the President does not sit in either House.

steps.title: Lok Sabha vs Rajya Sabha
steps.body:
**Lok Sabha**

- **543** elected seats today (constitutional maximum 550 elected members).
- MPs elected directly by voters in constituencies, by **first-past-the-post**.
- Term **5 years**, unless dissolved earlier.
- Minimum age to be a member: **25**.
- Presided over by the **Speaker**.

**Rajya Sabha**

- Maximum **250** members: up to 238 elected representatives of States/UTs + **12 nominated** by the President for art, literature, science and social service.
- Members elected by **elected MLAs** of each state, by proportional representation (single transferable vote).
- A **permanent House**: never dissolved; one-third of members retire every two years; each member serves **6 years**.
- Minimum age: **30**.
- Presided over by the **Vice-President** as Chairman.

steps.title: How Parliament holds the government accountable
steps.body:
- **Question Hour**: MPs ask ministers questions (starred questions get oral answers with follow-ups).
- **Zero Hour**: an Indian practice where urgent issues are raised after Question Hour.
- **Motions**: no-confidence motion (only in Lok Sabha), adjournment motion, calling-attention motion.
- **Debates** on the President's address and the **Budget**: no tax can be levied and no money spent without Parliament's approval.
- **Committees**: for example the **Public Accounts Committee** examines the CAG's audit reports on government spending and, by convention, is chaired by a member of the opposition. Department-related standing committees examine bills in detail.

steps.title: Anti-defection and reservation
steps.body:
**Tenth Schedule** (52nd Amendment, 1985): an MP or MLA can be disqualified for voluntarily giving up party membership or voting against the party whip without permission. A merger is protected only if at least two-thirds of the legislature party agree. The Speaker/Chairman decides, subject to judicial review.

**Reserved seats**: seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and Assemblies. The **106th Amendment (2023)** provides one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies; it will take effect after the next census and the delimitation that follows.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Rajya Sabha is dissolved every 6 years': it is **never dissolved**; members retire in batches every two years.
- 'Rajya Sabha members are elected by people directly': they are elected by elected **MLAs**.
- 'A no-confidence motion can be moved in either House': only in the **Lok Sabha**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Watch 15 minutes of Question Hour on Sansad TV or its official online archive. Note one question, the minister's answer, and whether the answer actually addressed the question.

lessons.title: How a bill becomes a law

scenes.text: After a friend is hurt in a road crash in Hyderabad and bystanders are too scared to help, Sana, 19, starts a campaign: 'Protect people who help accident victims.'
Thousands sign. An MP raises it in Parliament. Courts and the government had already issued guidelines protecting Good Samaritans.
Later, when Parliament amends the Motor Vehicles Act in 2019, a section protecting Good Samaritans is included and passed by both Houses.
After the President's assent, it becomes law. Sana learns every law starts as a bill, and citizens can shape it.

steps.title: Types of bills
steps.body:
- **Ordinary bill**: any matter other than money; can start in **either House**.
- **Money bill** (Article 110): only about taxes, borrowing, the Consolidated Fund and similar money matters. The **Speaker certifies** whether a bill is a money bill. It can be introduced **only in the Lok Sabha**, with the President's recommendation.
- **Financial bills**: involve money but also other matters; treated mostly like ordinary bills with some conditions.
- **Constitutional amendment bill** (Article 368).

A bill moved by a minister is a **government bill**; one by any other MP is a **private member's bill** (rarely passed).

steps.title: Journey of an ordinary bill
steps.body:
1. **First reading**: the bill is introduced and published.
2. It may be sent to a **committee** (standing, select or joint) for detailed study and public comments.
3. **Second reading**: general debate, then clause-by-clause consideration and voting on amendments.
4. **Third reading**: the House votes to pass the bill.
5. The same process happens in the **other House**. If it makes changes, the first House must agree.
6. **President's assent** (Article 111): the President may assent, withhold assent, or return it (if not a money bill) once for reconsideration. If both Houses pass it again, the President must assent.
7. It is **published in the Gazette** and comes into force on the notified date.

**Deadlock**: if the Houses disagree on an ordinary bill, the President may call a **joint sitting** (Article 108), presided over by the Speaker. Because the Lok Sabha is larger, its view usually prevails. Joint sittings have been rare (for example on the Dowry Prohibition Bill in 1961).

steps.title: Money bills: the Lok Sabha's special power
steps.body: The Rajya Sabha **cannot reject or amend** a money bill. It can only make **recommendations** within **14 days**; the Lok Sabha may accept or reject them. If the Rajya Sabha does not return it within 14 days, it is deemed passed. There is **no joint sitting** for money bills. This reflects the principle that the directly elected House controls public money.

steps.title: Amending the Constitution (Article 368)
steps.body:
Three ways:

- **Simple majority** of Parliament: for certain provisions outside Article 368's procedure, like creating new states or changing state names (Articles 2–4).
- **Special majority**: a majority of the **total membership** of each House **and** two-thirds of members **present and voting**, in **each House separately**. No joint sitting is allowed.
- **Special majority + ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures**: for federal matters, such as the election of the President, the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts, representation of States, and the Seventh Schedule lists (the GST amendment of 2016 went through this route).

The President **must** give assent to a constitutional amendment bill. But no amendment may destroy the **basic structure** (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'A joint sitting can resolve any deadlock': not for money bills or constitutional amendments.
- 'Rajya Sabha can block the budget': it can only delay a money bill by up to 14 days.
- 'Once Parliament passes a bill it is law': it needs the President's assent and usually a notification of the date it comes into force.

quiz.q: How long can the Rajya Sabha hold a money bill?
quiz.why: The answer is "14 days". Reason: After 14 days it is deemed passed by both Houses. The other choices, such as "6 months" and "30 days", do not fit the question.

options: Majority of total membership AND two-thirds of those present and voting
quiz.why: The answer is "Majority of total membership AND two-thirds of those present and voting". Reason: Both conditions must be met in each House. The other choices, such as "Unanimous vote" and "Half of members present", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which amendment needed ratification by at least half the State Legislatures?

lessons.title: Elections: your vote, step by step

scenes.text: Aisha in Kolkata turns 18. Her grandmother, who has voted in every election since the 1970s, says: 'Your first vote is your voice. Don't waste it.'
Aisha applies online with Form 6 on the Election Commission's voter portal. A Booth Level Officer visits to verify her address.
On polling day she shows her voter ID, gets ink on her left forefinger, presses the button on the EVM and watches the VVPAT slip appear for a few seconds.
Her friend Rahul, unhappy with every candidate, chooses NOTA. 'At least my dissatisfaction is counted,' he says.

steps.title: Universal adult franchise
steps.body:
**Article 326**: elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies are on the basis of **adult suffrage**. Every citizen aged **18 or above** who is not disqualified (for example for unsoundness of mind declared by a court, or certain corrupt practices) can vote. The voting age was lowered from **21 to 18** by the **61st Amendment (1988)**.

India gave the vote to all adults, women and men, rich and poor, from its **first general election in 1951–52**, when many established democracies had taken decades to do so.

steps.title: The Election Commission of India
steps.body:
**Article 324**: the **Election Commission of India (ECI)** superintends, directs and controls elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. It consists of the **Chief Election Commissioner** and other Election Commissioners.

At state level, a **Chief Electoral Officer** works under it; in each constituency, a **Returning Officer** conducts the election, and **Electoral Registration Officers** with **Booth Level Officers** maintain the voters' list.

Elections to **panchayats and municipalities** are run by separate **State Election Commissions** (Articles 243K and 243ZA).

steps.title: How to register and vote
steps.body:
1. **Register**: fill **Form 6** online on the ECI's voter services portal or Voter Helpline app, or offline with your BLO/ERO. You can apply in advance from age 17; your name is added once you turn 18 on a qualifying date. (Form 8 is used for corrections or shifting address.)
2. **Check** your name in the electoral roll and find your polling station. Voter helpline: **1950**.
3. On polling day take your **EPIC (voter ID)**; if you do not have it, the ECI usually allows other listed photo IDs (such as Aadhaar, passport, driving licence).
4. At the booth: identity check → **indelible ink** on the left forefinger → signature/thumb impression → press the button against your candidate on the **EVM**.
5. The **VVPAT** shows a slip with the candidate's name and symbol for about seven seconds behind glass, then it drops into a sealed box. This lets you verify your vote.

steps.title: NOTA and the Model Code of Conduct
steps.body:
**NOTA ('None of the Above')** was introduced after the Supreme Court's 2013 judgment in *PUCL v Union of India*. It lets you reject all candidates secretly. But in Lok Sabha and Assembly elections, **even if NOTA gets the most votes, the candidate with the highest votes among candidates still wins**; NOTA does not cancel the election.

The **Model Code of Conduct (MCC)** applies from the announcement of the election schedule until results. It is a set of guidelines agreed with parties, enforced by the ECI: no new government schemes or announcements to influence voters, no use of official machinery for campaigning, no appeal to caste or communal feelings, no bribing voters. Campaigning ends **48 hours** before polling ends in that area.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'If NOTA wins, a re-election is held': not for Lok Sabha/Assembly seats under current law.
- 'I need the voter ID card itself to vote': your **name must be on the roll**; the card is one of several accepted IDs.
- 'Offering money or gifts for votes is just politics': it is a **corrupt practice** and an electoral offence for both giver and taker. Report it through the ECI's cVIGIL app.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: If you are 17 or above, check your registration status online today, or help an elderly neighbour check theirs.

a.text: It is polling day. You are 19 and reach your booth, but your name is not on the voter list, though you have your EPIC card.

choices.label: Ask the Presiding Officer/BLO to check the roll carefully (name spelling, part number)
choices.feedback: Good. Names are sometimes in a different part of the list or misspelt.

choices.label: Ask a friend to vote for you in your name
choices.feedback: That is impersonation, an electoral offence.

b.text: They find you are listed in a neighbouring booth's part. You vote there. Outside, a party worker offers you ₹500 'for tea'.

choices.label: Refuse and report it on cVIGIL or to the polling official
choices.feedback: Right. Bribery is a corrupt practice; cVIGIL lets you upload a photo/video report.

choices.label: Take it; it is harmless
choices.feedback: Taking a bribe for voting is an offence, and it undermines free elections.

c.text: The officials notice the ink mismatch and refuse. You realise only you can cast your vote.

choices.label: Go back and ask officials to check the roll properly
choices.feedback: Better: use the proper process.

d.text: Your report is logged with location and time. You cast an honest vote and protected someone else's. Well done.

e.text: You later learn that accepting gratification to vote is punishable. Next time, refuse and report. Your vote is not for sale.

quiz.q: The voting age in India was reduced from 21 to 18 by…
quiz.why: The answer is "The 61st Amendment". Reason: The 61st Amendment Act, 1988. The other choices, such as "The original Constitution" and "The 42nd Amendment", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which Article gives the Election Commission control over elections?
quiz.why: The answer is "Article 324". Reason: Article 324. The other choices, such as "Article 32" and "Article 21", do not fit the question. (Question: Which Article gives the Election Commission control over elections?)

quiz.why: The answer is "Form 6". Reason: Form 6 is for new voter registration. The other choices, such as "Form A" and "Form 1", do not fit the question. (Question: Which form is used to register as a new voter?)

quiz.q: If NOTA gets the highest votes in a Lok Sabha seat…
options: No MP is chosen for 5 years
The candidate with the most votes among candidates wins
quiz.why: The answer is "The candidate with the most votes among candidates wins". Reason: Under current rules NOTA does not change the result. The other choices, such as "No MP is chosen for 5 years" and "The President nominates someone", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: What does VVPAT let a voter do?
options: See a printed slip verifying the candidate voted for
quiz.why: The answer is "See a printed slip verifying the candidate voted for". Reason: VVPAT displays a slip for about seven seconds for verification. The other choices, such as "Vote twice" and "Change their vote later", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which organ of the State makes laws?
questions.why: The answer is "Legislature". Reason: The legislature makes laws. The other choices, such as "Election Commission" and "Executive", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Minimum voting age in India is…
questions.why: The answer is "18". Reason: Article 326, after the 61st Amendment. The other choices, such as "16" and "21", do not fit the question. (Question: Minimum voting age in India is…)

questions.q: The PM is appointed by the President because the PM…
options: Commands a majority in the Lok Sabha
Is nominated by the Supreme Court
questions.why: The answer is "Commands a majority in the Lok Sabha". Reason: Parliamentary system: majority support in the Lok Sabha. The other choices, such as "Won the most votes personally" and "Is the oldest MP", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Minimum age to be a Lok Sabha member is…
questions.why: The answer is "25". Reason: 25 for Lok Sabha; 30 for Rajya Sabha. The other choices, such as "18" and "21", do not fit the question. (Question: Minimum age to be a Lok Sabha member is…)

questions.q: The Rajya Sabha is…
options: A permanent House; one-third retire every two years
questions.why: The answer is "A permanent House; one-third retire every two years". Reason: It is never dissolved. The other choices, such as "Headed by the Speaker" and "Elected directly by voters", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A money bill can be introduced…
questions.why: The answer is "Only in the Lok Sabha". Reason: Article 109. The other choices, such as "Only in a joint sitting" and "In either House", do not fit the question.

questions.q: What happens if the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion against the government?
options: The entire Council of Ministers must resign
questions.why: The answer is "The entire Council of Ministers must resign". Reason: Collective responsibility. The other choices, such as "Nothing" and "Only the PM resigns", do not fit the question.

questions.q: An ordinance issued by the President must be approved by Parliament within…
questions.why: The answer is "Six weeks of Parliament reassembling". Reason: Article 123(2). The other choices, such as "One year" and "It never needs approval", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which bill type requires a special majority and ratification by half the states?
options: Amendment affecting the Seventh Schedule lists
questions.why: The answer is "Amendment affecting the Seventh Schedule lists". Reason: Federal provisions need state ratification under Article 368(2). The other choices, such as "Annual budget" and "Private member's bill on traffic", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Who conducts elections to panchayats?
questions.why: The answer is "State Election Commission". Reason: Article 243K. The other choices, such as "Election Commission of India" and "The Governor", do not fit the question.

questions.q: The Council of Ministers sends advice to the President, who returns it once for reconsideration. They send the same advice again. The President must…
questions.why: The answer is "Act in accordance with it". Reason: Article 74(1) proviso. The other choices, such as "Dissolve Parliament" and "Ask the Supreme Court", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Why can the Rajya Sabha not reject a money bill?
options: Because control over public money rests with the directly elected House
questions.why: A core principle of parliamentary democracy: the elected House controls the purse.

questions.q: When does the women's reservation under the 106th Amendment (2023) take effect?
options: After the next census and the delimitation that follows
questions.why: The answer is "After the next census and the delimitation that follows". Reason: The amendment ties commencement to the census and delimitation. The other choices, such as "Immediately from 2023" and "Never", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Campaigning in a constituency must stop…
questions.why: The answer is "48 hours before polling ends". Reason: The 48-hour 'silence period' under election law. The other choices, such as "One week before polling" and "24 hours before polling ends", do not fit the question.

courses.summary: How India's courts are organised and kept independent, how judicial review and the basic structure doctrine protect the Constitution, how power is shared between the Union and the States (Seventh Schedule, Governor, Article 356, GST Council), and how panchayats and municipalities bring democracy to your street. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
