lessons.title: India's courts: structure and independence

story.title: Ramesh's land case climbs the ladder

scenes.text: Ramesh, a farmer near Nashik, files a suit against a neighbour who blocked the path to his field. The civil judge rules for the neighbour.
Ramesh appeals to the District Court, which reverses the decision. The neighbour then appeals to the Bombay High Court.
The High Court agrees with the District Court. The neighbour seeks special leave to appeal in the Supreme Court, which declines to hear it.
Ramesh's lawyer explains: 'Every court is bound by the Supreme Court's law, and you had the right to be heard at every level.'

steps.title: One integrated judiciary
steps.body:
Unlike the USA, India has a **single integrated system** of courts that applies both Union and State laws:

- **Supreme Court of India** (New Delhi): the highest court.
- **High Courts** (25): one for each state or for a group of states/UTs.
- **Subordinate courts** in each district:
  - Civil side: District Judge → Civil Judge (Senior Division) → Civil Judge (Junior Division).
  - Criminal side: Sessions Judge → Chief Judicial Magistrate → Judicial Magistrates (and Metropolitan Magistrates in some cities).
- Specialised **tribunals**, family courts, consumer commissions and **Lok Adalats** handle particular kinds of disputes.

steps.title: Supreme Court: composition and powers
steps.body:
**Article 124**: a Chief Justice of India and other judges fixed by Parliament (currently the CJI and up to **33** others). Judges retire at **65** (High Court judges at **62**).

Jurisdictions:

- **Original** (Article 131): disputes between the Union and States, or between States.
- **Writ** (Article 32): enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
- **Appellate**: appeals in civil, criminal and constitutional cases; plus **special leave to appeal** (Article 136) from any court or tribunal, at its discretion.
- **Advisory** (Article 143): the President may ask its opinion.
- **Review** (Article 137) and **curative petitions** to correct grave miscarriages of justice.

**Article 141**: law declared by the Supreme Court is **binding on all courts**. **Article 142**: it can pass orders to do **complete justice**.

steps.title: Independence of the judiciary
steps.body:
- **Appointment**: judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts are appointed by the President through the **collegium system** (senior-most judges recommend names), developed by the Supreme Court in the Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges cases. In 2015 the Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC).
- **Security of tenure**: a judge can be removed only by an order of the President after an address by **each House of Parliament** passed by a special majority, on grounds of **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
- **Salaries** are charged on the Consolidated Fund (not voted on), and cannot be reduced to their disadvantage during their term (except in a financial emergency).
- **Contempt powers** (Articles 129, 215) protect courts' authority.
- Retired Supreme Court judges cannot practise in any court in India.
- **Article 50** (DPSP) directs separation of the judiciary from the executive.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'High Courts are under the Supreme Court administratively': High Courts are bound by Supreme Court judgments, but they are not administratively subordinate to it. They supervise the district courts in their state (Article 227, 235).
- 'Special leave is an automatic right to appeal': Article 136 is **discretionary**.
- 'The government appoints any judge it wants': appointments follow the collegium's recommendation process.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Search your **district court** on the eCourts services portal or app. Look up the cause list for today: how many cases, which courts, what types. You can also track any case by its CNR number.

lessons.title: Judicial review, the basic structure and PIL

story.title: The case that saved the Constitution

scenes.text: In 1970, Swami Kesavananda Bharati, head of a math in Kerala, challenged land-reform laws affecting the math's property.
The case grew into the biggest question of all: can Parliament amend any part of the Constitution, even to destroy democracy?
In 1973, a 13-judge bench, the largest ever, ruled 7 to 6: Parliament can amend any provision, but not destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
Fifty years later, students like Neha in Kochi still study it. 'He lost his property case,' she says, 'but every Indian won.'

steps.title: Judicial review
steps.body:
**Judicial review** is the power of courts to check whether a **law** or an **executive action** is consistent with the Constitution, and to strike it down if not.

- **Article 13**: any law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
- **Articles 32 and 226** give the Supreme Court and High Courts power to enforce rights.

A law can be struck down if it: violates Fundamental Rights; was made by a legislature without power over the subject (federal division); or violates other constitutional provisions. Courts also review **executive action** for illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety and proportionality.

steps.title: The basic structure doctrine
steps.body:
- **Shankari Prasad (1951)** and **Sajjan Singh (1965)**: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights.
- **Golaknath (1967)**: Parliament **cannot** amend Fundamental Rights.
- **24th Amendment (1971)**: Parliament asserted its power to amend any part.
- **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**: Parliament can amend any part, **but not the basic structure**.
- **Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975)**: free and fair elections are part of the basic structure.
- **Minerva Mills (1980)**: limited amending power and judicial review are themselves basic features.
- **I. R. Coelho (2007)**: laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 can be reviewed against the basic structure.

Features courts have identified include: supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic government, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, rule of law, free and fair elections, and the essence of Fundamental Rights. The list is **not closed**; courts decide case by case.

steps.title: Public Interest Litigation (PIL)
steps.body:
Traditionally only a person whose own right was hurt could go to court (**locus standi**). From the late 1970s, the Supreme Court relaxed this so that any public-spirited person could approach it for those unable to do so (poor, imprisoned, illiterate).

Landmarks:

- **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**: thousands of undertrials in Bihar who had spent longer in jail than their possible sentence were released; speedy trial became part of Article 21.
- **S. P. Gupta (1981)**: broadened standing.
- **M. C. Mehta** cases: environment, including pollution control and the Ganga.
- **Vishaka (1997)**: guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace, later replaced by the POSH Act 2013.

Courts also warn against **frivolous PILs** filed for publicity or private gain, and can impose costs.

steps.title: Activism vs restraint
steps.body:
**Judicial activism**: courts actively protect rights and fill gaps (e.g., Vishaka guidelines when there was no law).

**Judicial restraint**: courts respect the choices of elected bodies on policy, intervening only when the Constitution is violated.

A healthy democracy needs both: courts that protect rights firmly, while leaving policy-making to Parliament and governments. Ask in each case: *Is a right being violated, or does the court simply prefer a different policy?*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Kesavananda Bharati won his case': the property claims largely failed; the lasting result was the basic structure doctrine.
- 'The basic structure is a written list in the Constitution': it is a **judge-made doctrine**.
- 'Courts can strike down a law because it is unwise': they strike down laws only for **unconstitutionality**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a one-paragraph PIL idea for a real problem in your area (e.g., a dangerous open drain near a school). Who is affected? Which right (Article 21?) and which authority's duty is involved?

lessons.title: Federalism: sharing power between the Union and the States

scenes.text: During a disease outbreak, Dr Leela, a district health officer in Odisha, receives orders from both the state health department and the Union government.
Her nephew Kabir asks, 'Who is actually in charge?'

Dr Leela explains: public health and hospitals are on the State List; but 'prevention of infectious diseases spreading from one state to another' is on the Concurrent List, and disaster management laws give the Union a coordinating role.
'So it is teamwork with rules,' Kabir says. 'That is federalism.'

steps.title: A 'Union of States'
steps.body:
**Article 1**: 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a **Union of States**.' India is federal (two levels of government, a written constitution, division of powers, an independent judiciary), but with a **strong Centre**: single citizenship, a single Constitution, all-India services, emergency powers and Parliament's power to reorganise states (Article 3). Scholars often call it **quasi-federal** or **cooperative federalism**.

Today India has **28 States and 8 Union Territories**. States were reorganised largely on linguistic lines from **1956**.

steps.title: The Seventh Schedule: three lists (Article 246)
steps.body:
- **Union List**: only Parliament legislates. Examples: defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, railways, banking, currency, posts and telecom, citizenship.
- **State List**: normally only States legislate. Examples: **police and public order**, public health and hospitals, agriculture, land, local government, betting and gambling.
- **Concurrent List**: both may legislate. Examples: **criminal law and procedure**, **marriage and divorce**, contracts, forests, **education** (moved here from the State List by the 42nd Amendment, 1976), electricity, trade unions.

**Residuary powers** (subjects in no list) belong to **Parliament** (Article 248), unlike the USA, where residuary powers lie with the states.

steps.title: Worked example: when laws clash (Article 254)
steps.body:
A State makes a law on a Concurrent List subject (say, rules on a type of contract). Parliament later makes a law on the same subject with different rules.

- **General rule**: the **Union law prevails** to the extent of conflict.
- **Exception**: if the State law was **reserved for the President and received assent**, it prevails **in that State**, unless Parliament later makes another law overriding it.

Parliament can also legislate on **State List** subjects: if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution by two-thirds that it is in the national interest (Article 249), during a national emergency (250), if two or more States request it (252), or to implement an international treaty (253).

steps.title: Money, the Governor and President's Rule
steps.body:
- **Finance Commission** (Article 280), every five years, recommends how central taxes are shared with States.
- **GST Council** (Article 279A, 101st Amendment, 2016): chaired by the Union Finance Minister with state finance ministers; the Union has one-third of the voting weight and the States together two-thirds; decisions need a three-fourths majority. A good example of shared decision-making.
- **Governor** (Articles 153–162): appointed by the President, the constitutional head of a State, acting mostly on the advice of the State Council of Ministers.
- **President's Rule** (Article 356): if the constitutional machinery in a State fails, the President may take over its administration. In **S. R. Bommai (1994)** the Supreme Court held that this is subject to **judicial review**, that the majority of a government must be tested **on the floor of the House**, and that federalism and secularism are basic features.

In August 2019, the special status of Jammu and Kashmir under Article 370 was ended and the state was reorganised into two Union Territories; the Supreme Court upheld the change in December 2023.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Police is a Union subject': **police and public order** are State subjects (there are central armed police forces, but local policing is with States).
- 'Criminal law is a State subject': **criminal law and criminal procedure** are on the **Concurrent List**, which is why Parliament could enact BNS, BNSS and BSA for the whole country.
- 'Residuary powers lie with States as in the USA': in India they lie with **Parliament**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take today's newspaper. For three news items (a new bridge, a school exam change, a railway fare), decide whether the subject is Union, State or Concurrent.

lessons.title: Panchayats and municipalities: democracy on your street

scenes.text: In a village in Jharkhand, women walk 2 km for water. At the Gram Sabha, Kamla Devi, elected sarpanch in a seat reserved for women, raises the issue.
Villagers vote in the Gram Sabha to make a water tank the year's top priority in the village development plan.
The panchayat uses its grants, puts the accounts on the notice board and holds a social audit.
The tank is built in eight months. A man who earlier mocked 'a woman sarpanch' now asks her for advice on the next project.

steps.title: The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992)
steps.body:
Article 40 (a Directive Principle) asked the State to organise village panchayats. The **73rd Amendment** (Part IX, **panchayats**) and the **74th Amendment** (Part IXA, **municipalities**) gave local bodies **constitutional status**. They came into force in **1993**; **24 April** is National Panchayati Raj Day.

Key features:

- **Three tiers** of panchayats: village, intermediate (block) and district (states with population under 20 lakh may skip the middle tier).
- **Gram Sabha**: all registered voters of the village; it approves plans, identifies beneficiaries and can hold social audits.
- **Elections every five years**, conducted by the **State Election Commission**; if dissolved early, fresh elections within six months.
- **Reservation** for SCs and STs in proportion to population, and **at least one-third** of seats and chairperson posts for **women** (many states provide 50%).
- A **State Finance Commission** every five years reviews local bodies' finances.
- The **Eleventh Schedule** lists **29** subjects for panchayats; the **Twelfth Schedule** lists **18** for municipalities (like urban planning, water supply, public health, slum improvement).

steps.title: Urban local bodies
steps.body:
- **Municipal Corporation**: large cities, headed by a mayor.
- **Municipal Council**: smaller urban areas.
- **Nagar Panchayat**: areas in transition from rural to urban.

Cities with population of 3 lakh or more must have **ward committees**. Metropolitan areas get a **Metropolitan Planning Committee**, and each district a **District Planning Committee** that consolidates rural and urban plans.

steps.title: PESA and Scheduled Areas
steps.body: The **Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act 1996 (PESA)** extends panchayat provisions to tribal Scheduled Areas with special powers for the Gram Sabha: to safeguard traditions and community resources, be consulted on land acquisition, and manage minor forest produce and village markets.

steps.title: Challenges and how citizens help
steps.body:
- **Proxy rule** ('sarpanch-pati'): male relatives sometimes act for elected women. This defeats the law; officials and Gram Sabhas should insist that the elected person acts.
- **Funds, functions, functionaries**: many states have not fully transferred all three.
- **Low attendance** at Gram Sabhas and ward meetings.

You can: attend your Gram Sabha or ward sabha, ask for the budget and works list, use RTI for details, and join social audits of schemes like MGNREGA.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find out when the next **Gram Sabha** (villages are typically required to hold several each year, including on days like 26 January, 1 May, 15 August and 2 October in many states) or **ward committee meeting** is in your area, and attend with one question ready.

questions.why: The answer is "Is subject to judicial review". Reason: Courts can examine the material on which it is based. The other choices, such as "Is beyond judicial review" and "Is permanent", do not fit the question.

questions.why: Epistolary PIL: letters treated as petitions for those unable to approach courts.

questions.q: Which tier of panchayat may a State with population under 20 lakh choose not to constitute?
questions.why: The answer is "Intermediate (block)". Reason: Article 243B(2). The other choices, such as "Gram Sabha" and "Village", do not fit the question. (Question: Which tier of panchayat may a State with population under 20 lakh choose not to constitute?)

questions.why: The US Tenth Amendment reserves powers not delegated to the states or the people.

courses.summary: Two of the most useful laws an ordinary person can use without a lawyer: the Consumer Protection Act 2019 (defective goods, poor service, misleading ads, online shopping) and the Right to Information Act 2005 (getting answers from government). lessons.title: Your rights as a consumer

scenes.text: Lakshmi in Coimbatore buys a washing machine for ₹28,000 with a two-year warranty. In the third month it starts leaking.
The technician visits four times, changes a pipe, and the leak returns. The company says, 'Warranty doesn't cover water damage.'
Her son Vivek reads that a product with a manufacturing defect and repeated failed repairs can be a 'defect' and the company's response a 'deficiency in service'.
Lakshmi decides to act, calmly and in writing. 'I paid for a working machine,' she says. 'The law is on my side.'

steps.title: The Consumer Protection Act 2019
steps.body:
The **Consumer Protection Act 2019** replaced the 1986 Act and came into force in **July 2020**. It covers **goods and services**, bought **offline or online**, including through teleshopping and multi-level marketing.

You are a **consumer** if you buy goods or hire services **for consideration** (money paid or promised) for your own use, not for resale or commercial purposes. Buying something to earn a livelihood by **self-employment** (like an autorickshaw for yourself) still counts.

steps.title: Six consumer rights
steps.body:
- **Right to safety**: protection against hazardous goods and services.
- **Right to be informed**: about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price.
- **Right to choose**: access to a variety of goods at competitive prices.
- **Right to be heard**: your interests will be considered at appropriate forums.
- **Right to seek redressal**: against unfair trade practices and exploitation.
- **Right to consumer awareness.**

steps.title: What you can complain about
steps.body:
- **Defect** in goods: any fault, imperfection or shortcoming in quality, quantity, potency, purity or standard.
- **Deficiency** in service: any fault or inadequacy in quality, nature or manner of performance (a bank wrongly charging you, a builder delaying possession, a courier losing a parcel).
- **Unfair trade practice**: false claims, misleading ads, not issuing a bill, refusing to take back defective goods within the stated period, disclosing your personal information given in confidence.
- **Restrictive trade practice**: forcing you to buy something else as a condition (tied selling).
- **Overcharging**: charging more than the **MRP** on packaged goods, or more than the displayed price.
- **Hazardous goods or services**, and **product liability**: the manufacturer, seller or service provider can be liable for harm caused by a defective product.

steps.title: Everyday examples
steps.body:
- A shop refuses to give a bill: you are entitled to a bill or cash memo.
- A cinema charges more than MRP for a bottle of water: overcharging is illegal under the Legal Metrology rules for pre-packaged goods.
- A restaurant adds a 'service charge' to the bill by default: the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2022 guidelines say service charge **cannot be added automatically**; it is **voluntary**.
- An app sells a 'new' phone that turns out to be refurbished: misrepresentation, an unfair trade practice.
- **E-commerce**: under the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020, platforms must display seller details and have a **grievance officer** who acknowledges complaints within 48 hours and resolves them within one month.
- **Misleading ads**: the **Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA)** can order ads withdrawn and impose penalties, including on endorsers who did not take due care.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not keeping the **bill, warranty card, screenshots and emails**. Evidence wins cases.
- Accepting 'no bill, cheaper price': you lose proof and warranty.
- Thinking free services are covered: a service given entirely free (with no consideration at all) is generally not a 'service' under the Act; but services paid for indirectly (like an insurance policy or a paid hospital) are.
- Buying for business resale and then filing as a 'consumer'.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Create a folder (paper or phone) called **'Bills and warranties'**. Add your last three big purchases with bill, warranty and a photo of the product's serial number.

lessons.title: How to file a consumer complaint, step by step

scenes.text: Lakshmi emails the company's customer care with her bill, warranty and photos, asking for a replacement within 15 days.
No reply. She calls the National Consumer Helpline 1915, which forwards her complaint to the company. The company offers another 'repair'.
She files a complaint on the e-Daakhil portal in the District Commission, Coimbatore. No lawyer, no fee for her claim size.
Five months later, the Commission orders a replacement plus ₹5,000 compensation and ₹3,000 costs. 'Patience and paper,' Lakshmi smiles.

steps.title: The ladder: start small, then go formal
steps.body:
1. **Talk to the seller/service provider** and write it down: email or registered letter with bill number, problem, what you want (repair/replacement/refund) and a deadline (e.g., 15 days).
2. **National Consumer Helpline (NCH)**: call **1915** or use the NCH app/website or WhatsApp. NCH sends your complaint to the company. Many cases end here.
3. **Legal notice** (optional but useful): a short letter stating facts and warning of a complaint before the Consumer Commission.
4. **File a complaint** before the right **Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission**, online via **e-Daakhil** or in person.
5. **Mediation**: the Commission may refer the case to mediation if both sides agree.
6. **Hearing and order**. If you disagree, **appeal** to the higher Commission within the time allowed (generally 45 days for an appeal from the District to the State Commission).

steps.title: Which Commission? (pecuniary jurisdiction)
steps.body:
The level depends on the **value of goods or services paid** (not the compensation you claim). Under the limits revised by rules in **2021**:

- **District Commission**: up to **₹50 lakh**
- **State Commission**: above ₹50 lakh up to **₹2 crore**
- **National Commission** (New Delhi): above **₹2 crore**

**Where**: you may file where the opposite party works **or where you live or work** (a big improvement of the 2019 Act).

**When**: within **two years** from the date the problem arose (Section 69). Delay can be excused only for sufficient cause, so do not wait.

**Fee**: currently **no fee** for claims up to ₹5 lakh; small fees above that. Check the current limits and fees on the official portal before filing.

steps.title: Template: a simple complaint
steps.body:
**Before the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, [District]**

**Complainant**: name, address, phone, email.
**Opposite parties**: (1) manufacturer, (2) seller/dealer, with addresses.

**Facts** (numbered): date of purchase, price, bill number; what went wrong; dates of complaints and repair visits; their replies.

**Deficiency/defect**: explain in one paragraph why this is a defect/deficiency/unfair trade practice.

**Reliefs sought**: replacement or refund of ₹___; compensation of ₹___ for harassment; litigation costs ₹___.

**Documents**: bill, warranty, emails, job cards, photos.

**Verification and signature.**

Keep it short, factual and polite. Commissions are designed for ordinary people; you do **not** need a lawyer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming a huge, unrealistic compensation: it does not change the court level (value paid decides), and it hurts credibility.
- Missing the **two-year** limit while 'waiting for the company'.
- No evidence of complaints: always **email or write**, and note complaint ticket numbers.
- Suing only the seller when the defect is a manufacturing one: name **both manufacturer and seller**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of a real consumer problem you or your family had. Write a **complaint email** to the company using the ladder: facts, what you want, deadline. Save it as a template.

lessons.title: RTI: asking the government for information

story.title: Where did the road money go?

scenes.text: In a town in Madhya Pradesh, the road outside Mohammed Irfan's shop has been 'repaired' three times in two years. Potholes return each monsoon.
Irfan writes a one-page RTI to the municipal council asking for work orders, amounts paid, contractor names and quality-inspection reports.
On day 27 he receives copies showing ₹38 lakh paid, but no quality inspection was ever done.
He shares the documents at the ward meeting. The council blacklists the contractor and orders an inspection before payment in future.

steps.title: The Right to Information Act 2005
steps.body:
The **RTI Act** (in force from **12 October 2005**) lets every **citizen** ask any **public authority** for information it holds. Courts treat it as part of the freedom of speech and expression (Article 19(1)(a)).

**'Information'** includes records, documents, emails, opinions, advice, reports, log books, contracts, samples, and electronic data. You may also **inspect files** and take certified copies.

**Public authorities**: government departments, ministries, municipalities, panchayats, public sector companies, government schools and hospitals, and bodies **substantially financed** by government. Purely private companies are not public authorities, though you can sometimes get their information through the regulator that oversees them.

steps.title: How to write an RTI application
steps.body:
1. Address it to the **Public Information Officer (PIO)** of the department (e.g., 'PIO, Office of the Municipal Commissioner, ___').
2. Write: 'Application under Section 6(1) of the RTI Act, 2005.'
3. Ask **clear, specific, numbered** questions about records. Good: *'Provide copies of work orders and payment vouchers for repair of X Road between 1 April 2024 and 31 March 2025.'* Bad: *'Why is the road bad?'*
4. **You need not give any reason** for asking (Section 6(2)), only contact details.
5. Pay the **fee**: ₹10 for central government bodies (by postal order, demand draft, court-fee stamp or online); states set their own fees. **People below the poverty line pay no fee** (attach proof).
6. Send by registered post or hand it in and get a receipt; for central bodies (and many states), you can file **online** on the official RTI portal.
7. Keep a copy and the proof of sending.

steps.title: Time limits
steps.body:
- **30 days** from receipt by the PIO: normal deadline.
- **48 hours**: if the information concerns the **life or liberty** of a person.
- **35 days**: if filed through an Assistant PIO.
- **40 days**: if third-party information is involved.
- If the PIO does not reply in time, it is treated as a **refusal**, and the information must then be given **free of charge** (Section 7(6)).
- Copying charges are small (for example ₹2 per page under the central rules).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Asking 'why' or for opinions not on record: the PIO gives **existing records**, not explanations created for you.
- Asking vague or very broad questions ('all files since 1990'): you may be asked for big fees or refused for diverting resources.
- Sending it to the wrong office: the PIO must transfer it within 5 days, but delays grow.
- Losing proof of filing, which you need for appeals.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Draft an RTI (do not send yet) on something that matters to you: attendance of doctors in your local PHC, money spent on a park, status of your passport file, or your own exam answer sheet (many bodies allow inspection of evaluated answer sheets).

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

lessons.title: RTI appeals, exemptions and using RTI wisely

scenes.text: Anjali, a nursing student in Shillong, has not received her state scholarship for a year. Her RTI asking for the status of her file gets no reply.
She files a first appeal to the First Appellate Authority, a senior officer in the same department.
Within weeks she receives file notings showing her application was stuck for a missing signature that no one told her about.
She submits the signature. The scholarship arrives in a month. 'RTI did what ten visits couldn't,' she says.

steps.title: First appeal and second appeal
steps.body:
**First appeal** (Section 19(1)): if you get **no reply**, a **refusal**, **incomplete** information, or excessive fees, appeal within **30 days** to the **First Appellate Authority (FAA)**, an officer senior to the PIO in the same public authority. There is usually **no fee** for central first appeals. The FAA should decide within **30 days** (up to 45 days with reasons).

**Second appeal** (Section 19(3)): if still unsatisfied, appeal within **90 days** to the **Central Information Commission** (for central bodies) or the **State Information Commission**. You may also file a **complaint** (Section 18) for problems like no PIO being appointed or refusal to accept your application.

The Commission can order disclosure, compensation to you, and impose a **penalty on the PIO** of **₹250 per day** of delay, up to **₹25,000** (Section 20).

steps.title: What can be refused? (Section 8 and others)
What ordinary people have used RTI for
steps.body:
- Tracking stuck **passports, pensions, scholarships, ration cards** and tax refunds.
- Getting **copies of one's own evaluated answer sheets** (the Supreme Court held in 2011 that examinees can access their evaluated answer books).
- Checking **ration shop stock** registers and **MGNREGA muster rolls** during social audits.
- Exposing fake bills in public works.

Most public authorities must also **proactively publish** basic information (Section 4): budgets, functions, officials, decision-making norms. Check the department's website before filing.

steps.title: Stay safe and fair
steps.body:
- RTI is powerful; some activists exposing big corruption have faced threats. For sensitive matters, file through a group, share information publicly once received, and report threats to the police (112).
- Do not use RTI to harass officials with dozens of repetitive applications; Commissions can decline such requests.
- Use it for **your own records** too: your service book, your FIR status, your land records.

lessons.title: Renting a home: tenant and landlord basics

scenes.text: Nikhil from Patna and his colleague Chloe from Shillong rent a 2BHK in Bengaluru. The broker hands them a 'standard' 11-month agreement.
Chloe reads it fully and finds: a 10-month deposit, a lock-in of 11 months, and a clause that the owner may enter 'at any time'.
They negotiate politely: a smaller deposit, a 3-month lock-in, and 24-hour notice before visits. The owner agrees and they both sign every page.
On moving day they take a dated video of every room. A year later, when the owner claims damage, the video settles it and the deposit is returned.

steps.title: Why the agreement matters
steps.body:
Renting is a **contract**. The written agreement is your main protection. Two common forms:

- **Lease** (a transfer of a right to enjoy property for a term, under the Transfer of Property Act 1882).
- **Leave and licence**: permission to use the premises without creating a tenancy interest; common in cities like Mumbai.

Rent control and tenancy laws are mostly **state laws**, so rules differ by state. The Union government's **Model Tenancy Act 2021** is a model that states may adopt or adapt; it proposes, for example, a security deposit cap of **two months' rent** for residential premises and a separate Rent Authority for disputes. Check whether your state has adopted it.

steps.title: Registration and stamp duty
steps.body:
- Under the **Registration Act 1908**, a lease of immovable property for **more than one year** (or year to year) must be **registered**. This is why many agreements are for **11 months**.
- Some states, such as Maharashtra, require registration of leave-and-licence agreements regardless of duration; many states offer online registration.
- **Stamp duty** must be paid as per your state's Stamp Act, even on 11-month agreements. An unstamped agreement may not be admissible as evidence until the duty and penalty are paid.
- Many cities require **police verification** of tenants; the landlord usually submits it, often online.

steps.title: Checklist of clauses
steps.body:
- Names, addresses and ID of both parties; property address and what is included (fans, beds, appliances).
- **Rent**, due date, mode of payment, and annual increase (if any).
- **Security deposit** amount and **when and how it will be refunded**, with what deductions allowed (only for unpaid dues or damage beyond normal wear and tear).
- **Duration**, **lock-in** period, and **notice period** for either side.
- Who pays **electricity, water, maintenance, society charges**.
- **Repairs**: who handles major structural repairs vs minor repairs.
- **Entry**: landlord's visits with prior notice.
- **Sub-letting**: usually not without consent.
- **Inventory list** signed by both, with photos/video.

steps.title: What a landlord generally cannot do
steps.body:
- **Throw you out by force**, lock you out or remove your belongings: eviction must follow the agreement and the legal process (notice, and if disputed, a court or rent authority order).
- **Cut water or electricity** to force you out: many state rent laws prohibit this, and the Model Tenancy Act also prohibits withholding essential supplies.
- **Keep the deposit without reason.**

And what a tenant must not do: stop paying rent, damage property, sub-let without consent, or overstay after the agreement ends and notice is given.

**Discrimination**: refusing tenants for their religion, caste, food habits or marital status is widespread; some housing societies' rules have been challenged, but the law here is still evolving. Document it and seek advice.

steps.title: Money tips
steps.body:
- Pay rent by **bank transfer/UPI** with a note, not cash, and ask for **rent receipts** (salaried people need them for HRA tax claims; if annual rent is above a threshold, the landlord's PAN is generally required).
- Never pay a large 'token amount' before seeing original ownership documents and the owner's ID. Fake listings are a common scam.

lessons.title: On the road: licences, rules, penalties and accidents

scenes.text: Kunal, 16, in Jaipur, borrows his father's 110cc scooter to reach tuition fast. No licence, no helmet.

At a checkpoint the police stop him. Because he is a juvenile driving without a licence, the law can hold the vehicle's owner, his father, responsible with a heavy fine, and the registration can be cancelled.
His father, Mr Sharma, is shocked. 'I thought it was just a small challan.'
Kunal takes the bus until he is 18. At 18 he gets his learner's licence, takes lessons and passes the test, and always wears a helmet.

steps.title: Licences and documents
steps.body:
Under the **Motor Vehicles Act 1988** (major amendment in **2019**):

- **Age**: 16 for a gearless two-wheeler up to 50cc engine capacity (with a parent/guardian's consent); **18** for cars and most motorcycles and scooters.
- **Process**: learner's licence (test on rules and signs) → practise with an L-sign and a licensed driver → driving test → **driving licence (DL)**. Apply online through the Parivahan Sarathi portal.
- **Carry** (physically or digitally via **DigiLocker or mParivahan**, which are accepted): driving licence, **registration certificate (RC)**, **insurance** certificate, and **Pollution Under Control (PUC)** certificate.
- **Third-party insurance is compulsory** (Section 146). It pays for injury or death of others and their property damage caused by your vehicle.

steps.title: Key safety rules
steps.body:
- **Helmets** for the rider and the pillion on two-wheelers (Section 129). A helmet must meet the BIS standard and be **fastened**.
- **Seatbelts** for all occupants, including the rear seat.
- **Children**: the law requires protective measures for children on two-wheelers, including helmets and safety harnesses for young children, under rules made after the 2019 amendment.
- **No mobile phone** handheld use while driving.
- **Drunk driving** (Section 185): the limit is **30 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood** (breath analyser). It carries a fine and/or imprisonment, higher for repeat offences, and licence suspension.
- **Speeding, red-light jumping, wrong-side driving, triple riding, no number plate** are all offences; challans are increasingly issued electronically using cameras (**e-challan**).

The 2019 amendment sharply increased fines. **Exact amounts** can vary because states may set compounding amounts; check your state transport department.

steps.title: Underage driving (Section 199A)
steps.body:
If a **juvenile** (under 18) commits an offence under the MV Act, the **guardian or vehicle owner is deemed guilty** unless they prove it happened without their knowledge or that they took care to prevent it. Consequences include a **large fine and possible imprisonment** for the guardian/owner, **cancellation of the vehicle's registration for a year**, and the juvenile becoming **ineligible for a licence until age 25**. The juvenile is dealt with under the Juvenile Justice Act.

Parents: handing your keys to a 15-year-old is not a favour; it is a serious legal risk for you and a life risk for them.

steps.title: At an accident: what to do
steps.body:
1. **Stay safe**: park away, switch on hazard lights.
2. Call **112** (or **108** ambulance in most states). Give the exact location.
3. Help the injured **without moving them** unless there is fire or danger; do not remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless needed for breathing.
4. **Good Samaritan protection** (Section 134A, added 2019): a person who helps an accident victim in good faith is **not liable** in any civil or criminal action for injury or death of the victim caused by negligence while helping. Guidelines say Good Samaritans **cannot be forced to reveal identity** or be detained, and hospitals must not demand payment before giving emergency care to victims.
5. If you are the **driver**, you must **take the injured to a hospital** (or ensure medical help) and **report to the police** as soon as possible (Section 134).
6. Compensation for victims is claimed before the **Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT)**; causing death by a rash or negligent act is an offence under the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) Section 106**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Helmet is only for long rides': most head injuries happen close to home at low speed.
- 'A half-face cap is fine': it must be a **BIS-certified**, properly fastened helmet.
- 'Insurance has lapsed but I'll renew next month': driving without valid third-party insurance is an offence, and you could be personally liable for huge damages.
- 'Paying a cop on the spot is faster': pay challans only through official modes and get a receipt.

steps.body: Check your family vehicles today: RC, insurance expiry, PUC validity. Add them to DigiLocker or mParivahan. Set a reminder a month before insurance and PUC expire.

lessons.title: Cyber fraud and identity theft: the law and how to report

scenes.text: Mrs Gomes, a retired teacher in Goa, gets a video call from a man in police uniform: 'A parcel in your name has drugs. You are under digital arrest. Do not disconnect.'
For hours they keep her on camera and demand she transfer her savings to a 'verification account'.
Her grandson Dev walks in, sees the screen and cuts the call. 'Aaji, there is no such thing as digital arrest. Real police never ask for money on video calls.'
They call 1930 immediately and report on cybercrime.gov.in. She had not transferred anything. They warn their whole building.

steps.title: The laws that apply
steps.body:
**Information Technology Act 2000** (amended 2008), with key provisions:

- **Section 43 + 66**: unauthorised access, data theft, introducing viruses; dishonest or fraudulent acts are offences.
- **Section 66C**: **identity theft**, fraudulent use of someone's password, electronic signature or other unique identification.
- **Section 66D**: **cheating by personation** using a computer resource (fake profiles, fake customer care).
- **Section 66E**: capturing or sharing images of a person's private areas **without consent**.
- **Sections 67, 67A, 67B**: publishing or transmitting obscene, sexually explicit, and child sexual abuse material (the last is also a serious POCSO offence).
- **Section 72**: breach of confidentiality by those with lawful access.

The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023**, in force from 1 July 2024, also applies: **cheating (Section 318)**, **extortion (Section 308)**, **criminal intimidation (Section 351)**, **stalking including monitoring a person's online activity (Section 78)**, **voyeurism (Section 77)**, **defamation (Section 356)**, and **organised crime (Section 111)**, which expressly covers cyber-crimes by organised gangs.

steps.title: Common frauds and their tell-tale signs
steps.body:
- **'Digital arrest'**: fake police/CBI/customs on video call. **No Indian agency arrests anyone over video call or asks for money to 'verify'.**
- **KYC/bank/electricity cut-off SMS** with a link or an app to install.
- **UPI 'collect request'** posing as a payment to you: **you never need to enter your PIN to receive money**.
- **Part-time job / task scams**: 'like videos and earn', then 'invest to unlock earnings'.
- **Investment and trading groups** promising sure-shot returns.
- **Sextortion**: a stranger video-calls, records, and threatens to share morphed or real images unless paid.
- **Fake customer care numbers** from search results.
- **SIM-swap**: your phone suddenly loses network; someone has your number.

Common thread: **urgency + fear or greed + secrecy + payment.**

steps.title: If money is lost: the golden hour
steps.body:
1. **Call 1930** (National Cyber Crime Helpline) immediately, or report at **cybercrime.gov.in**. Quick reporting lets banks **freeze** money moving through mule accounts.
2. Call your **bank**/UPI app to block cards, UPI and net banking.
3. **Save evidence**: screenshots, phone numbers, UPI IDs, transaction IDs, chat links. Do not delete chats.
4. You get an acknowledgement number; follow up with the local **cyber cell** or police station. You can also ask for an FIR; under the BNSS, a **Zero FIR** or **e-FIR** can be registered regardless of where the crime happened.
5. Report fraud calls or messages on the **Sanchar Saathi** portal (Chakshu) and block numbers.

RBI rules limit a customer's liability for unauthorised electronic transactions when reported promptly (zero liability in many cases if reported within three working days and the fault is not yours). Report fast.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sharing an **OTP** 'just to cancel' a transaction.
- Installing **screen-sharing apps** at a caller's request.
- Paying a sextortionist: payment usually leads to more demands. Stop contact, preserve evidence, report.
- Lending your bank account or SIM to a 'friend': **money-mule** accounts are prosecuted.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Today: switch on **two-factor authentication** for email and WhatsApp, set a UPI transaction limit, save **1930** in your phone and your parents' phones, and tell them about 'digital arrest' scams.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

lessons.title: Online harassment, image misuse and your data

scenes.text: Simran, 19, a college student in Ludhiana, finds a fake profile using her photos and a morphed picture, sending messages to her classmates.
She feels ashamed and wants to delete all her accounts. Her friend Grace says, 'You did nothing wrong. The person who did this broke the law.'
They screenshot everything with dates and links, report the profile to the platform as impersonation and non-consensual imagery, and file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in.
The platform removes the content within a day. Police trace the account to an ex-classmate, who is charged. Simran keeps her accounts and learns her privacy settings.

steps.title: What the law prohibits
steps.body:
- **Sexual harassment** including unwelcome sexually coloured remarks or showing pornography against a woman's will: **BNS Section 75**.
- **Voyeurism**: watching or capturing images of a woman in a private act or sharing them: **BNS Section 77**.
- **Stalking** including repeated unwanted contact and monitoring online activity: **BNS Section 78**.
- **Privacy violation**: capturing/sharing private-area images without consent: **IT Act Section 66E** (gender-neutral).
- **Publishing obscene or sexually explicit material**: IT Act **Sections 67 and 67A**.
- **Criminal intimidation** and **extortion** (threats to leak images for money): **BNS Sections 351 and 308**.
- **Defamation**: **BNS Section 356**.
- **Anything involving a person under 18** is also covered by **POCSO** and IT Act **Section 67B**, with very strict penalties, even if the child 'agreed'.

steps.title: Platforms must act fast
steps.body:
Under the **IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021**, social-media platforms must:

- have a **Grievance Officer** in India, acknowledge complaints within **24 hours** and resolve within a set time (generally 15 days);
- **remove within 24 hours** content that exposes a person's private area, shows nudity or sexual acts, or is an **impersonation including morphed images**, on complaint by the person or someone on their behalf.

If the platform does not act, you can appeal to the government's **Grievance Appellate Committee** online, and still pursue a police complaint.

steps.title: Step-by-step response plan
steps.body:
1. **Do not engage or pay** the harasser. Do not threaten them back.
2. **Preserve evidence**: screenshots with date/time, profile URLs, usernames, phone numbers, emails. Ask a trusted friend to help.
3. **Report on the platform**: use 'impersonation', 'non-consensual intimate imagery' or 'harassment' categories.
4. **Report to police**: on **cybercrime.gov.in** (there is a category for women/child-related crimes, and you may report anonymously for some content), or at any police station; a **Zero FIR** can be registered anywhere.
5. **Hash-blocking tools** such as StopNCII.org (for adults) can help prevent re-uploads on participating platforms without you sharing the image itself.
6. **Take care of yourself**: talk to someone you trust. Tele-MANAS **14416** offers free mental-health support. Women in distress: **181**.

steps.title: Your data rights in India
steps.body:
The **Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 (DPDP Act)** gives individuals ('data principals') rights over their digital personal data held by organisations ('data fiduciaries'): to get information about processing, to **correct and erase** data, to **withdraw consent**, to grievance redressal, and to nominate someone to exercise rights after death or incapacity. Processing children's (under 18) data needs **verifiable parental consent**. A **Data Protection Board of India** handles breaches and penalties. Its rules are being brought into force in phases, so check the current status.

The **right to privacy** is a Fundamental Right (Puttaswamy, 2017).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Blaming the victim ('why did you post photos?'). The **offender** is responsible.
- Deleting chats out of panic, which destroys evidence.
- Forwarding the harmful content 'to warn others': forwarding can itself be an offence and spreads harm.
- Thinking anonymous accounts can't be traced: police can obtain account data from platforms through legal process.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do a 10-minute **privacy check-up**: make your profile photo visible only to contacts, turn off location in photos, review who can add you to groups, and remove old public posts with personal details.

activity.prompt: Questions people hesitate to ask

items.q: Someone is threatening to post my private photo unless I pay. Should I pay?
items.a: No. Payment usually leads to more demands. Stop responding, keep the evidence (screenshots, usernames, payment requests), report on the platform and at cybercrime.gov.in or 1930, and tell someone you trust. Extortion and sharing private images are crimes; you are the victim.

items.q: I shared a photo willingly with my partner. Can they post it after a breakup?
items.a: No. Consent to share privately is not consent to publish. Publishing private images without consent can be an offence under the IT Act and BNS, and platforms must remove such content within 24 hours of your complaint.

items.q: I am under 18 and someone has my image. Will I get in trouble?
items.a: The law treats you as a child in need of protection. Tell a trusted adult or call 1098 (Childline). Anyone who possesses, shares or threatens with images of a minor commits a serious offence under POCSO and the IT Act.

items.q: Do I need to go to the police station in my own city?
items.a: No. You can report online at cybercrime.gov.in, or at any police station, which must register a Zero FIR for a cognizable offence and transfer it to the right station.
For content involving child sexual abuse material and some sexual content, the national portal allows anonymous reporting. For crimes against you personally, a named complaint lets police act faster.

items.q: Will my name be published if I complain?
items.a: The law protects the identity of victims of sexual offences; disclosing it is itself an offence under the BNS (Section 72).

lessons.title: Marriage laws in India: who is governed by what

scenes.text: Ayaan (Muslim, from Lucknow) and Tara (Hindu, from Kolkata), both 27, want to marry without either converting.
Their relatives argue: 'Do a nikah!' 'No, do pheras!' Tara asks, 'Is there a law where neither of us changes religion?'
A lawyer explains the Special Marriage Act 1954: give notice to the Marriage Officer, wait 30 days, then marry before three witnesses.
They register under the Act and also hold both families' ceremonies for joy. Their marriage certificate is their legal proof.

steps.title: Personal laws plus one secular law
steps.body:
Marriage and divorce are on the **Concurrent List**. India has several **personal laws** based on religion, plus a **secular** option:

- **Hindu Marriage Act 1955**: Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs.
- **Muslim personal law** (largely uncodified, applied through the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937; plus the Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act 1939 and the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019).
- **Indian Christian Marriage Act 1872** and **Divorce Act 1869**: Christians.
- **Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936**: Parsis.
- **Special Marriage Act 1954**: **any two persons**, of the same or different religions, without conversion.

Goa has its own civil code dating to the Portuguese era, and **Uttarakhand** enacted a Uniform Civil Code in 2024. Article 44 (a Directive Principle) asks the State to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code across India; this remains a subject of public debate.

steps.title: Conditions for a valid marriage (overview)
steps.body:
**Minimum age**: **21 for the groom, 18 for the bride** (Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 and the HMA/SMA). A child marriage is **voidable** at the option of the party who was a child (petition within two years of attaining majority), and those who perform or promote it can be punished. Report child marriages to **1098** or the Child Marriage Prohibition Officer.

**Monogamy**: under the HMA, SMA, Christian and Parsi laws, neither party may have a living spouse. A second marriage during the first is **void** and **bigamy** is an offence under the BNS (Section 82).

**Free consent** and capacity to consent (soundness of mind).

**Prohibited relationships**: close relatives cannot marry (the HMA allows exceptions where a custom permits).

**Muslim marriage (nikah)** is a civil contract requiring offer and acceptance, witnesses as per the school of law, and **mahr** (dower), which is the wife's right.

steps.title: Registration: why it matters
steps.body:
The Supreme Court in **Seema v Ashwani Kumar (2006)** directed that marriages of all religions be **registered**, and many states have compulsory registration laws.

A **marriage certificate** helps with passports, visas, bank nominations, insurance claims, property, maintenance and inheritance, and protects women and children from denial of marriage.

**Special Marriage Act process**:

1. Notice to the Marriage Officer of the district where at least one party has lived for **30 days**.
2. The notice is displayed; **objections** may be made within 30 days on legal grounds only (age, existing spouse, etc.).
3. Solemnisation before the Marriage Officer and **three witnesses**; the certificate is entered in the Marriage Certificate Book.

A marriage already held under religious rites (for example a Hindu wedding) can usually be registered under that law's rules too.

steps.title: Common myths
steps.body:
- 'A court marriage is a separate law': people usually mean marriage under the **Special Marriage Act** (or registration of a religious marriage).
- 'Adults need parents' permission to marry': **adults of marriageable age can marry by their own choice**; the Supreme Court has repeatedly protected this choice (e.g., Shafin Jahan, 2018; Lata Singh, 2006). Couples facing threats can seek police protection.
- 'Instant triple talaq ends a marriage': the Supreme Court held it invalid in **Shayara Bano (2017)**, and the **2019 Act** made pronouncing it **void and a punishable offence**.
- 'Live-in relationships are illegal': adults in a live-in relationship are not committing a crime, and a woman in a 'relationship in the nature of marriage' is protected by the Domestic Violence Act 2005.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Check whether your parents' or your own marriage is registered. If not, find your state's marriage-registration rules and the documents needed.

lessons.title: Divorce, maintenance and child custody

scenes.text: Rohan and Sneha in Pune have lived separately for 14 months. They agree the marriage is over but want to stay respectful for their son Aarush, 6.
They file a joint petition for divorce by mutual consent in the Family Court, with a settlement on maintenance, Sneha's jewellery and Aarush's custody and visitation.
Because they had already lived apart over a year and settled everything, the court considers waiving the six-month waiting period.
The decree is passed. Aarush lives with Sneha and spends weekends and half the holidays with Rohan. Both parents attend his school play.

steps.title: Ways a marriage can end (Hindu Marriage Act as the main example)
steps.body:
**Contested divorce** (Section 13): one spouse proves a ground, such as **cruelty** (physical or mental), **desertion** for at least two years, **adultery**, conversion to another religion, serious incurable mental disorder, renunciation of the world, or not being heard of as alive for seven years. Wives have some additional grounds.

**Divorce by mutual consent** (Section 13B):

1. The couple has lived **separately for one year or more**, cannot live together, and agree to divorce.
2. **First motion**: a joint petition before the **Family Court**.
3. **Second motion**: not earlier than **six months** (and within 18 months) after the first. The Supreme Court held in **Amardeep Singh (2017)** that this six-month period can be **waived** in suitable cases.
4. **Decree of divorce.**

The Supreme Court itself may dissolve a marriage on **irretrievable breakdown** using its special power under Article 142 (Shilpa Sailesh, 2023); lower courts do not have this power.

Other laws (Special Marriage Act, Divorce Act, Parsi Act, Muslim law including **khula** and the 1939 Act) have their own grounds and procedures.

steps.title: Maintenance: several routes
steps.body:
- **BNSS Section 144** (earlier CrPC Section 125): a **secular, quick remedy** for a wife (including a divorced wife who has not remarried), **children**, and **parents** who cannot maintain themselves, against a person with sufficient means who neglects them. It applies **regardless of religion**; in 2024 the Supreme Court reaffirmed that a divorced Muslim woman can also claim under this provision.
- **Hindu Marriage Act Sections 24 and 25**: interim maintenance and litigation costs during the case, and permanent alimony.
- **Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act 1956**: wife, children, aged parents.
- **Domestic Violence Act 2005**: monetary relief as part of protection.
- **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007**: tribunals can order children/relatives to pay maintenance (currently up to ₹10,000 a month) to parents and senior citizens.

Courts consider income, needs, standard of living and the number of dependants. The Supreme Court has required **both spouses to file affidavits disclosing assets and liabilities** in maintenance cases (Rajnesh v Neha, 2020).

steps.title: Child custody: the welfare principle
steps.body:
In every custody case, the court's **paramount consideration is the welfare of the child**, not the rights of the parents.

- **Laws**: the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act 1956, and the courts' wider powers.
- Custody of a child **below five years** is ordinarily with the **mother** under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, unless the child's welfare requires otherwise.
- Courts consider the child's age, wishes (if old enough), stability, schooling, health, each parent's ability to care, and siblings.
- **Visitation** (access) for the other parent is usually given. **Joint or shared parenting** arrangements are increasingly accepted.
- In **Gita Hariharan (1999)**, the Supreme Court held that the mother can also act as natural guardian in appropriate circumstances.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Moving out and not keeping records of **expenses, income and children's needs**: evidence matters in maintenance cases.
- Using children as messengers or weapons: courts notice, and it harms the child.
- Hiding income: courts can draw adverse conclusions; full disclosure is required.
- Not trying **mediation**: family courts encourage it, and many settlements happen there.
- If there is violence, do not wait for divorce: you can seek **protection orders** under the DV Act immediately (call 112 in an emergency, 181 for the women helpline).

steps.title: Free help
steps.body: Family courts have counsellors and mediators. **Legal Services Authorities** give free lawyers to **all women and children**, regardless of income (Section 12, Legal Services Authorities Act 1987). Call **15100**.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

Agree on terms: maintenance, custody, property
File joint petition (first motion) in the Family Court
Court records statements; waiting period begins (six months, may be waived)

quiz.q: Before filing for mutual-consent divorce under the HMA, the couple must have lived separately for at least…
quiz.why: The answer is "1 year". Reason: Section 13B(1). The other choices, such as "1 month" and "6 months", do not fit the question. (Question: Before filing for mutual-consent divorce under the HMA, the couple must have lived separately for at least…)

quiz.q: Can the six-month waiting period be waived?
quiz.why: The answer is "Yes, in suitable cases (Amardeep Singh, 2017)". Reason: The Supreme Court held it is directory, not mandatory. The other choices, such as "Only by Parliament" and "Only for celebrities", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The secular maintenance provision in the BNSS is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Section 144". Reason: BNSS Section 144 corresponds to the old CrPC Section 125. The other choices, such as "Section 35" and "Section 173", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: In custody cases, the court's paramount consideration is…
quiz.why: The answer is "Welfare of the child". Reason: The welfare principle. The other choices, such as "Who filed first" and "Mother's religion", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Who can get free legal aid regardless of income?
quiz.why: The answer is "All women and children". Reason: Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987. The other choices, such as "Only government employees" and "Only men", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: Buying property safely

story.title: The plot that was sold twice

scenes.text: Mr and Mrs Reddy, both teachers in Warangal, find a 'bargain' plot. The seller offers a power-of-attorney sale to 'save stamp duty'.
Their daughter Divya, a law student, insists on a title search. The encumbrance certificate shows a bank mortgage, and a 2019 registered sale of the same plot to someone else.
They walk away. Months later, the 'seller' is arrested for selling plots twice.
They later buy a RERA-registered flat with a registered sale deed, clear title and a home loan from a bank that did its own legal check.

steps.title: The documents that matter
steps.body:
- **Title deeds** for at least the last **30 years** (the 'chain of title'): who owned it, and how it passed down.
- **Encumbrance Certificate (EC)** from the sub-registrar: shows registered transactions (sales, mortgages) on the property.
- **Revenue records** (e.g., 7/12 extract, khata, patta, jamabandi, depending on the state) and **mutation** entries.
- **Approved building plan**, occupancy/completion certificate (for buildings), and land-use conversion if agricultural land is being used for housing.
- **Property tax receipts**, society **no-objection** certificate, and no-dues from utilities.
- Seller's **identity** and, if married or co-owners exist, all **co-owners' consent**.

steps.title: The sale deed and stamp duty
steps.body:
- A sale of immovable property worth ₹100 or more must be by a **registered instrument** (Transfer of Property Act Section 54; Registration Act Section 17).
- **Stamp duty** and **registration fees** are set by each state; some states offer **lower duty for women** buyers.
- In **Suraj Lamp & Industries (2011)**, the Supreme Court held that sales through **General Power of Attorney, agreement to sell and will** (so-called GPA sales) **do not transfer ownership**. Only a registered sale deed does.
- After registration, apply for **mutation** in municipal/revenue records. Note: mutation is for revenue/tax purposes and is **not itself proof of title**.

steps.title: Buying from a builder: RERA
steps.body:
The **Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act 2016 (RERA)** protects buyers of under-construction property:

- Projects above **500 sq m** of land or more than **eight apartments** must be **registered** with the state RERA before advertising or selling.
- Prices must be based on **carpet area**.
- **70%** of money collected from buyers must go into a **separate account** used only for that project's construction and land cost.
- The builder cannot take more than **10%** of the cost as advance before a written **agreement for sale** is registered.
- **Structural defects** reported within **five years** of possession must be fixed free.
- For **delay**, buyers can get **interest** or a **refund** with interest.

Check the project's registration number and quarterly updates on the state RERA website.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paying a large advance in **cash** with only a stamp-paper receipt.
- Skipping the **EC** and title search to save a few thousand rupees.
- Trusting a 'GPA sale' to save stamp duty.
- Buying 'agricultural land' for a house without checking conversion and local rules (some states restrict who can buy agricultural land).
- Not checking if the seller's **siblings/daughters** have a share in inherited property (see next lesson).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Search your state's **land records portal** for any property you know (many states offer free online access). Find the owner's name, survey number and any mutation entries.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

activity.prompt: Property purchase checklist
items: Title deeds for 30 years verified by a lawyer

Revenue records and mutation in seller's name
Approved plan / occupancy certificate (for buildings)
RERA registration verified (for builder projects)
All co-owners and legal heirs have signed
Payment only through bank channels
Sale deed stamped and registered

quiz.q: Which document shows registered mortgages or sales on a property?
quiz.why: The answer is "Encumbrance certificate". Reason: The EC lists registered transactions. The other choices, such as "PAN card" and "Ration card", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Does a GPA + agreement to sell transfer ownership?
options: No; only a registered sale deed does (Suraj Lamp, 2011)
quiz.why: The answer is "No; only a registered sale deed does (Suraj Lamp, 2011)". Reason: The Supreme Court held GPA sales do not convey title. The other choices, such as "Yes" and "Yes, after 3 years", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Under RERA, what share of buyers' money must go into a separate project account?
quiz.why: The answer is "70%". Reason: 70% for construction and land costs of that project. The other choices, such as "50%" and "10%", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Is mutation proof of ownership?
options: No, it is for revenue purposes and not proof of title
quiz.why: The answer is "No, it is for revenue purposes and not proof of title". Reason: Courts have repeatedly said so. The other choices, such as "Only for flats" and "Only if old", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A builder must fix structural defects reported within how long after possession?
quiz.why: The answer is "5 years". Reason: Section 14(3) of RERA. The other choices, such as "10 years" and "1 year", do not fit the question. (Question: A builder must fix structural defects reported within how long after possession?)
