lessons.title: Inheritance and wills

scenes.text: When Mr Pillai dies in Nashik without a will, his sons say the ancestral house is theirs. 'Daughters get married and leave,' says one.
His daughter Meenakshi learns that since the 2005 amendment, daughters are coparceners by birth with the same rights as sons.
With a mediator's help, the siblings and their mother agree to equal shares. Their mother, as a Class I heir, gets an equal share in Mr Pillai's own share too.
Meenakshi then writes her own will, signed and witnessed by two neighbours, so her children never face a fight.

steps.title: Which succession law applies?
steps.body:
- **Hindu Succession Act 1956 (HSA)**: Hindus, Buddhists, Jains, Sikhs.
- **Muslim personal law**: Muslims (shares fixed by religious law; differences between Sunni and Shia schools).
- **Indian Succession Act 1925**: Christians, Parsis (with special rules), people married under the Special Marriage Act and others not covered by the above; also governs **wills** for many communities.

**Intestate** succession means a person died **without a will**. **Testamentary** succession means property passes by **will**.

steps.title: Hindu succession basics
steps.body:
**When a Hindu man dies intestate**, his property goes first to **Class I heirs**, who take **equal shares**: **widow, sons, daughters, mother**, and the children of a predeceased son or daughter (among others). If there are none, it goes to Class II heirs (like father, siblings), and so on.

**Daughters as coparceners**: the **Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005** made a daughter a **coparcener by birth** in a joint Hindu family, with the **same rights and liabilities as a son**. In **Vineeta Sharma (2020)** the Supreme Court held this applies **whether or not the father was alive** on 9 September 2005.

**A Hindu woman's property** is her **absolute property** (Section 14). If she dies intestate, it goes first to her children (and children of predeceased children) and husband, with special rules for property inherited from her parents or in-laws.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Mr Pillai (Hindu) dies intestate. His self-acquired flat is worth ₹90 lakh. Survivors: wife, mother, two sons, one daughter. All are Class I heirs.

Shares: 5 heirs × equal share = **₹18 lakh each** (one-fifth each).

If one son had died earlier leaving two children, those children would together take that son's one-fifth.

*(Ancestral coparcenary property follows a slightly different calculation, because each coparcener, including daughters, already has a share by birth. A lawyer should work out real cases.)*

steps.title: Making a valid will
steps.body:
Under the **Indian Succession Act 1925**:

- Any person who is **18 or older** and of **sound mind** can make a will, without coercion or fraud.
- It must be **in writing**, **signed** by the testator, and **attested by at least two witnesses** who saw the signing (witnesses should not be beneficiaries).
- **Registration is optional**, but it adds credibility. Stamp paper is not required.
- You can **change or revoke** it any time; the **latest valid will** prevails. A small change can be made by a codicil.
- In some places and cases, a will must be **probated** (proved in court) before the executor can act.
- **Muslims** generally may bequeath only up to **one-third** of their property by will to non-heirs without the heirs' consent.

**Nomination is not a will**: in many cases (such as bank accounts), the **nominee receives** the money to hold for the **legal heirs**. To decide who finally gets what, write a will.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Married daughters have no share': **wrong** for Hindu families since 2005.
- 'A will must be on stamp paper and registered': neither is legally required, though registration helps.
- Using a beneficiary as a witness.
- Forgetting to list **bank accounts, insurance, shares, digital assets** and to name an **executor**.
- Making a will under pressure from a family member: wills obtained by undue influence can be challenged.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make a private **asset list** for your family (property, bank accounts, insurance, investments) and check nominations are updated. Adults: draft a simple will outline.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

activity.prompt: A Hindu woman dies intestate leaving self-acquired savings of ₹60 lakh. Her heirs are her husband and three children (no predeceased children). Under the HSA, they share equally. How much does each get (in lakh)?

quiz.q: Since the 2005 amendment, a Hindu daughter is…
options: A coparcener only if her father agrees
A coparcener by birth with the same rights as a son
quiz.why: The answer is "A coparcener by birth with the same rights as a son". Reason: Section 6 as amended; confirmed in Vineeta Sharma (2020). The other choices, such as "Not a coparcener" and "A coparcener only if her father agrees", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: How many witnesses must attest a will under the Indian Succession Act?
quiz.why: The answer is "At least two". Reason: Section 63. The other choices, such as "None" and "Five", do not fit the question. (Question: How many witnesses must attest a will under the Indian Succession Act?)

quiz.q: Is registration of a will compulsory?
quiz.why: The answer is "No, it is optional". Reason: Optional, though helpful. The other choices, such as "Only for land" and "Yes", do not fit the question. (Question: Is registration of a will compulsory?)

quiz.q: A nominee in a bank account is generally…
options: The person who receives the money, holding it for the legal heirs
quiz.why: The answer is "The person who receives the money, holding it for the legal heirs". Reason: Nomination does not override succession law in most cases. The other choices, such as "The final owner" and "Not allowed to receive anything", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A Muslim can generally bequeath by will to non-heirs up to…
quiz.why: The answer is "One-third of the estate". Reason: The one-third rule, beyond which heirs' consent is needed. The other choices, such as "One-half" and "Nothing", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Minimum marriage age for women in India is…
questions.why: The answer is "18". Reason: 18 for the bride, 21 for the groom. The other choices, such as "16" and "25", do not fit the question. (Question: Minimum marriage age for women in India is…)

questions.q: Which law lets two people of different religions marry without conversion?
questions.why: The answer is "Special Marriage Act 1954". Reason: SMA. The other choices, such as "Consumer Protection Act" and "Hindu Marriage Act 1955", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which court usually hears divorce cases in cities?
questions.why: The answer is "Family Court". Reason: Family Courts Act 1984. The other choices, such as "Lok Sabha" and "RERA", do not fit the question. (Question: Which court usually hears divorce cases in cities?)

questions.q: Ownership of land is transferred by…
questions.why: The answer is "A registered sale deed". Reason: TPA Section 54 and Suraj Lamp. The other choices, such as "A notarised GPA" and "Paying property tax", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Who is a Class I heir under the HSA?
questions.why: The answer is "Daughter". Reason: Daughters are Class I heirs. The other choices, such as "Neighbour" and "Cousin", do not fit the question. (Question: Who is a Class I heir under the HSA?)

questions.q: Which BNSS section allows parents to claim maintenance from their children?
questions.why: The answer is "Section 144". Reason: It covers wife, children and parents. The other choices, such as "Section 479" and "Section 173", do not fit the question.

questions.q: A child marriage under the PCMA 2006 is…
options: Voidable at the option of the party who was a child
questions.why: The answer is "Voidable at the option of the party who was a child". Reason: Section 3, petition within two years of majority. The other choices, such as "Always valid" and "Valid after age 18", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Under RERA, a builder cannot take more than what percentage as advance before a registered agreement for sale?
questions.why: The answer is "10%". Reason: Section 13. The other choices, such as "30%" and "50%", do not fit the question. (Question: Under RERA, a builder cannot take more than what percentage as advance before a registered agreement for sale?)

questions.q: Vineeta Sharma (2020) held that daughters' coparcenary rights…
options: Apply regardless of whether the father was alive in 2005
Apply only if the father was alive on 9 Sept 2005
questions.why: The answer is "Apply regardless of whether the father was alive in 2005". Reason: Rights arise by birth. The other choices, such as "Apply only if the father was alive on 9 Sept 2005" and "Were withdrawn", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which statement about a will is correct?
options: A will must be on stamp paper
The latest valid will prevails; earlier ones can be revoked
Only one will can ever be made
questions.why: The answer is "The latest valid will prevails; earlier ones can be revoked". Reason: Wills are revocable. The other choices, such as "A will must be on stamp paper" and "Only one will can ever be made", do not fit the question.

questions.q: In a maintenance case, the Supreme Court (Rajnesh v Neha, 2020) required…
options: Only the husband to file income details
Both parties to file affidavits of assets and liabilities
questions.why: The answer is "Both parties to file affidavits of assets and liabilities". Reason: Disclosure by both sides. The other choices, such as "Only the husband to file income details" and "No documents", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which court can dissolve a marriage on the ground of irretrievable breakdown using Article 142?
questions.why: The answer is "The Supreme Court". Reason: Shilpa Sailesh (2023) relates to the Supreme Court's Article 142 power. The other choices, such as "Any district court" and "Family Court", do not fit the question.

questions.q: Adults choose to marry against their families' wishes and receive threats. The legal position is…
options: Adults can marry by choice; they can seek police and court protection
questions.why: Right to choose a partner is protected (e.g., Shafin Jahan 2018, Lata Singh 2006).

courses.title: Work rights, how courts work, Lok Adalat and free legal aid
courses.summary: Know your rights at work (wages, hours, PF, gratuity, maternity benefit, notice and termination), understand how civil and criminal cases move through courts under the new BNSS, settle disputes faster through Lok Adalats and mediation, and get a free lawyer through the legal services system (NALSA 15100).
outcomes: Learners can check an offer letter and payslip for key legal entitlements
Learners can explain the steps of a civil suit and of a criminal case from FIR to judgment
Learners can state the key rights of an arrested person under the BNSS
Learners can explain how Lok Adalats and mediation work and which disputes suit them
Learners can identify who qualifies for free legal aid and how to apply

lessons.title: Your rights at work

scenes.text: Pooja, 22, joins a Chennai startup as a junior designer. There is no appointment letter, salary comes in cash, and nobody mentions PF.
Her manager expects 12-hour days and says, 'Leave is for the weak.' When she announces her pregnancy two years later, HR hints she should resign.
Her cousin Arul, an HR professional, explains PF, maternity benefit of 26 weeks, and that dismissing a woman because of pregnancy is prohibited.
Pooja asks in writing for an appointment letter and PF enrolment, and applies for maternity leave. With a labour lawyer's letter, the company complies.

steps.title: The legal framework (and the four Labour Codes)
steps.body:
Labour is on the **Concurrent List**, so both the Union and the States make labour laws. Parliament passed **four Labour Codes** in 2019–2020 that consolidate many older central laws:

- **Code on Wages 2019**
- **Industrial Relations Code 2020**
- **Code on Social Security 2020**
- **Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020**

They are being brought into force with rules framed by the Centre and the States, so **check the current status and your state's rules**. The core rights below appear in both the older laws and the Codes. Separately, each state has a **Shops and Establishments Act** for offices and shops, covering hours, holidays and leave.

steps.title: Wages, hours and social security
steps.body:
- **Minimum wages**: notified by governments for different jobs and regions; paying less is an offence. **Equal pay** for the same or similar work regardless of gender.
- **Timely payment** with a **wage slip** and no unauthorised deductions.
- **Working hours**: for factory workers, generally up to **9 hours a day / 48 hours a week**, with **overtime at twice the ordinary rate**. Offices follow the state Shops and Establishments Act.
- **EPF** (Employees' Provident Fund): generally for establishments with **20 or more** employees; the employee and employer each contribute (typically **12%** of basic wages plus DA). Check your passbook through your **UAN** on the EPFO portal.
- **ESI** (Employees' State Insurance): medical and cash benefits for lower-wage employees in covered establishments.
- **Gratuity** (Payment of Gratuity Act 1972): after **five years** of continuous service (earlier in case of death or disablement), at **15 days' wages for each completed year**, subject to a ceiling set by the government.

steps.title: Maternity benefit and other protections
steps.body:
- **Maternity Benefit Act 1961** (amended 2017): **26 weeks** paid leave for the first two children; **12 weeks** from the third child; **12 weeks** for adopting a child below three months and for commissioning mothers; a **creche** facility in establishments with **50 or more** employees; work-from-home may be allowed by agreement after the leave. Dismissing a woman **because of** her pregnancy or during maternity leave is **prohibited**.
- **POSH Act 2013**: every employer with **10+ employees** must have an **Internal Committee** for sexual harassment complaints.
- **Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016**: no discrimination; reasonable accommodation.
- **Freedom of association**: workers may form and join **trade unions** (Article 19(1)(c)).

steps.title: Termination, notice and full-and-final
steps.body:
- Your **appointment letter/contract** sets notice periods; **both sides** must follow them (or pay in lieu, if the contract allows).
- For **workmen** (broadly non-managerial staff) with one year of continuous service, **retrenchment** requires notice (or pay) and compensation, plus government permission in larger establishments.
- A **non-compete** clause that stops you from working **after you leave** is generally **void** under **Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act 1872**; confidentiality obligations and restrictions **during** employment are usually valid.
- On exit, ask for a **relieving letter**, **experience letter**, **full-and-final settlement** (pending salary, leave encashment as per policy, gratuity if eligible) and PF transfer/withdrawal.

**Worked example (gratuity)**: last monthly basic + DA = ₹52,000; 7 completed years. Gratuity = 52,000 × 15/26 × 7 = **₹2,10,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Working without an **appointment letter** or salary slips.
- Signing a resignation letter under pressure 'to avoid a bad record'. You can refuse, and record the pressure in writing.
- Not checking whether PF deducted from salary is actually **deposited** (check your passbook).
- Assuming 'at-will' employment like in some countries; Indian law and your contract give protections.

steps.title: Where to complain
steps.body:
- Your company's **HR / grievance redressal committee**.
- The **Labour Commissioner / labour department** of your state (conciliation officers can settle disputes); the central **SAMADHAN** portal for disputes in central-sphere establishments.
- **EPFO grievance portal** for PF issues.
- **Labour Courts / Industrial Tribunals** for formal disputes.
- Free legal advice: **NALSA 15100**.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** Laws, section numbers, fees and limits change, and many rules differ from state to state. For your own situation, speak to a lawyer, or get **free legal help: NALSA legal aid helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority (DLSA) at the district court. Emergencies: **112**. A child in danger: **1098**.

quiz.q: Maternity leave under the amended Maternity Benefit Act for a first child is…
quiz.why: The answer is "26 weeks". Reason: 26 weeks for the first two children. The other choices, such as "12 weeks" and "6 weeks", do not fit the question. (Question: Maternity leave under the amended Maternity Benefit Act for a first child is…)

quiz.q: Gratuity generally becomes payable after…
quiz.why: The answer is "5 years of continuous service". Reason: Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, with exceptions for death/disablement. The other choices, such as "1 year" and "10 years", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: A post-employment non-compete clause in India is generally…
options: Void under Section 27 of the Contract Act
quiz.why: The answer is "Void under Section 27 of the Contract Act". Reason: Restraint of trade after employment is generally void. The other choices, such as "Enforceable for 5 years" and "Fully enforceable", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Overtime for factory workers is generally paid at…
quiz.why: The answer is "Twice the ordinary rate". Reason: Twice the ordinary rate of wages. The other choices, such as "Half the rate" and "The same rate", do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Where can you check whether your PF contributions are deposited?
quiz.why: The answer is "EPFO passbook via UAN". Reason: The EPFO member passbook shows contributions. The other choices, such as "Income tax website only" and "Ration office", do not fit the question.

lessons.title: How courts work: civil cases and criminal cases

scenes.text: In Bhopal, Imran lent ₹4 lakh to a business friend who refuses to repay. In the same month, Imran's brother Salim's phone is snatched on the street.
For the loan, Imran's lawyer sends a legal notice, then files a civil suit for recovery. That is a dispute between two people.
For the snatching, Salim goes to the police station, which registers an FIR. That is a crime against society; the State prosecutes.
Imran learns the civil case follows the Code of Civil Procedure, while Salim's case follows the new BNSS. 'Two roads, two rulebooks,' he says.

steps.title: Civil vs criminal
steps.body:
**Civil cases**: disputes between persons about money, property, contracts, family matters, injunctions. The person suing (plaintiff) seeks **compensation or an order**. Procedure: **Code of Civil Procedure 1908 (CPC)**. Standard of proof: **balance of probabilities**.

**Criminal cases**: offences against society (theft, assault, cheating, murder). The **State prosecutes** through a public prosecutor; the result can be **punishment** (fine, imprisonment, community service for some petty offences). Since **1 July 2024**: **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS)** defines offences, **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS)** sets procedure, and the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA)** governs evidence. Standard of proof: **beyond reasonable doubt**.

The same facts can lead to both (for example, a cheque bounce can lead to a criminal complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act and a civil recovery suit).

steps.title: Journey of a civil suit
steps.body:
1. **Legal notice** (often useful; compulsory against the government under Section 80 CPC).
2. **Plaint** filed in the court with jurisdiction (by value and location) with **court fee**.
3. **Summons** to the defendant → **written statement** (generally within 30 days, extendable within limits).
4. Court frames **issues** (the questions to decide); may refer to **mediation**.
5. **Evidence**: documents and witnesses, cross-examination.
6. **Arguments** → **judgment** and **decree**.
7. **Appeal** if needed; **execution** of the decree to actually recover money/property.

**Limitation Act 1963**: suits must be filed within set periods, for example **three years** for most money-recovery claims. Late = barred.

steps.title: Journey of a criminal case (BNSS)
steps.body:
1. **Information**: for a **cognizable** offence, police must register an **FIR** (BNSS **Section 173**). You can file it **orally, in writing or electronically (e-FIR)**, at **any police station** (**Zero FIR**). You get a **free copy**.
2. For offences punishable with **3 to 7 years**, police may conduct a **preliminary enquiry** (up to 14 days) before registering.
3. If police refuse to register: send it to the **Superintendent of Police** (Section 173(4)), then apply to the **Magistrate** (Section 175(3)).
4. **Investigation**, possible arrest, collection of evidence (with **videography of searches** and **forensic examination** mandatory for offences punishable with 7 years or more).
5. **Police report (charge-sheet)** filed in court; the victim must be informed of progress **within 90 days**.
6. **Charges framed**, **trial**, **judgment** (the BNSS sets a target of judgment within 30 days after arguments, extendable to 45). Appeals follow.

**Non-cognizable** offences (minor ones): police record it and need a magistrate's order to investigate.

steps.title: Rights of an arrested person (BNSS + Constitution)
steps.body:
- To be told the **grounds of arrest** and, for bailable offences, the **right to bail** (Section 47).
- Police must **inform a relative or friend** of the arrest (Section 48).
- **Meet a lawyer** during interrogation (not throughout) (Section 38).
- **Medical examination** (Section 53).
- Production before a **magistrate within 24 hours** (Section 58; Article 22).
- For offences punishable up to **7 years**, police should generally issue a **notice of appearance** instead of arresting (Section 35), following the Supreme Court's guidance in Arnesh Kumar (2014).
- A **woman** should not be arrested after sunset and before sunrise except in exceptional circumstances with a magistrate's prior permission (Section 43(5)).
- **Bail**: a right in **bailable** offences; the court's discretion in **non-bailable** ones; **anticipatory bail** can be sought from the Sessions Court or High Court (Section 482). An undertrial first-time offender who has served **one-third** of the maximum sentence is generally to be released on bail (Section 479).

steps.title: Using eCourts
steps.body: Every case has a **CNR number**. On the **eCourts Services** website or app you can see next dates, orders and judgments for district courts and High Courts. Many courts allow **e-filing** and **virtual hearings**. Court complexes have **legal-aid front offices** for help.

A child in danger: **1098**.

lessons.title: Lok Adalat and mediation: faster, cheaper justice

story.title: The electricity bill and the accident claim

scenes.text: Gurmeet Kaur, a widow in Amritsar, has fought a disputed electricity bill for three years. Her neighbour Joseph's motor accident claim has been pending for four.
The District Legal Services Authority announces a National Lok Adalat. Both register their cases.
In one day, with retired judges and a lawyer as conciliators, the electricity board agrees to a corrected bill, and the insurance company agrees to pay Joseph's compensation.
No court fee, no appeal, final settlement. Joseph's court fee is refunded. 'Justice at last,' Gurmeet says.

steps.title: What a Lok Adalat is
steps.body:
**Lok Adalats** ('people's courts') are set up under the **Legal Services Authorities Act 1987** by legal services authorities. They settle disputes by **compromise**, with a panel usually including a judicial officer and a lawyer or social worker.

- Cases **pending in court** or at the **pre-litigation** stage can be referred.
- **No court fee**; if a pending case is settled, the **court fee paid is refunded**.
- The **award is final and binding**, **deemed to be a decree of a civil court**, and **no appeal** lies against it (Section 21).
- If no settlement is reached, the case goes back to the regular court; nothing is lost.

**National Lok Adalats** are held across the country on announced dates several times a year, and settle a very large number of cases in a single day.

steps.title: Which cases suit a Lok Adalat?
steps.body:
Good fits: **motor accident claims**, **bank loan recovery**, **cheque bounce** (Section 138 NI Act), **electricity, water and telephone bills**, **family disputes** (other than divorce itself), **labour disputes**, land acquisition compensation, **compoundable criminal offences** and many civil disputes.

Not suitable: **non-compoundable offences** (serious crimes that cannot be settled privately, like murder or rape), and matters where the law does not allow compromise.

**Permanent Lok Adalats** (Section 22B) deal with **public utility services** (transport, post, telecom, power, water, hospitals, insurance, and others notified). If conciliation fails, a Permanent Lok Adalat can **decide the dispute on merits** (within its monetary limit).

steps.title: Mediation and other ADR
steps.body:
**Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR)** methods (Section 89 CPC):

- **Mediation**: a trained neutral mediator helps the parties reach their **own** agreement. Court-annexed mediation centres exist in most district courts. The **Mediation Act 2023** provides for **pre-litigation mediation**, confidentiality, time limits and enforcement of mediated settlement agreements like court judgments.
- **Conciliation**: the conciliator may also suggest terms.
- **Arbitration** (Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996): a private arbitrator **decides** the dispute; the award is binding, with limited grounds of challenge. Common in business contracts.
- **Commercial disputes** above a specified value must generally try **pre-institution mediation** first (Commercial Courts Act 2015, Section 12A), unless urgent relief is needed.

steps.title: Before you settle
steps.body:
- A Lok Adalat award **cannot be appealed**, so **read the terms carefully** and agree only if you are satisfied.
- Nobody can force you to compromise; consent must be **free**.
- In accident claims, check the compensation against the usual tribunal calculation (ask your lawyer or legal-aid counsel).

steps.title: Try this

A child in danger: **1098**.

lessons.title: Free legal aid: your right to a lawyer

scenes.text: Shanti, a domestic worker in Delhi, is accused of theft by her employer and taken to the police station. She cannot afford a lawyer.
Her daughter calls 15100. The duty legal-aid counsel of the Legal Aid Defence Counsel office reaches the magistrate's court the next morning.
The lawyer secures her bail and later shows the 'missing' necklace was in the employer's own drawer, recorded on a CCTV clip.
The case is closed. 'I didn't know I had a right to a free lawyer,' Shanti says. 'Now my whole basti knows.'

steps.title: Why legal aid is a right
steps.body:
**Article 39A** directs the State to provide **free legal aid** so that justice is not denied because of economic or other disabilities. The Supreme Court has held that free legal aid to an accused who cannot afford a lawyer is part of **Article 21** (fair procedure); in **Khatri v State of Bihar (1981)** it said the magistrate must tell the accused of this right.

The **Legal Services Authorities Act 1987** created:

- **NALSA** (National Legal Services Authority),
- **State Legal Services Authorities (SLSA)**,
- **District Legal Services Authorities (DLSA)**, usually headed by the District Judge,
- **Taluk Legal Services Committees**, and legal services committees for the Supreme Court and High Courts.

steps.title: Who is entitled? (Section 12)
How to get legal aid
steps.body:
1. Call the **NALSA helpline 15100**, or visit the **legal services front office** at your district court complex or Taluk court.
2. Fill a simple **application** (in person, by post, or online through NALSA's legal services portal), with a short description of your problem and any eligibility proof (an affidavit is often enough for income).
3. The authority assigns a **panel lawyer** and may also pay **court fees**, costs of documents and copies.
4. In criminal cases, many districts have a **Legal Aid Defence Counsel** office with full-time defence lawyers.
5. **Legal-aid clinics** operate in villages, jails, law colleges and community centres, staffed by **para-legal volunteers**.
6. **Tele-Law**: free legal advice by video/phone through Common Service Centres.

Legal aid covers advice, drafting, representation in courts and tribunals, and Lok Adalats. If you are unhappy with your assigned lawyer, you can **ask the authority for a change**.

steps.title: Victim compensation
steps.body: Under **BNSS Section 396** and state **Victim Compensation Schemes**, victims of crime (and dependants) can apply to the DLSA/SLSA for **compensation**, including **interim relief**, even if the offender is not traced or identified. Special schemes cover women victims of sexual assault and acid attacks.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Save **15100** in your phone and write down the address of your **District Legal Services Authority** (usually in the district court complex). Tell one person who might need it.

courses.guardianNote: This course explains child-protection laws in plain, non-graphic language: what the law forbids (described in general terms only), how children are protected during police and court processes, children's rights if they are accused of an offence, and laws on ragging, child marriage and child labour. lessons.title: POCSO: what the law says and why

scenes.text: Neha, 14, in Jaipur, goes for extra maths coaching. The tutor starts sending her private messages and says, 'This is our secret. Your parents won't understand.'
Neha feels confused and uneasy. Her best friend Mehak says, 'A safe adult never asks you to keep secrets from your parents.'
Neha tells her mother, shaking. Her mother hugs her: 'Thank you for telling me. It is not your fault. We will handle this.'
They report to the police, who involve a woman officer and the Child Welfare Committee. The tutor is arrested under POCSO. Neha keeps studying, now with a new tutor.

steps.title: The POCSO Act 2012
steps.body:
The **Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act 2012 (POCSO)** is a special law to protect children from sexual abuse and exploitation.

- A **child** means **any person below 18 years**.
- It is **gender-neutral**: it protects **boys, girls and all children**, and anyone (of any gender) can be an offender.
- In India, the **age of consent is 18**. Sexual activity with a person under 18 is an offence under POCSO, **even if the child 'agreed'**. The law treats children as unable to give legal consent to sexual acts.
- The Act was **strengthened in 2019** with higher punishments for the most serious offences.

steps.title: What the law forbids (in general terms)
steps.body:
POCSO covers several kinds of offences:

- **Sexual assault** of a child, including any **touching with sexual intent**, and more serious **penetrative** assault.
- **Sexual harassment** of a child: sexual remarks or gestures, **showing sexual material** to a child, **repeatedly following, watching or contacting** a child (including **online**), or **threatening** to use a child's image.
- **Using a child for pornography**, and **storing or sharing** any sexual material involving children. Even **possessing** such material without deleting or reporting it is an offence.
- **Aggravated** offences carry heavier punishment, for example when the offender is a person in a position of trust or authority (a relative, teacher, police officer, doctor, staff of a school or institution), or when the child is very young or has a disability.

**Grooming** (building trust to abuse later, often with secrecy, gifts or special attention) is a common pattern. Abusers are **usually someone the child knows**.

steps.title: Everyone's duty to report
steps.body:
- **Section 19**: **any person** (including a child) who knows or suspects that an offence has been or is likely to be committed **must report** it to the **Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU)** or the **local police**.
- **Section 21**: **not reporting** is itself an **offence**. Heads of institutions who fail to report offences by their staff face a higher punishment.
- Professionals like **doctors, teachers, counsellors and hotel or media staff** who come across such material or cases also have reporting duties.
- **A child who reports is never punished** for reporting. Making a deliberately **false** complaint is punishable for adults, but **not for a child**.

**Where to report**: police (**112**), **Childline 1098**, the SJPU, or online for child sexual abuse material at **cybercrime.gov.in** (anonymous reporting is possible for such content).

steps.title: About teen relationships
steps.body:
Because the age of consent is 18 and POCSO has **no close-in-age exception**, sexual activity between two people **under 18** can technically fall under POCSO, and cases have been filed when two teenagers were in a relationship. Courts have discussed this problem in many judgments, and in **2023 the Law Commission advised against lowering the age of consent**, suggesting instead that judges be given guided discretion in sentencing in genuine adolescent cases.

What this means for teens: you have the right to be safe, to say **no** at any time, and to get **accurate information and help** without shame. Talk to a trusted adult or counsellor.

steps.title: If a child tells you
steps.body:
- **Listen calmly**; believe them; do not interrogate or ask leading questions.
- Say: **'Thank you for telling me. It is not your fault. I will help you.'**
- Do not promise to keep it secret; explain you will tell people who can help.
- **Report** (it is the law) and get medical care if needed. Do not confront the abuser yourself.
- Keep the child **away from the alleged abuser**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Name **three trusted adults** you could tell if something felt wrong, one at home, one at school and one outside. Save **1098** and **112** in your phone.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** If you or someone you know is in danger, call **112** now. Child in danger: **1098** (Childline). Women in distress: **181**. Cyber fraud: **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in. Mental-health support: **14416** (Tele-MANAS). **Free legal aid: NALSA 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority. Section numbers and procedures change, so confirm the details for your case with a lawyer or legal-aid counsel.

statements.s: POCSO protects only girls.
statements.why: It is gender-neutral and protects all children under 18.

statements.s: Under Indian law, a 16-year-old cannot legally consent to sexual activity.
statements.why: The age of consent is 18.

statements.s: Abusers are usually strangers.
statements.why: Most abusers are people the child knows and trusts.

statements.s: If you know a child is being abused, you have a legal duty to report it.
statements.why: Section 19; failing to report is an offence under Section 21.

statements.s: A child who reports abuse can be punished if the case is not proved.
statements.why: Children are not punished for reports; only deliberate false complaints by adults are punishable.

statements.s: Repeatedly messaging a child with sexual intent can be an offence under POCSO.
statements.why: This is sexual harassment of a child, including online.

lessons.title: After a report: how POCSO protects the child

scenes.text: Aman, 13, in Kolkata, tells his football coach's assistant, Ms Rita, that a senior coach touched him inappropriately and threatened to drop him from the team.
Ms Rita reports to the police that day, as the law requires. A police officer in plain clothes comes to Aman's home to record his statement with his mother present.
In the Special Court, Aman testifies from a separate room by video. He never has to face the coach; the judge asks the lawyers' questions gently.
A support person helps the family through each step. Aman gets counselling and is back on the field, at a new academy.

steps.title: Recording the child's statement
steps.body:
POCSO requires a **child-friendly** process:

- The statement is recorded at the **child's residence or a place of the child's choice**, as far as possible by a **woman police officer not below the rank of sub-inspector** (Section 24).
- The officer should **not be in uniform**.
- The child must **not be kept in a police station overnight** for any reason, and must be kept away from the accused.
- A **parent or trusted person** may be present (Section 26); an **interpreter, special educator or expert** must be provided if needed (for example for a child with a disability).
- The statement can also be recorded by a **Magistrate** (Section 25).
- Statements may be **audio-video recorded**.

steps.title: Medical care and support
steps.body:
- **Medical examination** is done in the presence of a parent or trusted person; for a girl, by a **woman doctor** (Section 27).
- **Emergency medical care** must be given immediately; hospitals cannot refuse or demand an FIR or documents first.
- The **Child Welfare Committee (CWC)** is informed within 24 hours and decides whether the child needs care and protection, including if the abuser is in the family.
- A **support person** can be assigned to help the child and family through the investigation and trial (POCSO Rules 2020).
- The Special Court can order **interim compensation** for the child's relief and rehabilitation, and **final compensation**.
- The **child's identity** (name, address, school, photo, family details) **must not be disclosed** by media or anyone (Section 23).

steps.title: In the Special Court
steps.body:
- Cases are tried by **Special Courts** (Section 28), often in a **child-friendly** room.
- The child does **not have to see the accused**; screens or video links are used (Section 36).
- Lawyers' questions go **through the judge**; no aggressive cross-examination (Section 33).
- The child gets **frequent breaks** and is not called repeatedly to court.
- Trials are held **in camera** (not open to the public).
- The court should record the child's evidence **within 30 days** of taking cognizance and complete the trial **within one year** as far as possible (Section 35).
- **Presumption** (Section 29): in certain serious offences, once basic facts are shown, the court presumes the accused committed the offence unless proved otherwise.

steps.title: Common mistakes by adults
steps.body:
- 'Let's settle this within the family/community.' POCSO offences **cannot be privately settled**; families who hide abuse may themselves commit the offence of non-reporting, and the child stays in danger.
- Bathing the child or washing clothes before medical help: this can destroy evidence (but the child's comfort and health come first; seek medical help quickly).
- Questioning the child again and again; this causes trauma. Let trained officers do it once.
- Posting about the case on social media with identifying details.

steps.title: Try this (for parents and teachers)
steps.body: Check whether your child's **school or sports academy** has a **child protection policy**, a named contact person, CCTV in common areas, and a rule that no adult is alone with a child behind closed doors.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** If you or someone you know is in danger, call **112** now. Child in danger: **1098** (Childline). Women in distress: **181**. Cyber fraud: **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in. Mental-health support: **14416** (Tele-MANAS). **Free legal aid: NALSA 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority. Section numbers and procedures change, so confirm the details for your case with a lawyer or legal-aid counsel.

lessons.title: The Juvenile Justice Act: children accused of offences and children needing care

scenes.text: Sunny, 15, in Ahmedabad, is caught with a stolen bicycle. His father is ill and the family has no money.
The police do not put him in a lockup or handcuff him. A Child Welfare Police Officer takes him to the Juvenile Justice Board within 24 hours.
The Board, a magistrate and two social workers, grants bail, asks a probation officer to report on his family, and orders community service and counselling.
The Board also links the family with a sponsorship scheme. Sunny stays in school. His record is not held against him later.

steps.title: Two kinds of children under the JJ Act 2015
steps.body:
The **Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015** (amended 2021) defines a child as a person **below 18** and deals with:

- **Child in conflict with law (CCL)**: a child **alleged or found to have committed an offence**. Handled by the **Juvenile Justice Board (JJB)**: a Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrate and **two social workers** (at least one a woman).
- **Child in need of care and protection (CNCP)**: for example a child who is **homeless, abandoned, orphaned, working, begging, abused, trafficked, at risk of child marriage**, or whose parent is unable or unfit to care. Handled by the **Child Welfare Committee (CWC)**.

The guiding principles include the **best interest of the child**, the **presumption of innocence**, dignity, family responsibility, privacy, **institutionalisation as a last resort**, and **no stigma**.

steps.title: Rights of a child in conflict with law
steps.body:
- **Not to be placed in a police lockup or jail**, and not handcuffed; kept in an observation home or place of safety.
- Produced before the **JJB within 24 hours**.
- **Bail is the norm** (Section 12), whether the offence is bailable or not, unless release would bring the child into association with criminals, expose them to danger, or defeat justice.
- Free **legal aid**; the right to be heard and to have parents informed.
- Most outcomes are **reformative**: advice, counselling, **community service**, group counselling, fines, probation, or a stay in a **special home** for **up to three years**.
- **No child** can be sentenced to **death** or to **life imprisonment without the possibility of release**.
- Records are **confidential** and generally removed afterward; the finding is **not a disqualification** later in life (Section 24).

steps.title: Heinous offences by 16–18-year-olds
steps.body:
The Act classifies offences as **petty** (up to 3 years), **serious** (3–7 years) and **heinous** (minimum 7 years or more).

If a child aged **16 to 18** is alleged to have committed a **heinous** offence, the JJB conducts a **preliminary assessment** (within three months) of the child's mental and physical capacity, ability to understand consequences, and circumstances. It may then transfer the case to a **Children's Court** (a Sessions Court) that can try the child **as an adult**. Even then, the child is kept in a **place of safety** until 21, and cannot get death or life without release.

This change was introduced in 2015 after intense public debate, including about the 2012 Delhi gang-rape case.

steps.title: Adoption and other protections
steps.body:
- **Legal adoption** happens only through the procedure under the JJ Act and the **Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA)** (or the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act for Hindus). Since the 2021 amendment, the **District Magistrate** issues adoption orders.
- **Buying or selling a child** for any purpose is a serious offence (Section 81).
- **Cruelty to a child** by a person in charge (Section 75), giving a child **liquor or drugs** (Section 77), and using children for **begging** (Section 76) are offences.
- **Corporal punishment** in schools is prohibited under the **Right to Education Act** (Section 17).
- Found an **abandoned baby**? Inform **1098** or the police immediately; failing to report a found child is an offence under the JJ Act.

steps.title: Common myths
steps.body:
- 'Juveniles get away with anything': the system focuses on reform, but serious offences by 16–18-year-olds can lead to adult trial.
- 'Police can keep a child in the lockup overnight for questioning': not allowed.
- 'Adopting a relative's baby informally is enough': informal arrangements are **not legal adoption** and leave the child without legal protection.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find your district's **Child Welfare Committee** and **Juvenile Justice Board** contact details (often on the district or state child-protection website).

lessons.title: Ragging, child marriage and child labour

scenes.text: Karan, 18, joins an engineering college hostel in Odisha. Seniors call freshers at midnight, force them to do humiliating tasks and threaten 'consequences'.
One fresher, Joel, is pushed to drink alcohol and collapses. Others are too scared to speak.
Karan calls the national anti-ragging helpline. The college's anti-ragging squad arrives within the hour; Joel is taken to hospital.
The seniors are suspended and removed from the hostel, and an FIR is filed. In a week, freshers feel safe again, and many seniors thank Karan quietly.

steps.title: What ragging is
Help and penalties
steps.body:
- **National Anti-Ragging Helpline**: **1800-180-5522** (toll-free, 24x7), email **helpline@antiragging.in**.
- Every institution must have an **Anti-Ragging Committee** and an **Anti-Ragging Squad**, and students and parents must submit an **anti-ragging undertaking** (affidavit), usually online, every year.
- Penalties include: **suspension** from classes, **withholding results or scholarships**, **debarring from exams**, **cancellation of admission**, **expulsion from hostel**, **rustication** for a period, and **expulsion** from the institution, plus an **FIR** where an offence is involved.
- If offenders are not identified, the institution may impose **collective punishment** on a group to deter silence.
- Institutions that fail to act can themselves face UGC action.

steps.title: Child marriage
steps.body:
Under the **Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006**, a 'child' is a male below **21** or a female below **18**.

- Child marriage is **voidable** by the child party; marriages involving trafficking, force or sale are **void**.
- Punishment for an adult male above 18 marrying a child, and for **anyone who performs, conducts, directs or abets** a child marriage (including parents and those who attend to promote it).
- Courts can issue **injunctions to stop** a planned child marriage; a marriage held in violation of an injunction is void.
- Each district has a **Child Marriage Prohibition Officer**.
- **Call 1098 or 112** if a child marriage is being planned. Many have been stopped by a single call.

The girl's **right to maintenance and residence** until remarriage, and children's legitimacy and custody, are protected.

steps.title: Child labour
steps.body:
Under the **Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986** (amended 2016):

- **Children below 14** may not be employed in **any occupation or process**, except helping their **family or family enterprise** in non-hazardous work **after school hours** or during vacations, or as a **child artist** under safeguards.
- **Adolescents (14–18)** may not be employed in **hazardous** occupations and processes.
- Employers face imprisonment and fines; rescued children are rehabilitated.
- Report on the government's **PENCiL** portal, to the labour department, police, or **1098**.

steps.title: If you are a bystander
steps.body: Silence is what lets ragging and abuse continue. You can **report anonymously** through the anti-ragging helpline, support the victim afterwards, refuse to join in, and record evidence safely. Bystanders who join in or encourage ragging are also liable.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Save the anti-ragging helpline **1800-180-5522** and **1098** in your phone. If you are joining college, find out who is on your institution's anti-ragging squad.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** If you or someone you know is in danger, call **112** now. Child in danger: **1098** (Childline). Women in distress: **181**. Cyber fraud: **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in. Mental-health support: **14416** (Tele-MANAS). **Free legal aid: NALSA 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority. Section numbers and procedures change, so confirm the details for your case with a lawyer or legal-aid counsel.

lessons.title: POSH: what workplace sexual harassment is

scenes.text: Ritika, 26, a software engineer in Gurugram, is the only woman in Team B. Her lead, Vikram, makes comments about her clothes and sends 'funny' memes with sexual content to her late at night.
When she ignores them, he says her appraisal 'depends on being a team player' and invites her for a 'one-on-one dinner'.
Her friend Farah shows her the company's POSH policy: unwelcome sexually coloured remarks, showing sexual content, and implied threats about her job are all covered.
Ritika saves screenshots and writes to the Internal Committee. 'I just want to do my job safely,' she writes.

steps.title: Background and coverage
steps.body:
In **Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (1997)**, after the gang-rape of Bhanwari Devi, a social worker who tried to stop a child marriage, the Supreme Court laid down guidelines against workplace sexual harassment, based on Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 and CEDAW. Parliament then enacted the **Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act 2013 (POSH Act)**.

- It protects an **'aggrieved woman'** of **any age**, whether **employed or not** (an employee, intern, trainee, contract worker, volunteer, visitor, client, or a **domestic worker**).
- **'Workplace'** is wide: government and private offices, factories, hospitals, sports facilities, universities, the unorganised sector, a **dwelling house** where a domestic worker works, and **any place visited in the course of employment**, including **transport** provided by the employer, client sites, offsites and, as generally understood today, virtual work settings.

steps.title: What counts as sexual harassment
Employer's legal duties
Common myths
steps.body:
- 'POSH applies only to physical touching': **remarks, messages and gestures** are covered.
- 'Only employees are protected': visitors, interns, clients and domestic workers are too.
- 'Small firms are exempt': the **Local Committee** covers them.
- 'Men can file POSH complaints': the **Act protects women**. Many companies have **gender-neutral policies** voluntarily, and men can use other laws (e.g., criminal law) for harassment.

steps.title: For managers and bystanders
steps.body:
- If someone tells you, **listen, don't judge**, and tell them about the IC. Don't try to 'settle it informally'.
- Don't share details; **confidentiality** is a legal duty.
- If you witness harassment, you can support the woman, record what you saw, and be a witness.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find your organisation's **POSH policy** and IC members' names. If you can't find them, that itself is a compliance gap to raise with HR.

lessons.title: Filing and handling a POSH complaint

scenes.text: The Internal Committee at Ritika's company, chaired by Ms Anjali Rao, receives her complaint with screenshots, within a month of the last incident.
Ritika asks for interim relief. The IC recommends she report to a different lead during the inquiry.
Vikram gets a copy and replies. Both are heard separately, witnesses are examined, and the hearing notes are kept confidential.
Within 90 days, the IC finds the allegations proved. The company issues a written warning, withholds his promotion, orders sensitisation training and compensation from his salary.

steps.title: How to file
steps.body:
1. **Write a complaint** to the IC (or the Local Committee). If she cannot write, an IC member must **help** her put it in writing. Include: who, what, when, where, witnesses, and evidence (messages, emails, screenshots).
2. **Time limit**: within **three months** of the incident, or of the **last incident** in a series. The IC may **extend by another three months** if circumstances prevented her from filing.
3. If she cannot file because of physical or mental incapacity or death, a **relative, friend, co-worker** or others specified by the Rules may file.
4. Ask for **interim relief** if needed.
5. She can **also** file a **police complaint** for criminal offences (for example under BNS Section 75 for sexual harassment, Section 78 for stalking); POSH is a civil workplace remedy and does not bar criminal action.

steps.title: The process and timelines
steps.body:
- **Conciliation** (Section 10): only **at the woman's request**, before inquiry; **no monetary settlement** can be the basis of conciliation.
- **Inquiry**: the IC sends the complaint to the respondent (generally within **7 working days**); the respondent replies (generally within **10 working days**). The IC follows principles of **natural justice**: both sides are heard and may give evidence. Lawyers are generally not allowed to represent parties at the hearing.
- **Complete the inquiry within 90 days.**
- **Report** to the employer within **10 days** after completion.
- The employer must **act on the recommendations within 60 days**.
- **Interim relief** (Section 12) during inquiry: transfer of the woman or respondent, **leave up to three months** for the woman (in addition to her regular leave), or restraining the respondent from reporting on her work or appraisal.
- **Appeal** against the recommendations: within **90 days** to the appellate authority under service rules or as notified.

steps.title: Outcomes, confidentiality and false complaints
steps.body:
If proved, the IC may recommend **action under service rules** (warning, withholding promotion or increment, termination, counselling, community service) and **compensation** to the woman, deducted from the respondent's salary or paid by him, considering her mental trauma, loss of career opportunity, medical expenses, and his income.

**Confidentiality** (Section 16): the identity and addresses of the woman, respondent and witnesses, and the inquiry details, **must not be published** or made known to the public or media. Breach is punishable under service rules.

**False or malicious complaints** (Section 14): action can be taken only if the complaint was **knowingly false or malicious**. **Mere inability to prove** a complaint is **not** malicious. This protects genuine complainants from retaliation.

steps.title: Mistakes ICs and HR must avoid
steps.body:
- Asking the woman why she 'waited so long' or about her clothing or personal life.
- Pressuring for a 'compromise' or settlement.
- Leaking details or letting the respondent supervise her during the inquiry.
- Having an IC without an **external member**, or with fewer than half women; such a committee can be challenged.
- Missing the **90-day** deadline.

steps.title: Other channels
steps.body: Women in government and private workplaces can also register complaints on the government's **SHe-Box** portal, which forwards them to the concerned IC/LC. In an emergency, call **112**. The women helpline **181** offers support and referral. Free legal aid: **15100**.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** If you or someone you know is in danger, call **112** now. Child in danger: **1098** (Childline). Women in distress: **181**. Cyber fraud: **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in. Mental-health support: **14416** (Tele-MANAS). **Free legal aid: NALSA 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority. Section numbers and procedures change, so confirm the details for your case with a lawyer or legal-aid counsel.

a.text: You are the IC Presiding Officer. A junior employee, Sana, files a complaint against a senior director about repeated sexual remarks over four months. The last incident was six weeks ago.

options: Three months from the (last) incident, extendable by three months

lessons.title: The Domestic Violence Act: protection at home

scenes.text: Fatima, 31, in Hyderabad, lives with her husband and in-laws. She is not beaten, but she is insulted daily, her salary is taken, and her phone is checked.
'It's not violence if he doesn't hit me,' she tells her sister Zainab. Zainab says, 'The law says emotional and economic abuse are violence too.'
Fatima calls 181. She is connected to a Protection Officer, who helps her file a domestic incident report and an application before the Magistrate.
The Magistrate passes a protection order, a residence order allowing her to stay in the home, and orders monetary relief. Her salary account is hers again.

steps.title: Who the Act protects
steps.body:
The **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 (PWDVA)** gives **quick civil remedies** to an **'aggrieved person'**: a **woman** who is or has been in a **domestic relationship** with the respondent.

A **domestic relationship** means living together (now or at any time) in a **shared household** and being related by **marriage**, a **relationship in the nature of marriage** (such as a live-in relationship), **blood**, **adoption** or as **family members in a joint family**. So **wives, live-in partners, mothers, sisters, daughters, widows** can all use it.

Respondents: the husband or male partner and his relatives; after **Hiral Harsora (2016)**, the Supreme Court held complaints can be against **female relatives** too, as the words 'adult male' were struck down.

steps.title: Four forms of domestic violence (Section 3)
steps.body:
- **Physical abuse**: hurting, endangering life, limb or health.
- **Sexual abuse**: any conduct of a sexual nature that abuses, humiliates, degrades or violates her dignity.
- **Verbal and emotional abuse**: insults, ridicule, humiliation, name-calling, especially about **not having a child or a male child**; repeated threats of violence to her or someone she cares about.
- **Economic abuse**: depriving her of money or resources she needs or is entitled to (including **stridhan**, household necessities, rent), disposing of her assets, or restricting her access to the shared household or resources.

**Harassing her or her relatives for dowry** is also domestic violence.

steps.title: What the Magistrate can order
steps.body:
- **Protection order** (Section 18): stop the violence, stop contact, stop entering her workplace, stop operating joint bank accounts or alienating assets.
- **Residence order** (Section 19): she **cannot be thrown out** of the **shared household**; the respondent may be removed, or alternative accommodation provided. In **Satish Chander Ahuja (2020)** the Supreme Court held a shared household can include the **in-laws' house** where she lived in a domestic relationship.
- **Monetary relief** (Section 20): expenses, loss of earnings, medical costs, maintenance for her and children.
- **Custody order** (Section 21): temporary custody of children.
- **Compensation** (Section 22): for injuries including mental torture and emotional distress.
- **Interim and ex parte orders** (Section 23): urgent relief, even before the other side is heard.

The first hearing should ordinarily be within **3 days**, and the case decided within **60 days**. **Breach of a protection order is a criminal offence** (Section 31).

steps.title: How to get help, step by step
steps.body:
1. In danger now: call **112**.
2. Call the **Women Helpline 181** or go to a **One Stop Centre (Sakhi)**, which provides medical aid, police help, legal aid, counselling and temporary shelter under one roof.
3. Contact the district **Protection Officer** (appointed under the Act) or a registered **service provider** (NGO). They help record a **Domestic Incident Report (DIR)** and file an application.
4. Or apply **directly to the Magistrate**, with a free legal-aid lawyer (**15100**; all women qualify).
5. Keep **evidence**: medical records, photos, messages, witnesses, bank statements.
6. Remedies under the DV Act can be sought **alongside** others: criminal complaint (BNS Section 85 for cruelty), maintenance (BNSS Section 144), divorce.

steps.title: Common myths
steps.body:
- 'It's only violence if he hits me': emotional and economic abuse are covered.
- 'I'll lose my home if I complain': a **residence order** protects her right to stay.
- 'Live-in partners have no rights': relationships in the nature of marriage are covered.
- 'I must first file a police case': the DV Act is a **civil** remedy before a Magistrate; police involvement is not a precondition.

steps.title: Being a good friend or relative
steps.body: Believe her, avoid blaming ('why don't you just leave?'), help make a **safety plan** (important documents, some money, a bag, a code word with a friend), and share 181, 112 and 15100. Leaving is a process; respect her pace, but act at once if her life is in danger.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** If you or someone you know is in danger, call **112** now. Child in danger: **1098** (Childline). Women in distress: **181**. Cyber fraud: **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in. Mental-health support: **14416** (Tele-MANAS). **Free legal aid: NALSA 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority. Section numbers and procedures change, so confirm the details for your case with a lawyer or legal-aid counsel.

lessons.title: Dowry, cruelty and dowry death

scenes.text: Before Priyanka's wedding in Kanpur, the groom's family asks for 'a car and ₹10 lakh, as everyone gives'. Her father, Mr Mishra, feels he has no choice.
After the wedding, the demands continue. Priyanka is taunted and denied food when her father cannot pay more.
Her friend Ruth convinces her to call 181. With legal aid, Priyanka files a complaint of cruelty for dowry and applies under the DV Act.
Police register a case; her stridhan is ordered returned. Mr Mishra realises that giving dowry was also an offence, and joins a campaign to end it in his community.

steps.title: The Dowry Prohibition Act 1961
steps.body:
**Dowry** means any property or valuable security **given or agreed to be given**, directly or indirectly, by one party to a marriage (or their parents or anyone else) to the other, **in connection with the marriage**, before, at, or any time after it. (Mahr under Muslim personal law is excluded.)

- **Giving, taking or abetting** dowry: imprisonment of **at least five years** and a fine of **at least ₹15,000** or the value of the dowry, whichever is more (Section 3).
- **Demanding** dowry directly or indirectly: imprisonment of **six months to two years** and fine (Section 4).
- **Advertising** an offer of money or property in exchange for marriage is also punishable.
- **Gifts** given **without any demand** at the time of marriage are not dowry, if they are customary, reasonable for the giver's means, and recorded in a **list** signed by both sides (Section 3(2)).
- Dowry received by anyone other than the bride must be **transferred to her** (Section 6).
- Offences are **cognizable** and **non-bailable**. States appoint **Dowry Prohibition Officers**.

steps.title: BNS provisions (in force from 1 July 2024)
steps.body:
- **Cruelty by husband or his relatives** (BNS **Section 85**, formerly IPC 498A): imprisonment up to three years and fine. **Cruelty** (Section 86) means wilful conduct likely to drive the woman to suicide or cause grave injury or danger to her life, limb or health (mental or physical), **or** harassment to coerce her or her relatives to meet an unlawful demand for property (such as dowry).
- **Dowry death** (BNS **Section 80**, formerly IPC 304B): if a woman dies by burns, bodily injury or otherwise than in normal circumstances **within seven years of marriage**, and it is shown that **soon before her death** she was subjected to cruelty or harassment by her husband or his relatives in connection with dowry, it is a dowry death. Punishment: **not less than seven years**, which may extend to **life imprisonment**.
- The law of evidence includes a **presumption** in such cases against the accused once these facts are shown.
- **Abetment of suicide** is also an offence.

steps.title: Stridhan: her property
steps.body: **Stridhan** (gifts to the woman before, at or after marriage, from her family, in-laws or friends, including jewellery) is the **woman's absolute property**. In-laws or the husband hold it, if at all, in **trust** for her. Refusing to return it can be a criminal offence (criminal breach of trust) and economic abuse under the DV Act. Keep **photos and lists** of jewellery and gifts.

steps.title: Balance: protection and fairness
steps.body: These laws protect women from serious, often deadly abuse. Courts have also cautioned against **false or exaggerated** complaints that rope in distant relatives. The Supreme Court in **Arnesh Kumar (2014)** directed that police must **not arrest automatically** in cruelty cases, but follow the necessity checklist (now reflected in **BNSS Section 35**). For complainants, the advice is simple: **state facts accurately**; accurate complaints are the strongest.

steps.title: Changing the culture
steps.body:
- Refuse to attend weddings where dowry is demanded; speak up in family groups.
- Many young people now write **'no dowry'** in their matrimonial profiles.
- Parents: investing in a daughter's **education and property rights** (equal inheritance since 2005) is the real security, not dowry.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write a short message you could send to a family WhatsApp group explaining, kindly but clearly, that **giving and taking dowry are both crimes**, with one fact from this lesson.

steps.title: General education, not legal advice
steps.body: **This is general education, not legal advice.** If you or someone you know is in danger, call **112** now. Child in danger: **1098** (Childline). Women in distress: **181**. Cyber fraud: **1930** or cybercrime.gov.in. Mental-health support: **14416** (Tele-MANAS). **Free legal aid: NALSA 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority. Section numbers and procedures change, so confirm the details for your case with a lawyer or legal-aid counsel.

statements.s: Cruelty by a husband or relatives is now punished under BNS Section 85.

statements.s: A dowry death can only be charged if death occurs within one year of marriage.
statements.why: Within seven years of marriage.

statements.s: Stridhan belongs to the in-laws once given at the wedding.

statements.s: Police should not arrest automatically in every cruelty complaint without assessing necessity.

lessons.title: The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act

scenes.text: In a village in Madhya Pradesh, Dalit groom Rakesh plans to ride a horse in his wedding procession. A group threatens to stop it and to 'boycott' his family.
His sister Sunita, a law student, calls the National Helpline Against Atrocities and the police.
Police register an FIR under the SC/ST Act for threats and social boycott, and provide protection. The procession goes ahead.
Later, the Special Court hears the case quickly. The family receives relief under the Act's rules. 'The Constitution rode with us,' says Rakesh.

steps.title: Why a special law?
steps.body: **Article 17** abolished untouchability, and the **Protection of Civil Rights Act 1955** punishes its practice. But violence and humiliation against Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes continued, often with weak enforcement. Parliament therefore passed the **Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989**, with stronger offences, special courts and duties on officials. It was **strengthened in 2015 and 2018**.

steps.title: Examples of atrocities (Section 3)
Procedure and victims' rights
steps.body:
- **Exclusive Special Courts** and Special Public Prosecutors; the **charge-sheet** should be filed within **60 days**, and the trial completed within **two months** of the charge-sheet as far as possible.
- **Chapter IVA (2015)**: rights of victims and witnesses: protection, to be informed of every court proceeding, to be heard on bail, to get relief, travel and maintenance expenses, and free legal aid.
- **Relief and rehabilitation** amounts under the SC/ST (PoA) Rules 1995, paid in stages.
- **2018 amendment (Section 18A)**: no **preliminary enquiry** is needed before registering an FIR, and no prior approval is needed for arresting an accused. This restored the law after the Supreme Court's 2018 *Subhash Kashinath Mahajan* guidelines; in **Prathvi Raj Chauhan (2020)** the Court upheld the amendment, while noting courts can still grant anticipatory bail where **no prima facie case** is made out.
- **National Helpline Against Atrocities**: **14566**.

steps.title: Manual scavenging is banned

lessons.title: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016

scenes.text: Arjun, 21, in Bhubaneswar, has a specific learning disability (dyslexia) and is preparing for a competitive exam.
The exam notice says scribes are allowed only for 'blind candidates'. Arjun's friend Nisha, who uses a wheelchair, faces an exam hall on the second floor with no lift.
Their professor shows them the RPwD Act and a 2021 Supreme Court judgment recognising the right to a scribe as a reasonable accommodation, even for disabilities below the benchmark.
They write to the exam body and the State Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities. Arjun gets a scribe and extra time; Nisha's centre is moved to the ground floor.

steps.title: A rights-based law
steps.body:
The **Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (RPwD Act)** replaced the 1995 Act and implements the **UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD)**, which India ratified in 2007. It shifts from charity to **rights**: equality, dignity, non-discrimination, full participation, accessibility and respect for difference.

It recognises **21 specified disabilities**, including blindness, low vision, locomotor disability, hearing impairment, speech and language disability, intellectual disability, **autism spectrum disorder**, **specific learning disabilities**, **mental illness**, cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophy, multiple sclerosis, **thalassemia, haemophilia, sickle cell disease**, Parkinson's disease, **acid attack victims**, dwarfism, leprosy-cured persons and multiple disabilities.

A **'person with benchmark disability'** has at least **40%** of a specified disability, certified by an authority; some benefits (like reservation) apply to benchmark disabilities.

steps.title: Key rights and entitlements
steps.body:
- **Non-discrimination**: no discrimination on the ground of disability unless shown to be a proportionate means to a legitimate aim.
- **Reasonable accommodation**: necessary and appropriate modifications that do not impose a disproportionate burden (ramps, scribes, extra time, accessible software, flexible hours).
- **Education**: free education for children with benchmark disabilities aged **6 to 18**; inclusive education in schools; at least **5%** of seats reserved in government and government-aided **higher education** institutions, with an upper age relaxation of five years.
- **Employment**: at least **4%** reservation in government jobs for persons with benchmark disabilities; private employers must have an equal opportunity policy.
- **Accessibility**: public buildings, transport and digital services must meet accessibility standards within timelines.
- **Legal capacity**: persons with disabilities have equal legal capacity; **limited guardianship** with joint decision-making instead of full substitution.
- **UDID card**: a Unique Disability ID card for certification and benefits.

steps.title: Enforcement and offences
steps.body:
- **Chief Commissioner** (national) and **State Commissioners** for Persons with Disabilities can inquire into complaints and recommend action.
- **Special Courts** in each district for offences under the Act.
- **Offences** (Section 92): intentionally insulting or intimidating a person with disability **in public view** to humiliate them, assaulting or using force to dishonour them, denying food or fluids by someone in charge, and sexually exploiting a dependent person with disability are punishable with **six months to five years** and fine.

In **Vikash Kumar v UPSC (2021)**, the Supreme Court held that the right to a scribe is part of reasonable accommodation and cannot be denied only because a disability is below the 40% benchmark, where the condition affects writing.

steps.title: Common mistakes (and better language)
steps.body:
- Saying 'suffering from', 'handicapped' or 'normal vs disabled'. Prefer **person with a disability** or the term the person uses.
- Treating accessibility as a favour: it is a **legal obligation**.
- Assuming invisible disabilities (learning disabilities, mental illness, thalassemia) are not 'real'; they are recognised.
- Talking to a companion instead of the person with a disability.

lessons.title: Gender identity and sexual orientation: what Indian law says

scenes.text: Ananya, 24, a transgender woman from Thiruvananthapuram, has a college degree in her old name and gender. Employers keep asking questions.
She applies on the National Portal for Transgender Persons for a certificate of identity from the District Magistrate.
With the certificate she updates her Aadhaar, PAN and degree. A company with an inclusion policy hires her as a data analyst.
When a landlord refuses to rent to her 'because she is transgender', she quotes the 2019 Act, which prohibits such discrimination, and finds a better flat.

steps.title: NALSA v Union of India (2014)
Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019
steps.body:
- **Prohibits discrimination** against transgender persons in **education, employment, healthcare, housing, access to public places and services**, holding public or private office, and the right to move freely.
- **Recognition of identity**: a transgender person may apply to the **District Magistrate** for a **certificate of identity** as transgender (no medical examination required for this certificate). A change to 'male' or 'female' after gender-affirming surgery can be applied for with supporting documents. Applications can be made online on the **National Portal for Transgender Persons**.
- **Right to residence** with one's family; a child cannot be separated from parents on the ground of being transgender except by court order.
- Governments must provide **healthcare** (including gender-affirming care and HIV care), **inclusive education** and welfare schemes; establishments must designate a **complaint officer**.
- **Offences**: forced or bonded labour (other than compulsory public service), denial of use of public places, forcing out of home or village, and **physical, sexual, verbal, emotional or economic abuse** are punishable (six months to two years, and fine).
- A **National Council for Transgender Persons** advises the government.

The Act has been **criticised** by many in the community, for example for the certificate process and for penalties lower than for similar offences against others; some of these issues are before the courts.

steps.title: Sexual orientation: Navtej Singh Johar (2018)
steps.body:
In **Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India (2018)**, a five-judge bench **decriminalised consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex** by reading down **Section 377 IPC**. It held that sexual orientation is a natural and essential part of identity, and that criminalising consensual adult relations violated equality, dignity, privacy and free expression. (Non-consensual acts and acts with minors remained offences.)

The **BNS (2023)**, in force from 1 July 2024, does **not include** an equivalent of Section 377. Commentators have pointed out that this left no specific provision for **non-consensual** sexual offences against adult men, an issue raised before the government and courts.

steps.title: Same-sex marriage: Supriyo Chakraborty (2023)
steps.body:
In **October 2023**, a five-judge bench of the Supreme Court **declined to legalise same-sex marriage** through interpretation, holding that changing the **Special Marriage Act** or creating a marriage right is for **Parliament**. All judges agreed that queer persons have the right to **choose a partner** and live together **without harassment or violence**, and that the State should protect them. The government said it would set up a committee to examine practical entitlements of queer couples (like ration cards, joint bank accounts, medical decisions).

So, as of this lesson's writing: **same-sex relationships are legal; same-sex marriages are not legally recognised in India**; transgender persons in heterosexual relationships can marry under existing laws (some High Courts have recognised such marriages).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up **gender identity** and **sexual orientation**.
- Saying 'homosexuality is illegal in India': **consensual adult** same-sex relations are **not** a crime since 2018.
- Forcing 'conversion therapy': the **National Medical Commission** has declared conversion therapy professional misconduct, and the Madras High Court has directed action against it.
- Outing someone without consent: it can endanger them and violates privacy.

steps.title: Support
steps.body: If you are facing family pressure, violence or discrimination: call **112** in danger, **14416** (Tele-MANAS) for mental-health support, and **15100** for free legal aid. Courts have granted **police protection** to couples (including same-sex couples) facing threats.

courses.title: India's new criminal laws: BNS, BNSS and BSA in plain language
courses.summary: Since 1 July 2024, India's criminal law runs on three new codes: the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), which replaced the IPC; the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which replaced the CrPC; and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), which replaced the Indian Evidence Act. This course explains what changed and what did not: new and removed offences, community service, Zero FIR and e-FIR, timelines, forensics, electronic evidence, victims' rights, and how old cases are handled. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can name the three new laws, what each replaced, and the date they came into force
Learners can map common offences from old IPC sections to new BNS sections
Learners can list new offences (organised crime, terrorism, mob lynching, snatching) and offences omitted
Learners can explain key BNSS procedures: Zero FIR, e-FIR, preliminary enquiry, forensics, timelines, trial in absentia
