lessons.title: The big picture: three new laws

scenes.text: Inspector Meenakshi Iyer in Chennai handles two theft cases on the same day in July 2024: one theft happened on 28 June 2024, the other on 3 July 2024.
Trainee constable Arif asks, 'Do we use the IPC or the BNS?'
She explains: the offence of 28 June is governed by the IPC, because criminal law cannot apply retrospectively; the 3 July case is under the BNS. Procedure for new FIRs follows the BNSS.
Arif makes a note: 'Date of offence decides the penal law. Pending old cases continue under old procedure.'

steps.title: What replaced what
steps.body:
- **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS)** replaced the **Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC)**. It defines **offences and punishments**. It has **358 sections** (the IPC had 511).
- **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS)** replaced the **Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC)**. It sets the **procedure**: FIR, investigation, arrest, bail, trial, appeals. It has **531 sections**.
- **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (BSA)** replaced the **Indian Evidence Act, 1872**. It governs **what evidence is admissible and how facts are proved**. It has **170 sections**.

Parliament passed them in **December 2023**; they came **into force on 1 July 2024** across India.

steps.title: Stated aims
steps.body:
The government described the aims as: replacing colonial-era laws with laws focused on **justice (nyaya)** rather than punishment (danda); **victim-centric** procedures; **speedier trials** through fixed timelines; use of **technology** (e-FIR, electronic summons, video hearings, digital evidence); and **forensics** in serious crimes.

Much of the substance **remains similar** to the old laws: most offences, defences (like private defence), and principles (like presumption of innocence, the bar on confessions to police) continue, often with new section numbers.

steps.title: Which law applies to old cases?
steps.body:
- **Penal law (what offence, what punishment)**: decided by the **date the offence was committed**. Offences committed **before 1 July 2024** remain governed by the **IPC**; under **Article 20(1)**, a person cannot be punished under a law that was not in force when the act was done, or more heavily than the law then allowed.
- **Procedure**: under the BNSS's savings clause (**Section 531**), appeals, applications, trials, inquiries and investigations **pending** immediately before 1 July 2024 continue under the **CrPC** as it stood. New proceedings started after that date follow the BNSS.

So for some years courts will apply **both** the old and new laws, depending on dates. **Never assume the IPC is the current law** for new offences: it is not.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Quoting 'Section 420' or 'Section 302' for a crime committed today: the BNS equivalents are **318 (cheating)** and **103 (murder)**.
- Thinking everything changed: much of the old law was carried over with re-numbering.
- Thinking old cases were cancelled: they continue under the old laws as explained above.

lessons.title: BNS: what's new, what's gone, what's renumbered

scenes.text: Every morning in Lucknow, law student Zoya reads crime news with her grandfather, a retired judge, who still says 'IPC 420'.
They play a game: for each story, Zoya names the new BNS section. Chain snatching? Section 304, a new specific offence. A group lynching? Section 103(2).
A drunk man creating a scene in public gets community service as punishment. Grandfather is surprised: 'That was never in the IPC!'
By Sunday, he is saying 'BNS 318' for cheating. 'Old judge, new tricks,' he laughs.

steps.title: Common offences: old IPC → new BNS
steps.body:
- Murder: IPC 302 → **BNS 103**
- Culpable homicide not amounting to murder: IPC 304 → **BNS 105**
- Causing death by negligence: IPC 304A → **BNS 106**
- Dowry death: IPC 304B → **BNS 80**
- Abetment of suicide: IPC 306 → **BNS 108**
- Attempt to murder: IPC 307 → **BNS 109**
- Rape: IPC 375/376 → **BNS 63/64**
- Sexual harassment: IPC 354A → **BNS 75**
- Voyeurism: IPC 354C → **BNS 77**
- Stalking: IPC 354D → **BNS 78**
- Cruelty by husband/relatives: IPC 498A → **BNS 85**
- Theft: IPC 379 → **BNS 303**
- Extortion: IPC 384 → **BNS 308**
- Cheating: IPC 420 → **BNS 318**
- Criminal intimidation: IPC 506 → **BNS 351**
- Defamation: IPC 499/500 → **BNS 356**

steps.title: New offences
steps.body:
- **Organised crime** (Section 111) and **petty organised crime** (Section 112): continuing unlawful activity by crime syndicates, including kidnapping, extortion, land grabbing, contract killing, economic offences, **cyber-crimes** and trafficking.
- **Terrorist act** (Section 113): brought into the general penal code (special laws like the UAPA also continue).
- **Murder by a group of five or more** on grounds of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any similar ground (Section 103(2), often called **mob lynching**): punishable with death or life imprisonment.
- **Snatching** (Section 304): a specific offence for suddenly seizing movable property (like chain or phone snatching).
- **Sexual intercourse by deceitful means** (Section 69), including a **false promise of marriage** made without intending to fulfil it, or false promises of employment or promotion, or suppressing identity.
- **Acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India** (Section 152).
- Offences against **children** are grouped together, and 'child' means a person under 18. 'Gender' is defined to **include transgender** persons.

steps.title: Omitted or changed
steps.body:
- **Sedition** (IPC 124A) is **not in the BNS** as such; the Supreme Court had put it on hold in 2022. **Section 152** now punishes acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; critics and supporters debate how it differs in practice.
- **Adultery** (IPC 497), already struck down in *Joseph Shine (2018)*, is omitted.
- **Section 377** is omitted (see *Navtej Johar, 2018*).
- **Attempt to suicide** is not a general offence; Section 226 punishes only an attempt to commit suicide to **compel or restrain a public servant**.
- The **marital rape exception** is retained for wives aged **18 and above**; challenges to its constitutionality are before the Supreme Court.
- Many **fines** and some **minimum punishments** were increased, for example for causing death by negligence (up to five years).

steps.title: Community service: a new punishment
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying 'sedition is gone so anything goes': Section 152 and other laws still apply to acts endangering India's sovereignty.
- Quoting 'BNS 302' for murder: **302 in the BNS** is a different offence (deliberately wounding religious feelings by words). Murder is **103**.
- Thinking community service applies to serious crimes: it is for **specified petty** offences only.

lessons.title: BNSS: new procedures from FIR to judgment

scenes.text: Kiran, a nurse travelling from Pune to Delhi, is assaulted and robbed on the train somewhere in Madhya Pradesh. She reaches Delhi shaken.
At the nearest Delhi police station, the officer registers a Zero FIR, gives her a free copy, and transfers it to the station with jurisdiction.
The investigating officer later updates her by SMS. A forensic team examines the evidence; her statement is recorded on video.
Within 90 days she is informed of the progress. 'I didn't have to go back to the place where it happened to start the case,' she says.

steps.title: FIR: Zero FIR, e-FIR and preliminary enquiry
steps.body:
- **Zero FIR** (Section 173): information about a cognizable offence can be given at **any police station**, **regardless of where the offence happened**; it is registered and transferred. This practice existed before, but is now written into the law.
- **e-FIR**: information can be given **by electronic communication**; the informant must **sign it within three days** for it to be taken on record.
- **Free copy of FIR** to the informant or victim.
- **Preliminary enquiry** (Section 173(3)): for offences punishable with **three to seven years**, police may, with a senior officer's permission, conduct a preliminary enquiry within **14 days** to see if a prima facie case exists, or proceed with investigation.
- If police refuse, send the complaint to the **Superintendent of Police** (173(4)) and then apply to the **Magistrate** (175(3)); the Magistrate may also consider the police officer's report.

steps.title: Investigation: technology and forensics
steps.body:
- **Audio-video recording** of search and seizure, including preparation of the list of seized items (Section 105).
- **Forensic experts must visit** the crime scene for offences punishable with **seven years or more** (Section 176(3)).
- Statements of victims of certain sexual offences are recorded by a **woman Magistrate** where possible, with audio-video recording.
- **Electronic summons** and warrants, and hearings by **electronic means**, are allowed.
- Police can seek **police custody** of up to 15 days in total, in **parts**, during the first 40 or 60 days of detention (depending on the offence), a change that has been debated.
- Police may use **handcuffs** at arrest in specified serious cases (such as habitual offenders, escapees, terrorism, organised crime) (Section 43(3)).
- Each police station displays information on **arrested persons**, and a **designated officer** maintains it (Section 37).

steps.title: Timelines for faster justice
steps.body:
- Victims are to be informed of investigation **progress within 90 days** (Section 193).
- **Framing of charges** generally within **60 days** of the first hearing on charge (Section 251).
- **Judgment** within **30 days** of the end of arguments, extendable to **45 days** for reasons (Section 258).
- **Trial in absentia** (Section 356): a **proclaimed offender** who absconds to avoid trial can be tried and judged in their absence, under conditions, so that cases don't stall.
- **Plea bargaining** applications within a fixed time after charges.
- **Undertrial bail** (Section 479): a **first-time offender** who has served **one-third** of the maximum sentence is to be released on bail (one-half for others), except for offences punishable with death or life imprisonment.

These timelines depend on enough judges, prosecutors and forensic labs; how well they work in practice is being studied.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Police must register FIR only where the crime happened': **Zero FIR** applies everywhere.
- 'An e-FIR is complete when I send the email': you must **sign within three days**.
- 'Section 154 CrPC' for an FIR today: it is **BNSS Section 173**.
- 'Anticipatory bail is gone': it remains, under **BNSS Section 482**.

lessons.title: BSA: evidence in the digital age, and putting it all together

scenes.text: Shopkeeper Harish in Indore is cheated by a supplier who took ₹3 lakh by UPI and vanished. All he has are WhatsApp chats and UPI screenshots.
'Will the court even accept phone screenshots?' he asks his lawyer, Advocate Pinto.
She explains: under the BSA, electronic records are documents; with the required certificate (Section 63) and the bank's records, they can prove the case.
The bank's statement, the platform's records and a certified copy of the chats are produced. The supplier is convicted of cheating under BNS Section 318.

steps.title: Electronic evidence under the BSA
steps.body:
- **'Document'** expressly includes **electronic and digital records**: emails, server logs, documents on computers, laptops or smartphones, messages, websites, locational evidence and voice-mail messages stored on digital devices.
- **'Evidence'** includes information given **electronically**, so witnesses and experts may depose by electronic means where allowed.
- An electronic or digital record can be **primary evidence** in specified situations (for example, where it is created or stored simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each file is primary evidence).
- **Section 63** (the successor to Section 65B of the old Evidence Act): to admit a copy of an electronic record, a **certificate** in the prescribed format is generally required, signed by the person in charge of the device **and** by an **expert**, describing the device and stating the record's integrity (such as hash values).
- **Secondary evidence** now expressly includes oral and written admissions and the evidence of a skilled person who has examined voluminous documents.

steps.title: Principles that did not change
steps.body:
- A **confession to a police officer** is **not admissible** against the accused (BSA Section 23), and a confession while in police custody is inadmissible unless made before a Magistrate. Only a **fact discovered** in consequence of information from an accused in custody may be proved.
- The **burden of proof** lies on the prosecution; the accused is presumed innocent.
- **Dying declarations**, expert opinion, documentary evidence and witness examination (examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination) continue with re-numbering.
- Colonial-era references (to the British Crown, London Gazette, etc.) have been removed.

steps.title: Putting it together: if you are a victim of a crime today
steps.body:
1. **Safety first**: call **112**.
2. **FIR** at any police station (Zero FIR) or online (e-FIR, sign within 3 days); get a **free copy** (BNSS 173).
3. **Preserve evidence**: photos, chats, CCTV locations, medical reports. Keep originals; note device details for a Section 63 certificate later.
4. **Medical examination** promptly if hurt (and for sexual offences, the report is to be sent within **seven days**).
5. **Follow up**: you are to be informed of progress within **90 days**.
6. **Victim compensation**: apply to the DLSA (BNSS 396).
7. **Free legal aid**: **15100**; women and children always qualify.

**If you are accused**: stay calm; ask for the **grounds of arrest**, inform a relative, ask for a **lawyer** (free legal aid if needed), insist on production before a **Magistrate within 24 hours**, and do not sign anything you don't understand.

steps.title: Debates to know about
steps.body: Supporters highlight technology, victims' rights and timelines. Critics and many lawyers have raised concerns, for example about **police custody in parts** across the first 40/60 days, **handcuffing**, the breadth of **Section 152** and organised-crime provisions, and the **retention of the marital rape exception**. Courts will interpret these provisions over time. A good citizen knows **both** the law and the debate.

lessons.title: What are human rights, and where did they come from?

scenes.text: In Dharamshala, 15-year-old Pema asks her grandmother Dolma what life was like before 'rights' were common words.
Dolma remembers her own father talking about the Second World War, when millions were killed and governments said, 'What we do to our own people is our business.'
'After that war,' she says, 'the world agreed that some things can never be done to any human, anywhere. They wrote it down in 1948.'
Pema looks at her school ID, her library card, her right to speak in class. 'So rights are promises the whole world made after learning the hard way.'

steps.title: The idea
steps.body:
**Human rights** are basic rights and freedoms that belong to **every person**, simply because they are human, regardless of nationality, sex, caste, religion, language, colour or any other status. They are often described as:

- **Universal**: for everyone, everywhere.
- **Inalienable**: they cannot be taken away, though some can be limited by law in specific situations (for example, liberty after a fair trial).
- **Indivisible and interdependent**: civil and political rights (like free speech and fair trial) and economic, social and cultural rights (like education, health and work) support each other.

Many cultures and religions taught dignity, justice and compassion long before modern law. The modern system of human rights was built mainly in the **20th century**.

steps.title: Milestones
steps.body:
- **1215** Magna Carta (England): limited the king's power; the idea that rulers are under the law.
- **1689** English Bill of Rights: limits on the monarchy, rights of Parliament.
- **1776** US Declaration of Independence: 'all men are created equal', though slavery continued.
- **1789** French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
- **1864** First Geneva Convention: care for wounded soldiers.
- **1919** International Labour Organization founded: workers' rights.
- **1945** United Nations Charter: promotes 'respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all'.
- **1948** Universal Declaration of Human Rights (10 December).
- **1966** Two International Covenants (civil-political; economic-social-cultural), in force from **1976**.

Early documents often protected only some people (property-owning men, citizens, one race). The struggle to include **everyone** (women, enslaved people, colonised peoples, minorities, children, persons with disabilities) is a big part of the story. India's freedom movement and leaders like **Gandhi** and **Ambedkar** contributed powerful ideas about dignity and equality.

steps.title: Rights and duties together
steps.body:
Rights create **duties**:

- **States** have the main duty: to **respect** (not violate), **protect** (stop others from violating) and **fulfil** (take steps so people can enjoy rights, such as building schools).
- **Individuals** also have duties to others and to the community (UDHR Article 29).

Example: your right to free speech means the government must not jail you for criticism (respect), must protect you from a mob attacking you for your views (protect), and should support a free press and public libraries (fulfil). Your duty: don't use speech to incite violence against others.

steps.title: Common misunderstandings
steps.body:
- 'Human rights are only for good people': they belong to **everyone**, including people accused of crimes (for example, the right to a fair trial and freedom from torture).
- 'Rights mean I can do anything I want': most rights have **limits** that protect others' rights and public order.
- 'Human rights are a Western idea': people from all regions, including India, China, Lebanon, Latin America and Africa, shaped the modern documents.

lessons.title: The UDHR: 30 articles that changed the world

scenes.text: In 1947–48, the UN Commission on Human Rights, with Eleanor Roosevelt as chair, drafts a declaration. An early draft of Article 1 says 'All men are born free and equal'.
India's delegate, Hansa Mehta, a freedom fighter and educationist, argues that 'men' may be read to exclude women.
The final text reads: 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.'
In Mumbai, college student Riya reads this in her textbook. 'Two words,' she says, 'and half the world was written in.'

steps.title: How it was made
steps.body:
The UDHR was drafted by the **UN Commission on Human Rights**, chaired by **Eleanor Roosevelt** (USA). Key contributors included **René Cassin** (France), **P. C. Chang** (China), **Charles Malik** (Lebanon), **John Humphrey** (Canada, who prepared the first draft), and **Hansa Mehta** (India).

It was adopted by the **UN General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948** with **48 votes in favour, none against, and 8 abstentions**. **10 December** is celebrated every year as **Human Rights Day**. It has been translated into hundreds of languages, more than almost any other document.

steps.title: The structure of the 30 articles
steps.body:
- **Articles 1–2: foundations**: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights; everyone is entitled to these rights **without distinction** of any kind.
- **Articles 3–21: civil and political rights**: life, liberty and security (3); no **slavery** (4); no **torture** or cruel punishment (5); recognition as a person before the law (6); **equality before the law** (7); remedy (8); no arbitrary arrest (9); **fair and public hearing** (10); **presumption of innocence** (11); **privacy** (12); freedom of **movement** (13); **asylum** (14); **nationality** (15); **marriage** with free and full consent (16); **property** (17); thought, conscience and **religion** (18); opinion and **expression** (19); peaceful **assembly** (20); take part in **government**, free elections (21).
- **Articles 22–27: economic, social and cultural rights**: social security (22); **work**, equal pay, and **trade unions** (23); rest and leisure (24); an adequate **standard of living**, including food, clothing, housing, medical care (25); **education**, free at least at elementary stages (26); cultural life and the benefits of science (27).
- **Articles 28–30: the framework**: a social and international order where rights can be realised (28); **duties to the community** and limits on rights by law to respect others' rights (29); no one may use the Declaration to destroy others' rights (30).

steps.title: Worked examples
steps.body:
- A journalist is jailed for reporting on corruption → **Article 19** (expression), and possibly **9** (arbitrary detention).
- A girl is married at 14 without her consent → **Article 16** (free and full consent), and 26 (education).
- Workers are paid less because they are women → **Article 23** (equal pay for equal work).
- A refugee fleeing war is sent back to danger → **Article 14** (asylum).
- A person is tortured to confess → **Article 5**.
- A child cannot attend school because there is none nearby → **Article 26**.

lessons.title: From declaration to law: treaties, bodies and courts

scenes.text: Mariam, a human-rights lawyer in Nairobi, represents a family whose son disappeared after arrest. National courts have not helped.
Because her country accepted the individual-complaints procedure of the ICCPR, she files a communication with the UN Human Rights Committee.
The Committee finds violations of the rights to life, liberty and a remedy, and asks the State to investigate and compensate.
The 'views' are not a court judgment, but the publicity and pressure lead to a new investigation. 'International law is slow,' Mariam says, 'but it is not silent.'

steps.title: The International Bill of Human Rights
steps.body:
- **UDHR (1948)**
- **International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR, 1966)**: life, liberty, fair trial, expression, religion, assembly, privacy, participation, equality. Monitored by the **Human Rights Committee**. Optional Protocols allow **individual complaints** (for states that accept them) and the **abolition of the death penalty**.
- **International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR, 1966)**: work, social security, family, adequate standard of living, health, education, culture. Rights are to be realised **progressively** to the maximum of available resources.

Both Covenants came into force in **1976**. **India acceded to both in 1979**.

steps.title: Other core treaties
steps.body:
- **CERD (1965)**: elimination of racial discrimination.
- **CEDAW (1979)**: elimination of discrimination against women (India ratified in 1993; the Supreme Court relied on it in *Vishaka*).
- **CAT (1984)**: against torture (India has signed but not ratified).
- **CRC (1989)**: rights of the child; the **most widely ratified** human-rights treaty (India ratified in 1992).
- **CRPD (2006)**: rights of persons with disabilities (India ratified in 2007).
- Others protect migrant workers and people from enforced disappearance.

Each treaty has a **committee of independent experts** (a 'treaty body') that reviews states' periodic reports and issues recommendations.

steps.title: UN bodies and regional systems
steps.body:
- **Human Rights Council** (Geneva, created in **2006**, replacing the Commission on Human Rights): **47 member states** elected by the General Assembly. Its **Universal Periodic Review (UPR)** examines the human-rights record of **every UN member** in turns, every few years.
- **Special Rapporteurs** and working groups report on themes (e.g., freedom of expression, housing) or countries.
- **Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR)** supports the system.

**Regional systems** can be stronger:

- **Europe**: the **European Convention on Human Rights (1950)** and the **European Court of Human Rights** in Strasbourg, where individuals can bring cases against member states; its judgments are binding.
- **Americas**: the Inter-American Commission and Court of Human Rights.
- **Africa**: the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (1981) and the African Court.

There is **no regional human-rights court for Asia**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the **Human Rights Council** (states) with the **Human Rights Committee** (independent experts under the ICCPR).
- Thinking the UN can directly overrule national courts: UN bodies mostly **recommend**; enforcement depends on states, courts and public pressure.
- Confusing the **European Court of Human Rights** (Council of Europe, Strasbourg) with the **EU's Court of Justice** (Luxembourg).

lessons.title: Human rights in India: Commissions and you

scenes.text: In a small town, 22-year-old Raju dies in police custody. Police say he 'fell ill'. His mother, Kamla, does not believe it.
A local activist, Mr Thomas, helps Kamla file a complaint with the National Human Rights Commission online.
The Commission calls for reports, the post-mortem and video records, and directs an independent inquiry.
It recommends compensation for Kamla and disciplinary and criminal action against the officers. Kamla says, 'They thought no one would ask. Someone asked.'

steps.title: The Protection of Human Rights Act 1993
What the Commissions can do
steps.body:
- Inquire into complaints of human-rights violations, or negligence by a public servant in preventing them, on a **complaint** or **on its own** (suo motu), for example from news reports.
- Visit **jails and detention centres**.
- Intervene in court cases involving human-rights issues.
- Recommend **compensation**, **prosecution**, disciplinary action and interim relief to governments; governments must report back on action taken.
- Review laws and promote **human-rights literacy** and research.

NHRC guidelines require authorities to report **custodial deaths** and certain other incidents to it promptly.

**Limits**: the Commissions generally do not take up matters **more than one year** old, matters already **pending before a court or another commission**, or purely private disputes. Their recommendations are **not court decrees**, but courts have held that governments must give them due weight.

steps.title: How to file a complaint
steps.body:
1. Write a short complaint in **any language** (English, Hindi or another language in the Eighth Schedule): who, what, when, where, which official/authority, what relief you seek.
2. Attach evidence: medical reports, FIR copy, photos, news reports.
3. File **online** on the NHRC's complaint portal or by post/hand; State Commissions have their own portals. There is **no fee**.
4. Note your **complaint number** and track it online.
5. For urgent issues (life in danger), also call **112** and approach the High Court through a lawyer or legal aid (**15100**).

steps.title: Other bodies that protect rights in India
steps.body:
- **National Commission for Women**, **National Commission for Scheduled Castes**, **National Commission for Scheduled Tribes**, **National Commission for Minorities**, **National Commission for Protection of Child Rights**, and state equivalents.
- **Courts**, especially through writs and PIL (Articles 32 and 226).
- **Legal Services Authorities** for free legal aid.
- **Civil society**: NGOs, journalists, lawyers and human-rights defenders. The UN Declaration on Human Rights Defenders (1998) recognises everyone's right to promote and protect human rights.

courses.title: How legal systems differ: common law, civil law, religious and customary law
courses.summary: Why a trial in London looks different from one in Paris, Riyadh or a village court in South Africa. The main legal families of the world (common law, civil law, religious law, customary law and mixed systems), how judges, lawyers, codes and precedents work in each, and where India fits.
outcomes: Learners can describe the main features and origins of common-law and civil-law systems
Learners can explain precedent (stare decisis), ratio decidendi and obiter dicta
Learners can compare adversarial and inquisitorial trials, and juries with professional or lay judges
Learners can explain how religious and customary law operate in different countries
Learners can explain why India is a mixed system

lessons.title: Common law: judges, precedent and the adversarial trial

scenes.text: Emily, an exchange student from Manchester, joins a moot court competition in Mumbai with her Indian teammate Aditya.
Aditya cites a 1932 British case about a snail in a ginger-beer bottle. Emily is amazed: 'You still use Donoghue v Stevenson here?'
'It's persuasive, not binding,' Aditya explains, 'but our Supreme Court has built the law of negligence partly on it. Precedent travels across the common-law world.'
The judges, impressed by how they combine Indian and English precedents, award them best memorial.

steps.title: Origins and spread
steps.body:
**Common law** developed in **England** after 1066, as the king's judges travelling the country created rules 'common' to the whole kingdom by deciding cases. Alongside it, the **Court of Chancery** developed **equity** (fairness-based remedies like injunctions and trusts).

Through the British Empire it spread to the **USA** (except Louisiana's private law), **Canada** (except Quebec's private law), **Australia**, **New Zealand**, **India**, **Pakistan**, **Bangladesh**, **Singapore**, **Malaysia**, **Nigeria**, **Kenya** and many others. Today, common-law countries also have huge amounts of **statute law** made by legislatures; the 'common law' part is the body of judge-made principles that fills gaps and interprets statutes.

steps.title: Precedent (stare decisis)
steps.body:
**Stare decisis** ('stand by things decided'): courts follow earlier decisions on similar facts.

- **Binding precedent**: a decision of a higher court binds lower courts in the same hierarchy (in India, Article 141 makes Supreme Court law binding on all courts).
- **Persuasive precedent**: decisions of foreign courts, lower courts, or other benches may be followed if convincing.
- **Ratio decidendi**: the legal reason necessary for the decision; this part binds.
- **Obiter dicta**: remarks 'by the way'; persuasive only.
- Courts can **distinguish** a precedent (show the facts are materially different), and higher courts can **overrule** earlier decisions.

This gives **predictability** while allowing the law to grow.

steps.title: The adversarial trial
steps.body:
In the **adversarial** model, the two sides (prosecution and defence, or plaintiff and defendant) **present their cases**; the judge is a **neutral umpire** who ensures fair procedure and decides (or, with a jury, decides the law while the jury decides facts).

- Heavy use of **oral evidence** and **cross-examination**.
- Strict rules of evidence (what can and cannot be shown to the court).
- **Juries** of ordinary citizens are used in serious criminal trials in England and Wales and in the USA (where the Constitution guarantees jury trial in many cases). India once used juries in some courts, but they faded out in the 1960s; the famous Nanavati case (1959–61) is often linked to this.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Common law means no written law': common-law countries have constitutions, codes and many statutes. India has the BNS, BNSS, Contract Act and more.
- 'Precedent can never change': higher courts can overrule; legislatures can change the law by statute.
- 'Common law = law common to all countries': it means law common to the whole realm of England, as opposed to local customs.

lessons.title: Civil law: codes, scholars and the inquisitorial judge

scenes.text: Lucas, a French-Indian engineer, is a witness in a fraud case in Lyon. He expects a TV-style courtroom battle.
Instead, a judge reads a thick written file (dossier) prepared during the investigation, and asks him most of the questions herself.
Lawyers speak, but less dramatically. Lucas's cousin Ananya, a lawyer in Delhi, explains on the phone: 'France is a civil-law system. The code is the star, and the judge leads the inquiry.'
Lucas laughs: 'So India's courts are like London's, and France's are like a very organised investigation.'

steps.title: Origins: Roman law and the great codes
steps.body:
The **civil-law** tradition (also called **Romano-Germanic**) grew from **Roman law**, especially the **Corpus Juris Civilis** compiled under Emperor **Justinian** (529–534 CE), rediscovered and taught in medieval European universities.

Modern civil law is built on **comprehensive codes**:

- **French Civil Code (Code Napoléon), 1804**, which spread across Europe, Latin America, parts of Africa and the Middle East.
- **German Civil Code (BGB), in force 1900**, influential in Japan, South Korea, Greece and others.
- Others: the Swiss Civil Code (1907), and more recent codes (e.g., China's Civil Code, 2021).

Civil law is the **most widespread** legal family in the world: most of continental Europe, Latin America, much of Africa and Asia (Japan, China, South Korea, Indonesia), and Louisiana's and Quebec's private law.

steps.title: Key features
steps.body:
- **Codes** are the primary source; judges apply and interpret them, starting from general principles.
- **Precedent** is not formally binding in the same way, but a consistent line of decisions (*jurisprudence constante*) is highly persuasive, and top courts' rulings are followed in practice.
- **Legal scholars** (the 'doctrine') have great influence; commentaries on codes guide courts.
- **Judges** are often **career professionals** who join the judiciary after special training, rather than senior lawyers appointed later in life.
- **Separate court systems** are common: for example, **administrative courts** for disputes with the government (France's Conseil d'État) and **constitutional courts** (Germany's Federal Constitutional Court).

steps.title: The inquisitorial process
steps.body:
In the **inquisitorial** model, the court (or a judicial officer) **actively investigates** to find the truth:

- A written **case file** (dossier) is assembled during investigation.
- The **judge questions** witnesses and the accused; lawyers play a more limited role.
- Fewer technical rules excluding evidence; the judge weighs everything.
- Many systems use **mixed panels** of professional and **lay judges** (e.g., Germany's *Schöffen*; Japan's *saiban-in* system since 2009) instead of juries.

No system is purely one or the other today: many civil-law countries have added adversarial elements, and common-law systems use case management and written submissions.

steps.title: Side by side
steps.body:
- **Main source**: common law: statutes + judge-made precedent | civil law: codes and statutes.
- **Judges**: common law: often appointed from senior lawyers | civil law: career judiciary.
- **Trial style**: adversarial | inquisitorial.
- **Role of precedent**: binding | persuasive (in theory).
- **Who decides facts in serious criminal trials**: jury (in some countries) or judge | professional judges, sometimes with lay judges.
- **Influential writing**: judgments | academic commentaries.

lessons.title: Religious law, customary law and mixed systems (and India's place)

scenes.text: Global friends compare notes on a video call: Aisha in Kuala Lumpur, Noa in Tel Aviv, Thabo in Johannesburg, and Kabir in Pune.
Aisha says Muslim family matters in Malaysia go to Syariah courts. Noa says marriage in Israel is handled through religious authorities of each community.
Thabo explains that South Africa recognises customary marriages under its Constitution and a specific law, alongside civil marriage.
Kabir laughs: 'In India, it depends on your religion, unless you choose the Special Marriage Act. We're a mix of everything!'

steps.title: Religious law
steps.body:
Some systems draw law from **religious sources**:

- **Islamic law (Sharia)**: derived by scholars (**fiqh**) from the **Qur'an** and **Sunnah** (the Prophet's practice), with tools like **ijma** (consensus) and **qiyas** (analogy). Major schools include **Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali** (Sunni) and **Ja'fari** (Shia). Countries apply it very differently: as a main source of law in some (e.g., Saudi Arabia, Iran), only for **family and personal matters** for Muslims in many others (e.g., Malaysia, India), and not at all in others.
- **Jewish law (Halakha)**: in Israel, marriage and divorce are handled by the religious courts of each recognised community.
- **Canon law**: the internal law of the Catholic Church.
- **Hindu law**: historically drew on Dharmashastra texts, custom and commentaries; in India it was largely **codified by Parliament in the 1950s** (Hindu Marriage Act, Succession Act, etc.) and is applied by ordinary civil courts.

Religious law is often interpreted differently over time and place; generalisations should be careful.

steps.title: Customary law
steps.body:
**Customary law** consists of long-standing practices accepted as binding by a community, often unwritten and applied by elders or traditional authorities.

- Important in many **African** countries, the **Pacific** islands and indigenous communities worldwide, especially for **land, family and local disputes**.
- **South Africa's Constitution** recognises customary law, subject to the Bill of Rights.
- In **India**, many tribal communities in the North-East have constitutional protection for their **customary law and practices** (for example, Article 371A for Nagaland and Article 371G for Mizoram), and custom can override general rules in some areas (the Hindu Marriage Act recognises customs allowing certain marriages).

A recurring challenge: aligning custom with **equality**, especially for women's land and inheritance rights.

steps.title: Mixed systems, and India
steps.body:
**Mixed systems** combine traditions: **Scotland** (civil and common law), **South Africa** (Roman-Dutch, English and customary law), **Louisiana**, **Quebec**, **Sri Lanka**, the **Philippines**, **Israel**.

**India** is often described as a **common-law system with mixed features**:

- **Common-law** base: English-style courts, precedent (Article 141), adversarial trials, and laws first codified in the colonial era (now replaced in criminal law by the BNS, BNSS, BSA).
- **Strong written Constitution** with judicial review and the basic structure doctrine.
- **Codified statutes** for most areas, like a civil-law country.
- **Personal laws** by religion for family matters, plus the secular Special Marriage Act; **Goa** has its own civil code of Portuguese origin, and Uttarakhand enacted a Uniform Civil Code in 2024.
- **Customary laws** protected in some tribal areas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Countries with Muslim majorities all apply Sharia the same way': practice varies enormously.
- 'Customary law is primitive': it can be sophisticated and community-centred, though it must respect human rights.
- 'India is purely common law': it is a common-law system with codes, personal laws and a powerful constitution.

courses.title: International law and the United Nations
courses.summary: How law works between nations without a world government: the sources of international law, treaties and custom, the UN Charter and its organs (General Assembly, Security Council and veto), the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court, the laws of war, refugees and the sea, and how India brings international law home. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can list the sources of international law in Article 38 of the ICJ Statute
Learners can explain how a treaty is made and the principle pacta sunt servanda

lessons.title: What is international law, and where does it come from?

scenes.text: Two neighbouring countries share a great river. In a dry year, farmers downstream accuse the upstream country of taking too much water.
Diplomat Farida from the downstream country opens a decades-old water treaty: it fixes shares and creates a joint commission.
The joint commission meets. Both sides argue about what the treaty means; neither can simply ignore it, because breaking a treaty damages trust and invites consequences.
They agree on a temporary arrangement and refer a technical question to a neutral expert, as the treaty allows. The rivers keep flowing; so does diplomacy.

steps.title: Law without a world government
steps.body:
**Public international law** governs relations between **states** and **international organisations**, and increasingly protects **individuals** (human rights, international criminal law).

There is **no world parliament, no world police and no compulsory world court**. So why do states follow it? Because of **reciprocity** (I respect your diplomats, you respect mine), **reputation**, **trade and cooperation**, domestic courts and pressure, and sometimes **sanctions** or force authorised by the UN Security Council. Most international law (posts, aviation, trade, telecommunications, maritime traffic) is followed every day without anyone noticing.

(**Private international law** is different: it decides which country's law and courts apply to cross-border private disputes, like an international marriage or contract.)

steps.title: Sources: Article 38(1) of the ICJ Statute
steps.body:
The International Court of Justice applies:

- **(a) International conventions (treaties)** recognised by the states in dispute.
- **(b) International custom**, as evidence of a general practice accepted as law. Custom needs two elements: **state practice** (what states actually do, widely and consistently) and **opinio juris** (the belief that they do it because it is legally required).
- **(c) General principles of law** recognised by nations (such as good faith, and that no one may be a judge in their own cause).
- **(d) Judicial decisions and the teachings of the most highly qualified publicists**, as **subsidiary** means of determining the law.

Some norms are **jus cogens** (peremptory): no treaty may violate them, such as the prohibitions of **genocide, slavery, torture** and **aggression**.

steps.title: How treaties work
steps.body:
Treaties are governed by the **Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969)**.

1. **Negotiation** and **adoption** of the text.
2. **Signature**: shows intent; a signatory must not defeat the treaty's object and purpose.
3. **Ratification** (or accession for states joining later): the state's formal consent to be bound, after its internal procedures.
4. **Entry into force**: often after a set number of ratifications.
5. **Reservations**: a state may exclude or modify certain provisions, unless prohibited or incompatible with the treaty's object.

**Pacta sunt servanda**: every treaty in force is binding and must be performed **in good faith**. A state cannot use its own internal law as an excuse for not performing a treaty.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Signing a treaty makes it binding': usually **ratification** is needed.
- 'International law is not real law because there's no police': it has different enforcement mechanisms, and most of it is complied with.
- 'UN General Assembly resolutions are binding laws': they are generally **recommendations**, though they can reflect or help form custom.

lessons.title: The United Nations: Charter, organs and the veto

scenes.text: At a Model UN conference, Bhaskar represents a small island state in the Security Council simulation on a humanitarian crisis.
His draft resolution gets 13 votes in favour. One permanent member votes against.
The chair announces: 'The resolution is not adopted.' Bhaskar is stunned: 13 out of 15 wasn't enough?
His teacher explains the veto. Next day, he takes the issue to the General Assembly simulation, where every country has one equal vote, though its resolution is a recommendation.

steps.title: The UN Charter
steps.body:
The **UN Charter** was signed in **San Francisco on 26 June 1945** and came into force on **24 October 1945** (now **UN Day**). There were **51 original members, including India** (then still under British rule). Today there are **193** member states.

**Purposes** (Article 1): maintain international **peace and security**, develop friendly relations based on **equal rights and self-determination**, achieve **international cooperation** (including on human rights), and be a centre for harmonising actions of nations.

**Key principles** (Article 2): **sovereign equality**; settle disputes **peacefully**; **refrain from the threat or use of force** against any state's territorial integrity or political independence (Article 2(4)); no intervention in matters essentially within domestic jurisdiction (except enforcement under Chapter VII).

**Exceptions to the ban on force**: **self-defence** against an armed attack (Article 51), and action **authorised by the Security Council** under Chapter VII.

steps.title: Six principal organs
steps.body:
- **General Assembly (GA)**: all 193 members, **one vote each**. Discusses any matter, approves the budget, elects non-permanent Security Council members, and (with the Council) the Secretary-General and ICJ judges. Its resolutions are generally **recommendations**.
- **Security Council (SC)**: **15 members**: **5 permanent** (**China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States**) and **10 elected** for **two-year** terms. Primary responsibility for peace and security; its decisions under **Chapter VII** are **binding** (sanctions, peacekeeping mandates, authorising force). Substantive decisions need **nine votes** and **no veto** by a permanent member. India has served as an elected member several times, most recently in **2021–22**, and seeks a permanent seat.
- **Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC)**: coordinates economic, social and environmental work.
- **Trusteeship Council**: supervised trust territories; **suspended operations in 1994** after the last one (Palau) became independent.
- **International Court of Justice (ICJ)**: the principal judicial organ, at The Hague.
- **Secretariat**: headed by the **Secretary-General**, appointed by the GA on the SC's recommendation.

The UN **system** also includes specialised agencies like **WHO, UNESCO, ILO, FAO, UNICEF** (a fund/programme), and the **World Bank** and **IMF**.

steps.title: Worked example: does a Security Council resolution pass?
steps.body:
A substantive draft needs **at least 9 'yes' votes** out of 15 **and** **no permanent member voting 'no'**.

- 13 yes, 1 no (by a permanent member), 1 abstain → **fails** (veto).
- 9 yes, 0 no, 6 abstain (including two permanent members) → **passes**; an **abstention** by a permanent member is **not** a veto (by long practice).
- 8 yes, 0 no, 7 abstain → **fails** (fewer than 9 votes).
- 11 yes, 4 no (all elected members) → **passes**.

Procedural matters (like adopting the agenda) need 9 votes and are **not** subject to veto.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'The UN is a world government': it has **no power to tax** people or make laws for them directly; it works through states.
- 'An abstention by a permanent member is a veto': **no**.
- 'GA resolutions are binding law': generally **no** (except internal matters like the budget).

choices.feedback: Correct. An abstention is not a veto.

choices.feedback: No. By long practice, abstention does not block adoption.

choices.feedback: Good recovery.

d.text: After the veto, members take the issue to the General Assembly, which can debate and recommend measures. Since 2022, when a veto is cast the GA meets to discuss it. You managed the session correctly.

lessons.title: World courts: the ICJ and the ICC

scenes.text: On a study trip to The Hague, students Rohan and Hiba visit the Peace Palace, home of the International Court of Justice.
Their guide mentions the Jadhav case (India v Pakistan), where the ICJ held in 2019 that Pakistan had breached the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations by denying India consular access.
Later they visit the International Criminal Court on the city's edge. 'This one tries individuals for genocide and war crimes,' the guide says.
Hiba writes: 'ICJ = states vs states. ICC = individuals for the worst crimes.' Rohan adds: 'And India is a party to one, not the other.'

steps.title: International Court of Justice (ICJ)
steps.body:
- The **principal judicial organ** of the UN, at the **Peace Palace, The Hague**, established in **1945** (succeeding the Permanent Court of International Justice).
- **15 judges**, elected for **nine-year** terms by the General Assembly and Security Council; no two from the same country.
- **Contentious cases**: only between **states**, and only if they have **consented** to the Court's jurisdiction (by special agreement, a treaty clause, or a declaration accepting compulsory jurisdiction).
- **Advisory opinions**: on legal questions referred by UN organs and agencies (e.g., on the legality of the threat or use of nuclear weapons, 1996).
- Judgments are **binding** on the parties; non-compliance can be taken to the Security Council (Article 94 of the Charter).

**Kulbhushan Jadhav (India v Pakistan), 2019**: the Court found Pakistan breached Article 36 of the **Vienna Convention on Consular Relations (1963)** and directed an effective review and reconsideration of his conviction and sentence.

steps.title: International Criminal Court (ICC)
steps.body:
- Created by the **Rome Statute (adopted 1998, in force 2002)**; located in The Hague; **not a UN organ**, though it cooperates with the UN.
- Tries **individuals** (including heads of state) for four core crimes: **genocide**, **crimes against humanity**, **war crimes** and the **crime of aggression**.
- **Complementarity**: it acts only when national courts are **unwilling or unable** genuinely to prosecute.
- Jurisdiction over crimes on the territory of, or by nationals of, **states parties**, or situations **referred by the Security Council**, or states accepting jurisdiction.
- More than 120 states are parties; **India, China and the United States are not**.

Other tribunals: the ad hoc tribunals for the former Yugoslavia (1993) and Rwanda (1994), and the **Nuremberg** and **Tokyo** tribunals after the Second World War, which established that individuals, not just states, can be criminally responsible under international law.

steps.title: ICJ vs ICC side by side
steps.body:
- **Who is before it?** ICJ: **states**. ICC: **individuals**.
- **Founded by**: ICJ: UN Charter (1945). ICC: Rome Statute (1998/2002).
- **Part of the UN?** ICJ: yes. ICC: no (independent treaty body).
- **Typical cases**: ICJ: borders, treaties, diplomatic and consular rights, maritime boundaries. ICC: genocide, war crimes.
- **India**: party to the UN Charter and so to the ICJ Statute; **not** a party to the Rome Statute.
- **Other dispute bodies**: the **Permanent Court of Arbitration** (The Hague), the **International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea** (Hamburg), and the **WTO** dispute settlement system.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing the ICJ and ICC: both are in The Hague, but they are very different courts.
- 'The ICJ can hear any case against any country': it needs the states' **consent**.
- 'The ICC replaces national courts': it is a **court of last resort**.

lessons.title: Laws of war, refugees, the sea, and India's approach

scenes.text: Fisherman Selvam from Rameswaram strays across the maritime boundary into a neighbouring country's waters and is detained with his boat.
His daughter Kavitha calls the district fisheries office. The Ministry of External Affairs seeks consular access through the Indian mission.
She learns about territorial seas, exclusive economic zones and why boundaries at sea matter as much as on land.
After diplomatic talks, Selvam is released and returns home. Kavitha starts a WhatsApp group sharing GPS boundary alerts with fishermen.

steps.title: International humanitarian law (laws of war)
steps.body:
**International humanitarian law (IHL)** limits the effects of armed conflict. Its core is the **four Geneva Conventions of 1949** (ratified by every state) and their **Additional Protocols (1977)**, plus the Hague rules on means and methods of war.

Key principles:

- **Distinction**: attacks only on military objectives, never on civilians or civilian objects.
- **Proportionality**: no attack where expected civilian harm would be excessive compared to the concrete military advantage.
- **Precaution**: take feasible steps to avoid or minimise civilian harm.
- **Humane treatment** of the wounded, sick, prisoners of war and detainees; **no torture**.
- Protection of **medical personnel** and the Red Cross / Red Crescent emblems.
- Bans on certain weapons (e.g., chemical and biological weapons).

Serious violations are **war crimes**. India is a party to the four Geneva Conventions and has implementing legislation (the Geneva Conventions Act 1960).

steps.title: Refugee law
steps.body:
- The **1951 Refugee Convention** and its **1967 Protocol** define a **refugee** as a person outside their country with a **well-founded fear of persecution** for reasons of **race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion**, unable or unwilling to return.
- **Non-refoulement**: refugees must not be sent back to a place where they face serious threats to life or freedom; widely regarded as customary law.
- The **UNHCR** supports refugees worldwide.
- **India is not a party** to the 1951 Convention or the 1967 Protocol. It has hosted many refugee groups (for example from Tibet and Sri Lanka) under its own policies and laws, and Indian courts have sometimes protected refugees under **Article 21** (the right to life applies to all persons).

steps.title: The law of the sea (UNCLOS 1982)
steps.body:
The **UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)** is sometimes called the 'constitution of the oceans'. India ratified it in 1995. Zones measured from the **baseline** (usually the low-water line along the coast):

- **Territorial sea**: up to **12 nautical miles**; full sovereignty, but foreign ships have a right of **innocent passage**.
- **Contiguous zone**: up to **24 nm**; control for customs, immigration, sanitation and fiscal laws.
- **Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ)**: up to **200 nm**; sovereign rights over **fish, oil, gas** and other resources; other states keep freedoms of navigation and overflight.
- **Continental shelf**: seabed resources, which can extend further in some cases.
- **High seas**: beyond national jurisdiction; free for all; the deep seabed is the 'common heritage of mankind'.

Disputes can go to the **International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS)** in Hamburg, the ICJ or arbitration. In **2014**, an arbitral tribunal under UNCLOS delimited the **Bay of Bengal** maritime boundary between **Bangladesh and India**, and India accepted the award.

steps.title: How India brings international law home
steps.body:
- **Article 51** (Directive Principle): the State shall endeavour to promote international peace and security and foster respect for **international law and treaty obligations**.
- **Article 253**: Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of India to **implement treaties**, even on State List subjects.
- India generally follows a **dualist** approach: a treaty does not automatically become domestic law; Parliament implements it. But courts **read domestic law consistently** with treaty obligations where there is no conflict, and have used treaties to fill gaps (e.g., **Vishaka (1997)** using CEDAW; environmental principles like 'polluter pays').
- **Customary international law**, where not contrary to Indian law, is treated as part of the law of the land by Indian courts.

courses.title: Data privacy laws (GDPR, DPDP) and how laws differ across countries
courses.summary: The world's most influential privacy law, the EU's GDPR, explained principle by principle, compared with India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and other laws; then a careful tour of how countries differ on age of majority, voting age, compulsory voting, alcohol and drug laws, and why such differences exist. lessons.title: GDPR: principles and lawful bases

scenes.text: Priya runs a small fitness-app startup in Bengaluru. A gym chain in Berlin wants to offer her app to its members.
The gym's lawyer asks: 'Are you GDPR compliant? What is your lawful basis? Where is your data stored? Who is your processor?'
Priya learns the GDPR applies to her even though her company is in India, because she will offer services to people in the EU.
She maps her data, cuts out data she doesn't need, writes a clear privacy notice and signs a data processing agreement. The deal goes through.

steps.title: What the GDPR is and whom it covers
steps.body:
The **General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)** is an EU regulation adopted in **2016** and applicable from **25 May 2018**. It protects **personal data**: any information relating to an identified or identifiable living person (name, ID number, location data, online identifiers like IP addresses and cookies, and factors specific to their identity).

**Territorial scope** (Article 3):

- organisations **established in the EU**, wherever the processing happens; and
- organisations **outside the EU** that **offer goods or services** to people in the EU, or **monitor their behaviour** there.

Key roles: the **data subject** (the person), the **controller** (decides why and how data is processed), and the **processor** (processes on the controller's behalf, like a cloud provider).

steps.title: The seven principles (Article 5)
steps.body:
1. **Lawfulness, fairness and transparency**: have a legal basis; don't deceive; tell people clearly.
2. **Purpose limitation**: collect for specified, explicit, legitimate purposes; don't reuse for unrelated purposes.
3. **Data minimisation**: only what is adequate, relevant and necessary.
4. **Accuracy**: keep data correct and up to date.
5. **Storage limitation**: keep it no longer than necessary.
6. **Integrity and confidentiality**: appropriate security.
7. **Accountability**: the controller must be able to **demonstrate** compliance (records, policies, assessments).

steps.title: Six lawful bases (Article 6)
steps.body:
Processing is lawful only if at least one applies:

- **Consent**: freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; as easy to withdraw as to give; no pre-ticked boxes.
- **Contract**: necessary to perform a contract with the person (e.g., the delivery address for an order).
- **Legal obligation**: e.g., keeping tax records.
- **Vital interests**: to protect someone's life.
- **Public task**: official functions in the public interest.
- **Legitimate interests**: the organisation's interests, if not overridden by the person's rights (requires a balancing test).

**Special categories** (health, genetic and biometric data, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, trade-union membership, sex life or sexual orientation) need an **additional condition**, such as explicit consent.

**Children**: for online services offered directly to children, consent must come from a parent below age **16**, though EU countries may set it between **13 and 16**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'We need consent for everything': often another basis (contract, legal obligation) is more appropriate; consent is only valid if truly free.
- 'We're outside the EU, so GDPR doesn't apply': it can, if you target or monitor people in the EU.
- 'Collect everything, it might be useful later': violates **minimisation** and **purpose limitation**.
- 'Privacy policy = compliance': you also need security, records, contracts with processors, and a way to handle requests.

lessons.title: Rights, breaches, fines, and India's DPDP Act compared

story.title: Arjun asks, 'What do you know about me?'

scenes.text: Arjun, an Indian student in Dublin, keeps seeing ads about a health condition he once searched for. He feels watched.
He emails the shopping site's data protection officer: 'Under Article 15 GDPR, please send all personal data you hold about me.'
Within a month he receives a file with his purchase history, inferred interests and ad partners. He objects to profiling and asks for erasure of the health inferences.
The company complies. Back in Pune for holidays, he reads that India's DPDP Act also gives rights of access and erasure. 'Same idea, different details,' he notes.

steps.title: Data subject rights under the GDPR
steps.body:
- **Information** (Articles 13–14): clear notice of who, why, how long, rights.
- **Access** (Article 15): a copy of your data and details of processing, generally free, within **one month** (extendable in complex cases).
- **Rectification** (Article 16): correct inaccurate data.
- **Erasure ('right to be forgotten')** (Article 17): in specified cases, e.g., data no longer needed, or consent withdrawn. The idea gained fame in the **Google Spain** judgment of the EU Court of Justice (**2014**).
- **Restriction** of processing (Article 18).
- **Data portability** (Article 20): get your data in a machine-readable format and move it.
- **Object** (Article 21): including an **absolute right to object to direct marketing**.
- Rights related to **automated decision-making and profiling** (Article 22): not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, with exceptions and safeguards.

steps.title: Breaches, transfers and fines
steps.body:
- **Breach notification**: notify the supervisory authority **within 72 hours** of becoming aware of a personal-data breach (unless unlikely to result in risk), and tell affected people without undue delay if the risk is high.
- **Data Protection Officer (DPO)** required for public bodies and organisations doing large-scale monitoring or special-category processing.
- **Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)** for high-risk processing.
- **International transfers** outside the EU need safeguards (adequacy decisions, standard contractual clauses). In **Schrems II (2020)** the EU Court of Justice invalidated the EU–US Privacy Shield.
- **Fines**: up to **€20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover**, whichever is higher, for the most serious violations. In 2023 the Irish regulator fined Meta **€1.2 billion** over data transfers to the US, the largest GDPR fine so far at that time.

steps.title: India's DPDP Act 2023 compared
steps.body:
- **Scope**: **digital** personal data (and non-digital data later digitised); applies outside India if offering goods/services to people in India. Excludes personal data a person has made **publicly available** themselves.
- **Terms**: **Data Principal** (person), **Data Fiduciary** (controller), **Data Processor**; **Significant Data Fiduciaries** have extra duties (DPO in India, independent audits, impact assessments).
- **Grounds**: **consent** (with a clear notice; withdrawal as easy as giving) or certain **'legitimate uses'** (like data voluntarily provided for a specified purpose, State functions, legal obligations, medical emergencies, employment). There are **no six bases** like GDPR, and **no separate 'special category'** of sensitive data.
- **Children**: anyone under **18**; **verifiable parental consent**, and no tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising directed at children (with possible exemptions).
- **Rights**: information about processing, **correction and erasure**, **grievance redressal**, and **nomination** (someone to exercise rights after death or incapacity). There is no general right to data portability.
- **Duties of Data Principals** too (e.g., not to file false complaints).
- **Enforcement**: **Data Protection Board of India**; penalties up to **₹250 crore** per instance for serious failures like inadequate security safeguards.
- **Cross-border**: allowed except to countries the government restricts.
- Its **rules are being phased in**; check what is currently in force.

steps.title: Other privacy laws worldwide
steps.body:
- **USA**: no single federal privacy law; sector laws (health, children's online privacy) and state laws like the **California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)**, as amended.
- **Brazil**: **LGPD**, closely modelled on GDPR.
- **China**: **Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL), 2021**.
- **UK**: the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 after Brexit.

Privacy as a **fundamental right**: in India, *Puttaswamy (2017)*; in the EU, the Charter of Fundamental Rights (Articles 7 and 8).

lessons.title: Snapshots: age of majority, voting and civic duties around the world

scenes.text: On a video call, four cousins compare: Lena in Vienna voted at 16. Gabriel in São Paulo voted at 16 too, by choice.
Jack in Sydney says voting is compulsory in Australia and he'd be fined if he skipped without a valid reason.
Meera in Bhopal had to wait until 18, and nobody fines you for not voting in India.
'Same democracy idea, different rules,' Meera says. 'Each country decides based on its own history and debates.'

steps.title: Age of majority
steps.body:
The **age of majority** is when a person becomes a legal adult for most purposes (making contracts, suing in their own name).

- **18** in most countries, including **India** (Indian Majority Act 1875).
- **Japan** lowered it from 20 to **18** in **April 2022**.
- **South Korea**: **19**.
- In the **USA**, it is set by states: **18** in most; **19** in Alabama and Nebraska; **21** in Mississippi.
- **Scotland** gives legal capacity for many transactions from **16**.

Other ages can differ from majority: in India, marriage is 21/18, driving 18 (16 for small gearless two-wheelers), and some state laws set drinking ages above 18.

steps.title: Voting age
steps.body:
- **18** is the most common voting age (India since 1989; the USA since 1971 by the 26th Amendment; the UK since 1969).
- **16**: **Austria** (national elections, since 2007); **Brazil**, **Argentina** and **Ecuador** allow optional voting from 16; **Malta** (2018); **Scotland and Wales** for their own parliaments and local elections.
- **17**: e.g., **Greece**.
- **20**: e.g., **Taiwan** for most elections.

Arguments for lowering: young people are affected by long-term decisions; early voting builds habits. Arguments against: maturity concerns; consistency with other age limits. Debates continue in many countries.

steps.title: Compulsory voting
steps.body:
Some countries make voting a **legal duty**:

- **Australia**: compulsory enrolment and voting for federal elections since the 1920s; a small fine if you don't vote without a valid reason.
- **Belgium** (one of the oldest, since 1893), **Brazil** (compulsory from 18 to 70), **Argentina**, **Peru**, **Singapore** (non-voters are removed from the register until they apply to be restored), and others.

**India**: voting is a **right**, not a legal duty, at national level. (Gujarat passed a law in 2009 to make voting compulsory in local-body elections, but its implementation was stayed by the High Court.)

steps.title: How to read comparisons
steps.body:
- Ages and rules **change**; always check official, current sources before relying on them.
- A country may have **different ages for different things** and **different rules in different regions** (states, provinces).
- 'Different' does not mean 'better or worse': each rule reflects that society's history, values and debates.

bands.text: Under 16: a child under POCSO, the JJ Act and child-labour law (no work in any occupation below 14, except narrow exceptions). Cannot drive any motor vehicle.

16–17: still a child under the law (under 18). May get a licence for a gearless two-wheeler up to 50cc with guardian consent. Can apply in advance to be added to the voter list from 17. No hazardous work.
18–20: a legal adult (majority). Can vote, sign contracts, get a car licence, and a woman can legally marry (men from 21). Drinking age depends on the state; some states prohibit alcohol entirely.

lessons.title: Snapshots: alcohol, drugs and travelling under other countries' laws

scenes.text: Vikram, 24, from Delhi, travels to Amsterdam and then on to Singapore with friends. In Amsterdam he sees cannabis 'coffee shops'.
A friend suggests carrying 'a little' to Singapore. Their travel buddy Mei Ling, from Singapore, is horrified.
She explains that Singapore has some of the world's strictest drug laws, with heavy penalties including death for trafficking above set amounts, and that even transit can be risky.
They carry nothing. Vikram later reads that even in the Netherlands, cannabis is technically illegal but tolerated in a regulated way. 'Every border is a different rulebook,' he says.

steps.title: Alcohol laws differ widely
steps.body:
- **USA**: the minimum legal drinking age is effectively **21** nationwide (since the National Minimum Drinking Age Act 1984 linked highway funds to it).
- Most of **Europe**: generally **18** (some allow beer and wine from 16).
- **India**: alcohol is a **State subject**, so rules differ by state. Minimum drinking ages range from **18 to 25** depending on the state, and some states, such as **Gujarat, Bihar and Nagaland**, **prohibit** alcohol sales.
- Some countries **ban** alcohol entirely or for their citizens.

Everywhere, **drunk driving** is an offence; in India the limit is **30 mg per 100 ml of blood**, and many countries have similar or stricter limits.

steps.title: Drug laws: a spectrum
steps.body:
Countries take very different approaches:

- **Strict prohibition with severe penalties**: e.g., **Singapore** and several other countries impose very heavy penalties, including the **death penalty**, for trafficking above specified quantities.
- **India**: the **Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act 1985** prohibits production, possession, sale and use of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances except for medical or scientific purposes. Penalties depend on whether the quantity is 'small', 'intermediate' or 'commercial'. **Ganja** (cannabis flowering/fruiting tops) and **charas** (resin) are prohibited, while **bhang** (made from leaves) is not covered by the NDPS definition of ganja and is regulated by state excise laws. A person with a small quantity who **volunteers for de-addiction treatment** can get immunity from prosecution under certain conditions (Section 64A).
- **Decriminalisation**: **Portugal (2001)** made personal possession of all drugs an administrative offence (not a crime), referring people to 'dissuasion commissions' and treatment, while trafficking remains a crime.
- **Toleration**: the **Netherlands** tolerates regulated sale of small amounts of cannabis in licensed coffee shops, though it is not fully legal.
- **Legal regulated markets for cannabis**: **Uruguay (2013)** was the first country; **Canada (2018)**; **Germany** partly legalised cannabis for adults in **2024**. In the **USA**, cannabis remains illegal under **federal** law, while many **states** have legalised it for adults.

**Health facts don't change at borders**: drugs and alcohol carry real risks of dependence and harm, especially for the developing brain.

steps.title: Travellers: local law applies
steps.body:
- **You are subject to the laws of the country you are in**, including airports and transit areas. 'It's legal back home' is no defence.
- Never carry packages for strangers. Check medicines: some prescription drugs legal in India are **controlled** abroad (and vice versa); carry prescriptions and check embassy guidance.
- If arrested abroad, ask for **consular access** to the Indian embassy (a right under the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations).
- Some countries impose penalties on their **citizens** for certain acts done **abroad**.

steps.title: Help in India
steps.body: If you or someone you know is struggling with alcohol or drugs, help is available without judgment: the national toll-free **drug de-addiction helpline 14446**, **Tele-MANAS 14416** for mental health, or a doctor. Seeking treatment is a sign of strength.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Before your next trip (even to another Indian state), look up **three local laws** that differ from home: alcohol, smoking in public places, and any rule on medicines or plastic bags.

In India, **free legal aid: NALSA helpline 15100** or your District Legal Services Authority. Emergencies in India: **112**.
